title: Patek Philippe Water Drop
description: The 'Holy Trinity' of watch brands: Audemars Piguet, Patek Philippe, and Vacheron Constantin. Perhaps the most celebrated of the three, Patek Philippe has an unrivaled reputation for crafting some of the most complicated — and some of the simplest, yet most beautiful — timekeepers the market has seen. Sports watches came later to Patek, as pressure from the new 'luxury sports watch' category introduced in the early 1970s forced the storied brand to evolve — but historically, classically-styled dress pieces is where the maison cut its teeth. This particular timepiece is a classic representation of the jewelry/ watch intersections of midcentury that helped build Patek's reputation. Measuring 16mm in yellow gold, it boasts a smooth bezel, with a brilliantly supple multi link waterdrop bracelet, an unsigned winding crown, and a petite black dial with diamond shaped gold indexes. Powered by a hand-wound movement, this watch is equal parts watchmaking and fine jewelry. Few brands produce watches of this kind in the modern market, and it is pieces like this one that are the types of watches that made Analog:Shift the place it is today. So much personality, packaged with the class of Patek Philippe!

title: Patek Philippe Chronograph
description: Patek Philippe has sat atop the horological mountain for going on two centuries, having earned near-universal acclaim for its proficiencies in designing, engineering, and manufacturing some of the most exquisite timepieces the world has ever seen. The celebrated maison has a tradition of creating watches that transcend generations. Leaning on the pillars of timeless design, refinement, and mechanical ingenuity, there’s arguably no other manufacture that does it better . Within Patek's collections, few complications are more attractive than the manually-wound chronograph. Complicated to get right, and beautiful both on the wrist and on the caseback, these pieces make a statement. This piece, a Reference 5170J-001, features a 39mm 18K yellow gold case with a polished bezel, signed crown, rectangular pushers, and a sapphire exhibition caseback framing the maison's Calibre 29-535 manual-winding movement. Its dial may be one of our favorite configurations for several reasons. Firstly, the applied 'Roman' gold indices paired with a matching, polished handset add a certain glint to a monochromatic dial. Furthermore, the 'Roman' layout in particular adds a traditional flair to a contemporary piece. Finally, the chemin de fer minute track and pulsations scale...well, those should speak for themselves. But in case they don't, we believe that a pulsations scale — which is used to take a patient's pulse — has a distinguishable aesthetic compared to a traditional tachymeter scale. And frankly, it adds a bit more fun and a breath of fresh air to a watch design. If you're on the hunt for a chronograph with classic looks, excellent build quality, and a tremendous pedigree, this Ref. 5170J will set you straight!

title: Cartier Tank Louis Cartier
description: There are certain designs that just resonate throughout the years and remain evergreen despite changing trends and tastes. The Cartier Tank, in all its one hundred-plus years of production, is one such design. Whether in gold (yellow, pink, or white), stainless steel, or vermeil; whether Française, Chinoise, Americaine, or Normale; the Tank by Cartier is one watch that truly deserves to be called ‘iconic.’ Cartier introduced the Tank in 1917, with a run of six pieces — given, or so the legend goes, to American General Joseph Pershing and his staff. The design of the Tank was supposedly inspired by the Renault FT-17 tanks Cartier glimpsed on the battlefield of the Great War. (Cartier took the look of the Renault tank's treads and applied it to the lugs, which were integrated via brancards into the case itself.) That first run of six pieces increased to 33 by 1920, and by the end of the 20th century, that number stood well in the thousands. In sheer volume alone, the Tank — in all its various models — is Cartier's largest line of watches. The Tank Louis was introduced in 1922, following close on the heels of the Asian-influenced Tank Chinoise. With the Tank Louis, Cartier went back to basics, with the classic lugs that resemble the treads that inspired them. Louis Cartier himself wore the watch that bore his name — and the association with him marks the Tank Louis as the quintessence of the Cartier Tanks. This particular Tank Louis features a 22mm x 29.5mm rose gold case with a sapphire crystal, a sapphire cabochon winding crown, a lovely satin silver dial with printed black 'Roman' indices, a guilloche center section, and a matching blued-steel 'sword' handset. Powered by a manual winding Cartier's movement, this piece comes fitted to a brown alligator strap with a signed rose gold 'Ardillon' pin buckle. What better way to break into the Cartier world than with this prototypical icon?

title: Cartier Roadster
description: Some watches arrive ahead of their time. Introduced at the dawn of the 21st century, the Cartier Roadster broke from the maison's traditional playbook, pairing Cartier's unmistakable elegance with the muscular stance of a modern sports watch. Inspired by the streamlined curves of 1950s European sports cars, its tonneau-shaped case, flowing bracelet, and distinctive magnified date window made it one of the brand's boldest contemporary designs. Long appreciated by collectors, the Roadster enjoyed a remarkable resurgence in 2026, when Cartier reintroduced the collection to widespread acclaim. The revival underscored what enthusiasts had known all along: the Roadster's sculptural design had aged exceptionally well, feeling every bit as fresh today as when it first debuted. This Ref. W62031Y4-2510 features the collection's versatile 38mm x 43mm two tone stainless steel and 18K gold case, topped by a scratch-resistant sapphire crystal with the Roadster's signature integrated Cyclops magnifier over the date display. The silver sunray dial showcases bold, radial black Roman numerals surrounding an inner railroad minute track, while luminescent sword-shaped hands provide excellent legibility in classic Cartier fashion. A reliable automatic winding movement ticks within to ensure everyday wearing convenience. Fitted to its two tone original stainless steel bracelet with double deployant clasp, the Roadster also incorporates Cartier's ingenious quick-change system, allowing the bracelet or strap to be swapped in seconds without tools—a feature that was years ahead of its time and remains one of the collection's defining innovations. The Roadster occupies a unique place within Cartier's storied catalog. Sportier than a Tank, more unconventional than a Santos, yet unmistakably Cartier in every detail, it represents one of the maison's most distinctive modern designs. With the renewed enthusiasm surrounding the collection, there has rarely been a better moment to rediscover one of Cartier's most charismatic creations.

title: Cartier Tank Americaine
description: Cartier is responsible for some of the most recognizable and successful wristwatches in the history of modern horology. The definitive expert on watch design, the French maison has always been a leader in challenging conventional approaches to watchmaking while pioneering new styling as a fixture in the broader fashion world. Few watches have played a larger role in solidifying this brand identity than the Tank. Undoubtedly the most iconic watch in Cartier’s history and conceived based on a simple idea, it’s evolved to take myriad forms over the years, with over a dozen sub-designs that each has its own identity and presence. After the release of the Tank, the watch space was changed forever. Introduced in 1917 based on the conception of Louis Cartier, the great grandson of Cartier’s founder, the Tank took inspiration from a French military tank from the First World War— the Renault FT-17. The look of the Tank was striking and revolutionary— rectangular and unconventional for the period, the Tank was also one of the earliest wrist watches to be popularly accepted by the broader fashion space. After 1917, Cartier saw a surge in interest in its unique watches, and more and more Cartier Tank models were born, building on the underlying design philosophy that made the Tank an initial success in the 1910s. The Tank Cintrée was introduced in 1921, the Louis and Chinoise in 1922, the Basculante in 1933, the Asymetrique in 1936, and so on. In 1989, Cartier released a particularly exciting reference, targeted at the American collector market. Cartier recognized that New York customers loved more fashion-forward designs like the Cintrée. Making a specialty design for these customers, Cartier released the Tank Americaine. Featuring many of the characteristics of the Cintrée, the Americaine had an elongated scalloped case, lightly curved caseback, and beautiful case layout. The Americaine had the classic Roman numeral dial with railroad minutes track, blued steel hands, and cream dial that made the Tank so iconic and recognizable. This particular Americaine Reference W2603256 , powered by an automatic movement, features a beautiful blue sword handset and octagonal 'cabochon' crown. Executed in 18K white gold, this watch is probably the most classic layout for an Americaine with a cream white guilloche dial and date window at 6 o'clock. The brancards of the 26mm X 45mm 18K white gold case are fully polished, while the center case bridges are brushed for some subtle, tasteful contrast. As effortlessly comfortable as it is elegant, this piece is appropriate for virtually any wrist. If you're Cartier-curious but the Tank Louis or the Santos don't speak to you, the Tank Americaine might just be the watch for you!

title: Patek Philippe Annual Calendar
description: Few complications have had as much influence on modern watchmaking as the Annual Calendar. Introduced by Patek Philippe in 1996, the complication bridged the gap between simple calendar watches and the lofty perpetual calendar, offering remarkable practicality while requiring adjustment just once per year, at the end of February. It was a genuine innovation—one so significant that Patek patented the mechanism and created an entirely new category of complication. The Ref. 5396 traces its lineage directly to that groundbreaking first-generation Ref. 5035, refining the concept into one of the most elegant and enduring Annual Calendars in the manufacture's catalog. Its balanced display, classical proportions, and exceptional legibility have made it a favorite among collectors who appreciate complications designed for everyday use. This Ref. 5396G-011 is housed in a beautifully proportioned 38.5mm white gold case featuring a sapphire crystal, signed crown, and polished bezel. The silver opaline dial is a study in understated sophistication, fitted with applied white gold hour markers, dauphine hands, twin apertures for the day and month, a pointer date display, moonphase indication, and a 24-hour display integrated within the subsidiary register at 6 o'clock. Despite the wealth of information presented, the dial remains remarkably clean and harmonious—a hallmark of Patek Philippe's finest calendar watches. Powering the watch is the automatic Caliber 324 S QA LU 24H, visible through the sapphire caseback and finished to the exacting standards that have defined the manufacture for generations. It is paired with a signed black alligator strap and a matching white gold deployant buckle. The beauty of the Annual Calendar lies in its balance. Complex enough to fascinate, practical enough to wear every day, and elegant enough to accompany any occasion, the Ref. 5396 represents Patek Philippe at its most thoughtful—transforming the passage of days, months, and lunar cycles into something both useful and beautiful. Some watches tell time. The best remind us how thoughtfully it passes.

title: Patek Philippe Annual Calendar Regulator
description: In 1991, the soon-to-be graduates at the Geneva School of Engineering were presented with their final project prior to receiving their diploma — simplify the perpetual calendar. Although the task was easier said than done, their work led to the inception of the annual calendar complication, patented by Patek Philippe in collaboration with the bright engineering minds at the GSE. Five years later, Patek debuted the Reference 5035 — the watch that marked the world’s first-ever annual calendar movement and finally bridged the gap between a triple-date function and the formidable quantième perpétuel . This example, a Reference 5235/50R-001, features a neat ‘regulator’ display for optimal legibility and is housed in a sleek, 40.5mm 18K rose gold case with a sapphire crystal, a signed crown, and a smooth, polished bezel. It features a vertically brushed, black/ gray satin-finished dial with a pair of recessed subsidiary registers indicating hour and minutes, as well as day and month apertures flanking the 12 o’clock marker and a central seconds hand. Powered by Patek Philippe's Calibre 31-260 self-winding micro-rotor movement, it comes fitted to its signed, black alligator leather strap with a signed, 18K rose gold pin buckle and includes all of its factory paperwork. There’s no doubt the Nautilus and Aquanaut have gotten their time in the sun, and even vintage Patek Philippe in general continues to demand the attention of any savvy collector. But why not zig when everyone else zags with this high-complication, heavy-hitter from one of the best watchmakers on the planet!

title: Omega Seamaster Aqua Terra Shades
description: The Omega Seamaster Aqua Terra has always occupied a particularly useful place in the watch world: sporty enough for every day, polished enough to dress up, and largely free of the visual baggage that comes with a traditional dive watch. The Aqua Terra Shades collection pushes that versatility a little further with an emphasis on color, and this 38mm stainless-steel example features the aptly named Atlantic Blue dial, a deep, shifting blue that can move from almost black to electric depending on the light. The proportions are especially good. At 38mm across, 12.26mm thick, and 44.92mm lug-to-lug, the case has plenty of presence without feeling oversized. A polished bezel frames the sun-brushed dial, with faceted applied indexes, luminous hands, and a neatly integrated date aperture at 6 o’clock. The watch is fitted to Omega’s beautifully finished stainless-steel bracelet, while a domed sapphire crystal with anti-reflective treatment on both sides keeps everything exceptionally clear. Despite the more refined appearance, this remains a Seamaster, with water resistance to 150 meters. Inside is Omega’s self-winding Calibre 8800, a Co-Axial Master Chronometer movement with a 55-hour power reserve and the serious technical credentials that have become a hallmark of modern Omega. This example comes as an especially complete and versatile package, including its inner and outer boxes, warranty cards, papers and pamphlets, plus an additional black alligator-leather strap with a steel pin buckle and a stainless-steel mesh bracelet. Bracelet, mesh, or alligator: three very different personalities for one exceptionally easy-to-wear Aqua Terra.

title: Omega Seamaster Planet Ocean 600M
description: There are Planet Oceans, and then there are Planet Oceans with a little personality. This Omega Seamaster Planet Ocean 600M Co-Axial Chronograph pairs serious dive-watch engineering with a fantastic shot of orange, a color that has been part of the Planet Ocean vocabulary since the collection debuted in 2005. Against the black dial, the orange aluminum bezel and matching accents give the watch a distinctly sporty, almost racing-inspired character. Even better is the size. At 37.5mm, this is a surprisingly compact Planet Ocean, particularly considering everything Omega packed inside. The stainless-steel case surrounds a black dial with luminous applied indexes, three chronograph registers, a date display, and the familiar broad-arrow hands. The orange dive bezel provides the visual punch, while a helium escape valve at 10 o’clock and an extraordinary 600 meters of water resistance remind you that beneath all the color is a very serious dive watch. This example is paired with a complementary orange leather strap. Power comes from Omega’s self-winding Calibre 3313, a Co-Axial column-wheel chronograph movement with a 52-hour power reserve. A domed sapphire crystal with anti-reflective treatment on both sides completes the package. Originally marketed as a ladies’ model, the 37.5mm case feels particularly relevant today, as collectors rediscover smaller sports watches regardless of the category printed in an old catalog. Add the original Omega warranty cards, and this is a compact, colorful, and slightly unexpected take on one of Omega’s modern dive-watch signatures.

title: Breguet Classique Tourbillon '5 Days'
description: There are tourbillons, and then there are Breguet tourbillons. Abraham-Louis Breguet patented the tourbillon in 1801, devising the rotating escapement to counteract the effects of gravity on the accuracy of a pocket watch. More than two centuries later, the complication remains one of watchmaking’s great technical spectacles, and few executions carry quite the historical legitimacy of the name that invented it. This Breguet Classique Tourbillon 5 Days Reference 5317, dating to the 2000s, packages that history in quintessential Breguet form. Its 18K yellow-gold case frames a beautifully elaborate silvered dial, decorated with contrasting hand-guilloché patterns and surrounded by a traditional Roman numeral chapter ring. Blued Breguet hands indicate the time, while a fan-shaped five-day power-reserve indicator sits prominently at 12 o’clock. The star of the show, naturally, appears at 6 o’clock. The exposed tourbillon carriage turns once per minute, simultaneously providing a running-seconds indication and giving the otherwise classical dial a wonderful mechanical focal point. It’s an appealing collision of old-school elegance and unabashed horological theater. Turn the watch over and things become even more impressive. The sapphire exhibition caseback reveals the hand-wound movement in all its glory, with extensive engraving that transforms the bridges and plates into an almost baroque composition of gears, scrollwork, jewels, and polished steel. It’s the sort of movement that makes a solid caseback seem positively unreasonable. This example is fitted with a Breguet brown alligator-leather strap and a signed yellow-gold deployant clasp. For all its complication, the 5317 remains unmistakably a Breguet: elegant, intellectually serious, beautifully decorated, and just extravagant enough. When the complication on your wrist was invented by the man whose name is printed on the dial, provenance doesn’t get much better.

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava Pilot Travel Time
description: Patek Philippe caused something of a commotion when it introduced the Calatrava Pilot Travel Time in 2015. A 42mm pilot’s watch with oversized luminous Arabic numerals, prominent pushers, and military inspiration? From Patek? It was an unexpected departure from the traditional Calatrava playbook, which is precisely why the Reference 5524 has become such a fascinating chapter in the manufacture’s modern history. This Reference 5524G-001 pairs a 42mm 18K white-gold case with a rich white/ivory dial whose oversized applied white-gold numerals and broad luminous hands make legibility the priority. The vintage aviation influence is unmistakable, but the execution is pure Patek: beautifully proportioned, impeccably finished, and far more refined than the traditional pilot’s watch. The clever bit is the Travel Time complication. Two central hour hands display local and home time, with the skeletonized hand indicating home time. The knurled pushers at 8 and 10 o’clock advance or retreat the local hour in one-hour increments without disturbing the watch’s timekeeping. Separate LOCAL and HOME day/night indicators eliminate any AM/PM guesswork, while the pointer date at 6 o’clock is synchronized to local time. It’s a genuinely useful complication dressed up in something unusually sporty for Patek Philippe. Inside, the self-winding Calibre 324 S C FUS can be admired through the sapphire caseback, providing the haute-horlogerie finishing expected from the manufacture beneath that decidedly adventurous exterior. This example is fitted to a khaki composite fabric-look strap with a signed 18K white-gold pin buckle, a combination that plays beautifully against the cool white-gold case and ivory dial. It is accompanied by its Certificate of Origin, papers and pamphlets, hang tags, and setting tool. The 5524G remains one of modern Patek’s great curveballs: part Calatrava, part travel watch, part military fantasy, and unmistakably Patek Philippe. Let’s jet!

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava
description: There are dress watches, and then there are watches that define what a dress watch is supposed to be. Since its introduction in 1932, the Patek Philippe Calatrava has served as the blueprint. Born during the economic uncertainty of the Great Depression, it represented a new direction for the manufacture—one that emphasized purity of design rather than mechanical complexity. Drawing inspiration from Bauhaus principles, the Calatrava distilled watchmaking to its essentials: proportion, legibility, and timeless elegance. Nearly a century later, its influence remains impossible to overstate. This particular Reference 6119R-001 is a contemporary expression of that philosophy, proving that the original formula still feels remarkably fresh. Housed in a 39mm rose gold case, it strikes a perfect balance between traditional dress-watch restraint and modern wrist presence. Framing the dial is the iconic Clous de Paris bezel, a Patek Philippe signature whose intricate hobnail pattern adds depth and texture without disturbing the watch’s overall simplicity. The silver-toned dial features a finely grained finish that catches the light beautifully, serving as the backdrop for applied rose gold markers, a subsidiary seconds register at 6 o’clock, and an elegant 'dauphine' handset. Every detail feels deliberate, every proportion carefully considered. Inside beats the hand-wound Caliber 30-255 PS, a modern Patek movement that combines traditional architecture with contemporary performance. Visible through the sapphire caseback, it offers the level of finishing collectors have come to expect from the Genevan maison . Paired with a brown alligator strap and signed rose gold pin buckle, and accompanied by its leather folio, and Certificate of Origin, this 6119R-001 represents the Calatrava at its most refined. Some watches follow trends. The Calatrava created its own category.

title: Jaeger-LeCoultre Reverso 1935
description: Some vintage watches come with boxes and papers. Occasionally, one comes with a life story. This extraordinary LeCoultre Reverso, dating to circa 1935, comes from the first few years of one of the most important wristwatch designs of the 20th century. The Reverso had been patented only in 1931, famously conceived as a solution for British officers in India who needed a watch capable of surviving the rigors of polo. Its ingenious answer was a rectangular case that could slide from its cradle, rotate, and turn its metal back outward to protect the crystal. What began as a piece of sporting ingenuity became an Art Deco icon. This example captures the design in beautifully pure early form. Its rectangular case features the signature horizontal gadroons above and below the dial, while the wonderfully aged silvered dial has developed a warm patina across more than 90 years. Applied baton indexes, slender hands, a geometric minute track, and a distinctive rectangular small-seconds display at 6 o’clock create a design that feels almost architectural. The dial is signed simply LeCoultre, appropriate for a watch produced before the Jaeger and LeCoultre names were formally united as Jaeger-LeCoultre in 1937. But flip this Reverso over, and the story becomes personal. The reverse is engraved with the initials “AK,” and unusually, we know something about the person behind them. Accompanying the watch are its original British bill of sale from the Goldsmiths & Silversmiths Company, a period photograph of the original owner, and a written family provenance tracing the watch back to Archibald Kelso. According to the accompanying history, the watch was a wedding gift from Lilian Simpson, his future wife. Simpson had worked as a ladies’ companion to Lady Bluckstein of the J. Lyons & Co. family. At the same time, Kelso was a Glasgow master confectioner and, reportedly, a baking tutor or supplier to Lyons. Suddenly those two engraved letters mean considerably more. The best vintage watches are objects that somehow survive after the people who originally owned them are gone. With an early Reverso, that history is especially poignant: the blank reverse of the case was conceived from the beginning as a place for initials, inscriptions, and personal expression. Here, the initials are still present, and remarkably, so is the story behind them.

title: Ikepod Duopod 'Staying Alive 005'
description: If some Ikepods are designed to make you look twice, the Duopod Staying Alive 005 takes the opposite approach. This is Ikepod at its most restrained: the familiar pebble-shaped case, stripped-back two-hand display, and an almost entirely monochromatic palette that lets Marc Newson’s original design language do most of the talking. The dial is particularly good. Finished in silvery grey with a circular brushed effect, it uses simple applied baton markers and a crisp railroad-style minute track around its perimeter. The signature Ikepod hands provide just enough contrast, while the absence of a running seconds hand makes the whole thing feel unusually calm. It’s minimalism without becoming anonymous; that bulbous, lugless profile ensures that. Like the other modern Duopods, the brushed stainless-steel case measures 42mm, yet wears considerably smaller thanks to the complete absence of traditional lugs. The integrated black silicone strap disappears neatly beneath the case, emphasizing its smooth UFO-like form, while a curved sapphire crystal continues the rounded architecture. Inside, a Japanese Miyota quartz movement keeps things deliberately simple and dependable. This example comes with its original recycled Ikepod box and papers. Named Staying Alive, it’s an amusingly appropriate watch for the reborn Ikepod: proof that one of the most distinctive designs of the 1990s didn’t need to be reinvented. It just needed to keep on going.

title: Ikepod Seapod 'Zale' Automatic
description: What happens when Ikepod makes a proper dive watch? Thankfully, it still looks like an Ikepod. The Seapod Zale takes the brand’s unmistakable UFO silhouette and gives it genuine underwater credentials, resulting in a diver that looks unlike almost anything else in the category. The 46mm brushed stainless-steel case retains Ikepod’s signature lugless architecture, with the strap disappearing beneath the case rather than attaching to conventional lugs. As a result, it wears considerably smaller than its dimensions suggest, closer to a conventional 42mm watch. Most clever is the rotating dive bezel, integrated so smoothly into the case that the familiar 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 markings almost appear to be engraved directly into the flying-saucer profile. The dark dial brings some welcome Ikepod weirdness. Circular orange hour markers surrounded by luminous white rings give it a wonderfully graphic, almost Pop quality, while the broad orange-and-white hands and oversized minute track make the watch highly legible. That same vivid orange continues onto the integrated silicone strap, turning a functional dive watch into something considerably more fun. Inside is the automatic Miyota 9039, a slim, high-beat Japanese movement with approximately 42 hours of power reserve. A screw-down crown and 200 meters of water resistance mean the Seapod isn’t merely playing dress-up as a diver; it has the specifications to back up the look. This example is accompanied by its original recycled Ikepod boxes and papers. Big, bright, and unapologetically unconventional, the Zale proves that even when Ikepod heads underwater, it has absolutely no interest in swimming with the rest of the fishes.

title: Ikepod Duopod Dots 004
description: Few contemporary watches are as immediately recognizable as an Ikepod. The smooth, lugless case originally conceived by Marc Newson in the 1990s helped turn the watch into an object of industrial design, and the modern Duopod carries that radical simplicity forward. It is round, slightly strange, and unmistakably Ikepod. The Duopod Dots 004 is one of the more graphic interpretations of the formula. Its convex black dial is covered in concentric fields of raised dots that grow larger toward the center, creating an almost three-dimensional optical effect. Tiny orange hour markers punctuate the otherwise monochromatic surface, while white minute hashes circle the perimeter. Against all that texture, the two black-and-white hands are almost comically simple. There isn’t even a running seconds hand to disturb the composition. The brushed 316L stainless-steel case measures 42mm, but without conventional lugs it wears considerably smaller, closer to a traditional 39mm watch. A curved sapphire crystal exaggerates the rounded, pebble-like profile, while the integrated black silicone strap continues directly from the case. Inside is a reliable Japanese Miyota quartz movement, an appropriately fuss-free engine for a watch in which the design is very much the main event. This example is accompanied by its original recycled Ikepod packaging and papers. The Duopod may be the more accessible descendant of those cult Newson-era Ikepods, but that’s precisely its charm. It takes one of the most distinctive watch designs of the past three decades, removes the preciousness, and leaves behind something playful, wearable, and wonderfully weird.

title: Cartier Tank Basculante
description: The famed Cartier Tank comes in all shapes and sizes, perhaps none of them as unique and compelling as the Basculante. With its elegant engraved dial and unique reversible case, the Tank Basculante stands out amongst Cartier's Tank models. Released in 1932, a year after the Jaeger-LeCoultre Reverso, it certainly shares functional similarities with the better-known model from Le Senrtier: a carriage case in which the dial and movement are housed pivoting inside an outer case, to reverse and protect the dial side - much like the Reverso's. However, unlike Jaeger-LeCoultre’s design, which uses a single track 'slider' mechanism, the Basculante employs a swinging frame. When deployed, the inner carriage case looks as if it's on a seesaw. Hence the name, which comes from the French bascule , or seesaw. The Tank Basculante may seem to some a pale imitation of the Reverso, but the subtle differences set it apart. Small details such as the winding crown at 12 o'clock and subtle pattern work on the dial make the Basculante truly original. This particular Basculante comes with a unqiue darker dial (unlike the conventional white or silver iterations) and matching sword handset. Sized 36mm x 24mm in stainless steel the Arabic dial and compact proportions make this watch a standout from the collections. Choosing a Cartier Tank is always a formula for dress watch success — but choosing a Basculante, with its signature reversible design, signals a particularly refined level of taste.

title: Patek Philippe Aquanaut
description: The Patek Philippe Aquanaut may be one of the most important modern luxury sport watches on the market. The Reference 5060J, launched in 1996 for the 20th anniversary of the Nautilus, was a sort of transitional watch. Borrowing features from the Nautilus but doing away with the famed case “ears” of that porthole-inspired model and adding lugs, it provided the basis for the Reference 5060A in 1997, the first model actually bearing the Aquanaut name. The Aquanaut would go on to form the basis of a full collection of luxury sports watches that provided the entry point into the Patek Philippe catalog. This piece, a Reference 5167/1A-001 features a 40mm stainless steel case with a satin-finished bezel, sapphire crystal, a signed screw-down crown and all its Patek sport watch glory. On the dial you'll find all of the signature Aquanaut features present — offered in an ombre anthracite tone that fades to black towards the edges, 'hobnail' texturing, luminous Arabic indices, a matching luminous handset and a date indicator at 3 o’clock. In great condition throughout and fitted to a Patek Philippe signed, uncut, integrated rubber strap with steel deployant, this piece is everything that made the Aquanaut one of the most coveted models in Patek's collections. Once misunderstood, thanks to the 5167, the Aquanaut is the pinnacle of collectable sports watches. With more presence on the wrist compared to its older siblings, the 5167 remains one of most highly-coveted steel sport watches on the market. Try it on and you'll see why!

title: Cartier Must de Cartier Tri-Tone Tank Vermeil
description: There are iconic watches, and then there are watches that have transcended watchmaking altogether. The Cartier Tank belongs firmly in the latter category. Since its introduction in 1917, its clean geometry and architectural lines have remained remarkably unchanged, proving that truly great design rarely requires reinvention. Artists, royalty, tastemakers, and collectors have all worn the Tank, yet somehow it continues to feel as modern today as it did more than a century ago. This particular example comes from the celebrated Must de Cartier collection, introduced in the late 1970s as a more accessible expression of Cartier's most famous designs. While many Must models embraced bold monochromatic dials, this reference takes a different approach, showcasing one of the most distinctive dial executions of the era. Housed in a gold vermeil case, the watch features a captivating tri-frame metallic dial whose layered geometric design transforms the familiar Tank into something altogether more playful and expressive. The stepped framing effect creates depth and dimension, while retaining the clean elegance that has always defined the model. Cartier's signature blued-steel hands sweep across the dial beneath the original double Cartier signature, complete with the intertwined "CC" monogram—a charming reminder of the period in which it was produced. The classic sapphire cabochon crown remains present, of course, while inside beats a manually wound movement that reinforces the mechanical appeal collectors increasingly seek in vintage Must models. Paired with a black leather strap and gold tone pin buckle, this Tank occupies a sweet spot in the Cartier universe: instantly recognizable, undeniably stylish, and just unusual enough to stand apart from the crowd. The Must de Cartier line was never intended to be ordinary. Pieces like this remind us just how creative Cartier was willing to be when given the freedom to experiment. Because even an icon like the Tank occasionally benefits from a little disco-era swagger.

title: Patek Philippe Annual Calendar Flyback Chronograph
description: The Annual Calendar may seem like a given today, but in 1991 it was still a dream—and one considered nearly impossible. The soon-to-be graduates of the Geneva School of Engineering were handed a final challenge that bordered on audacity: simplify the perpetual calendar. Their work, in collaboration with Patek Philippe, became a breakthrough. Five years later, Patek unveiled the Reference 5035—the world's first annual calendar—a complication born not from ornamentation, but from logic and elegance. Fast forward, and we arrive at one of the most compelling evolutions of that idea: the 5960/1A-001. This is Patek Philippe embracing modernity with confidence. A 40mm stainless steel case—featuring sculpted lugs, a concave bezel, and pump pushers—wears purposefully without losing its refinement. The white dial is crisp and legible, featuring day-date-month apertures at the top, a power reserve indicator at 12 o'clock, and the signature monocounter at 6 o'clock that tracks both elapsed minutes and hours in one beautifully efficient register. It's a complication, streamlined. Inside beats the self-winding Caliber CH 28-520 C—column wheel chronograph, vertical clutch, annual calendar logic—and visible through a sapphire caseback where the 21k gold rotor catches the light like a quiet flex from one of the greatest manufactures on earth. It's fitted to Patek's multi-link steel bracelet with a double deployant clasp and comes with its original inner and outer boxes. The Nautilus and Aquanaut may be the poster children of modern Patek collecting, but pieces like the 5960/1A are where the true connoisseurs stop and take notice. It's a high complication in steel. It's intelligent. It's distinctive. And it's hiding in plain sight. A thinking person's Patek. And one of the smartest plays in the current market.

title: Cartier Must de Cartier Tank Vermeil Large
description: There are iconic watches, and then there are watches that have transcended watchmaking altogether. The Cartier Tank belongs firmly in the latter category. Since its introduction in 1917, its clean geometry and architectural lines have remained remarkably unchanged, proving that truly great design rarely requires reinvention. Artists, royalty, tastemakers, and collectors have all worn the Tank, yet somehow it continues to feel as modern today as it did more than a century ago. This particular example comes from the celebrated Must de Cartier collection, introduced in the late 1970s as a more accessible expression of Cartier's most famous designs. While many Must models embraced bold monochromatic dials, this reference takes a different approach, showcasing one of the most distinctive dial executions of the era. Housed in a gold vermeil case, the watch features a captivating gold applique dial whose layered geometric design transforms the familiar Tank into something altogether more playful and expressive. The framing effect creates depth and dimension, while retaining the clean elegance that has always defined the model. Cartier's signature blued-steel hands sweep across the dial to help add a pop of color to the beautiful design language. The classic sapphire cabochon crown remains present, of course, while inside beats a manually wound movement that reinforces the mechanical appeal collectors increasingly seek in vintage Must models. Paired with a brown leather strap and deployant clasp, this Tank occupies a sweet spot in the Cartier universe: instantly recognizable, undeniably stylish, and just unusual enough to stand apart from the crowd. The Must de Cartier line was never intended to be ordinary. Pieces like this remind us just how creative Cartier was willing to be when given the freedom to experiment. Because even an icon like the Tank occasionally benefits from a little disco-era swagger.

title: IWC Porsche Compass
description: 1972’s Chronograph 1 — strikingly cool as it is — is far from Porsche Design’s only notable wristwatch. In fact, we’d argue that there’s another that’s just as important, though for different reasons. That watch is the Porsche design compass. Designed by none other than Ferdinand “Butzi” Porsche himself — the man behind the iconic 911 — this model family incorporated a particularly unique case and bracelet architecture to make for one of the most other-worldly designs on the market. 39mm with anodized aluminum case and matching bracelet, this piece has the timekeeping display set on a pivot to reveal a second layer with a compass underneath. The ultimate tool watch for lovers of Porsche, this watch proves that Porsche knows more than just cars. Despite its unconventional design, this unusual watch — which was produced by none other than the International Watch Company is a perfect companion for adventurers the world over. Now considered a horological classic, it looks just as futuristic today as it did upon its release. Snag it before someone else has the same idea!

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava
description: Patek Philippe has long been known for its complicated watchmaking, but following the stock market crash of 1929, fewer clients had the means to purchase these high-end timepieces. After securing a controlling interest in the firm, Jean and Charles Henri Stern decided to create a simple watch that would come in at a lower price point and appeal to the firm’s clientele. Using the principles espoused by the Bauhaus school and its minimalist, function-first philosophy, Patek conceived the Calatrava, taking its name from the Spanish military order established in the 12th century which had become the symbol of Patek Philippe. Since its debut in 1932, the Calatrava has become a byword for a simple, time-only dress watch — even from brands other than Patek itself. This piece, a Reference 6007G-011, isn’t your run-of-the-mill Calatrava. Debuted in 2023 in three individual colorways — red, blue and yellow — this particular Calatrava features an array of automotive-eqsque design cues that easily makes it the sportiest 'Trava in their modern lineup. Housed in a 40mm 18K white gold case, this piece features a polished bezel and case complemented by a sapphire crystal and a signed crown. The black luminous dial features a matching white gold handset and radially configured, luminous, white gold Arabic indices. Straying away from the traditional dressier aesthetics of the Calatrava model, the Patek Philippe design team elected to add sportier design notes with its center dial adorned with a 'carbon' finish and a red accented, checker-style, minute track. Outfitted to a signed black leather strap with a matching 'carbon' embossing, contrast red stitching and a spade-style 18K white gold pin buckle, this piece comes with its matching paperwork and 'Certificate of Origin' dated 2025. Traditional Calatrava aesthetics were thrown out the window on this one and we're here for it!

title: IWC Big Pilot
description: The IWC Big Pilot's Watch can trace its history back to the oversized timepieces produced for military aviators in 1940. These enormous pieces were originally designed for maximum legibility in a cockpit setting, and were originally designed to be worn on the pilot's thigh! Today the Big Pilot's line is perhaps IWC's most identifiable collection, featuring a variety of case and dial configurations suited for any taste - provided your wrist can handle the oversized dimensions! This particular example is what you might consider to be the prototypical Big Pilot — a thoroughbred 46mm example cased in steel with an oversized 'onion' crown. It features a luminous matte black dial with printed white 'Arabic' numerals, a recessed power reserve indicator, and a date at 6 o'clock, a matching 'sword' handset, a polished faceted bezel, and a sapphire crystal. Powering this beast is IWC's Calibre 51111 automatic winding movement with a massive 8-day power reserve. It comes fitted to a IWC black 'rivet' leather strap with a signed steel deployant clasp. When you hear the term ‘pilot’s watch,’ there’s a healthy chance that what comes to mind is a timepiece from the International Watch Company.... and that is because of the ancestors to this watch. That is to say: The Big Pilot represents the very essence of IWC.

title: Bulova Accutron 218
description: In the early 1970s, the future didn’t tick — it hummed. This Bulova Accutron 218 is a reminder that the Space Age wasn’t all silver and white—it had depth, warmth, and serious design confidence. Housed in a sharp cushion case with crisp edges and original factory finishing intact, this is the kind of honest survivor collectors hope for. But the dial is the headline. A dark charcoal black dial is sectored from the center, with Steel hands with white stripes echo the dial furniture, with beautiful applique lume plots at their tips for a subtle functional touch. At 3, a date window rounds out the dial. The signed crown—correctly bearing the Accutron tuning fork logo—anchors the case at 4 o’clock. Inside beats the later Caliber 218 tuning fork movement, widely regarded as one of the more robust executions of Bulova’s revolutionary electronic platform. Instead of ticking, the seconds hand glides in a perfectly smooth sweep, powered by vibration rather than escapement. The Accutron line famously found its way onto the wrists of astronauts, pilots, and even into cockpit instrumentation, cementing its reputation as the watch of the electronic age. This 218 captures that spirit in a form that feels both forward-thinking and distinctly vintage. The sound of 1960s, still resonating. The Accutron 218 isn’t just a watch—it’s a piece of American technological optimism.

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava Diamonds
description: Patek Philippe has long been known for its complicated watchmaking, but following the stock market crash of 1929, fewer clients had the means to purchase these high-end timepieces. After securing a controlling interest in the firm, Jean and Charles Henri Stern created a simple watch that would come in at a lower price point and appeal to the firm’s clientele. Using the principles espoused by the Bauhaus school and its minimalist, function-first philosophy, Patek conceived the Calatrava, taking its name from the Spanish military order established in the 12th century which had become the symbol of Patek Philippe. Since its debut in 1932, the Calatrava has become a byword for a simple, time-only dress watch — even from brands other than Patek itself. This particular Calatrava, a ladies Reference 5108G, is one of the most exquisite references in the collection. Housed in a thoroughly modern 37mm 18K white gold case with a sapphire crystal, a signed crown, and a diamond-encrusted bezel and dial, it features a stunning, baguette and diamond-set dial, a dauphine handset and a pointed central seconds hand. Powered by the automatic Patek Philippe Calibre 315/290 movement with central rotor and finished with a sapphire caseback, it comes paired to a signed, blue alligator leather strap with a white gold pin buckle. This watch truly is a girl’s best friend!

title: Patek Philippe Nautilus
description: The Patek Philippe Nautilus is without question one of the great horological icons of the 1970s, and one of the most in-demand timepiece models on the planet. Collectors and prospectors alike are clamouring to get their hands on what is arguably one of Genta's greatest watch designs, and with the discontinuation of the flagship Reference 5711 in steel, this continued rise in popularity shows no signs of slowing down. Interestingly, most demand for Nautilus models is centered around Jumbo models in steel, something we can't fully wrap our heads around … This midsize Nautilus, a Reference 3800/1G, embodies all of the porthole-inspired character of its larger siblings, just with a slightly smaller 37mm case clad in solid 18K white gold. Outfitted with a crispy integrated bracelet with a signed locking clasp, this piece features one of our favorite Nautilus dial configurations with applied, luminous, white gold Roman indices; a date indicator at 3 o’clock; a matching luminous f euille handset and a white accented chemin de fer set against a gloss black dial. Absolutely fantastic. Powered by the maison’s self-winding Calibre 335SC movement, this piece is in outstanding condition retaining deep hallmarks and engravings. A standard stainless steel Nautilus with a blue ‘teak’ dial is as classic as it gets, but this unique dial configuration blended with a white gold case and bracelet is a perfect marriage of sport and elegance. Some may say that smaller watches are back with a vengeance — we say they never left!

title: Breitling Co-Pilot Chronograph
description: Like the Breguet Type 20, the Breitling Reference 765 or AVI was designed for helicopter pilots in the French army. Eager to secure the contract, in 1953 Breitling designed a watch that they thought would be perfect for the job. Unlike the Navitimer, the dial of the AVI displayed only the most essential information pilots needed — the requisite hours and minutes, indicated by large luminescent hands, and registers for running seconds, 12 hours, and 30 minutes. Unfortunately, the French military specification — Type 20 —required a flyback function, which the AVI lacked. Not to be deterred, Breitling adapted it for civilian use, and in 1964 it debuted as the Co-Pilot. This watch was worn to perfection by Raquel Welch in the 1967 film Fathom , in which an Italian skydiver (played by Welch as the title character) finds herself embroiled in international espionage. Breitling ads promoted the watch’s appearance on film, stating that either the watch or the woman “[Steals] the scenes, in film and real life.” Though the Co-Pilot retained the diameter of its predecessor (a whopping 41mm, large for the period), it underwent some cosmetic changes that made it stand out amidst Breitling’s chronograph offerings: The rotating 12h steel bezel, previously steel, was now anodized aluminum. (The bezel was also released in other variants, like the ‘Double-Scale,’ which displayed scales for both 60 minutes and 12 hours. The ‘Double-Scale’ bezel found its way to a cousin of the Co-Pilot, the 765 Yachting.) Additionally, the dial — previously black-on-black — was given a distinctive black-and-white colorway now known as ‘reverse panda’ by collectors.The new variant of Co-Pilot with the white chronograph registers found its way on the wrist of someone less glamorous (but no less exciting) than Raquel Welch — Jean-Claude Killy. Though best associated with the Rolex Dato-Compax that now bears his name in collecting circles, Killy also sported a Reference 765 Co-Pilot before pledging himself to the Crown as a brand ambassador. Most notably, he wore the Co-Pilot during the 1968 Winter Olympics in Grenoble, France, where he won gold medals in downhill, giant slalom, and slalom — the “Triple Crown” of alpine skiing — thus securing his legacy. This particular Co-Pilot, a Reference 765CP, dates to circa 1965 and comes in with a 42.5mm stainless steel case with dual barrel pushers, a signed crown, and a bidirecitonal rotating black aluminum bezel with a 12-hour markers. It features a matte black Tritium 'reverse panda' dial with recessed, silver sub registers, a an outer white minute track, and a matching white painted 'sword' handset. Powered by a Venus Calibre 178 manual winding chronograph movement, this piece comes fitted to one of our red Analog:Shift Montone leather straps with a steel pin buckle. Whether plunging toward Earth from a De Havilland DH-89A like Welch in Fathom, slaloming down the slopes in the French Alps ﻿a la ﻿Killy, or are a seasoned Breitling collector, this piece makes for a great option! While these are not exactly scarce, finding one in excellent overall condition such as this is always a treat.

title: Piaget Onyx Dial
description: There’s nothing more classic and appealing than a simple dress watch. Though to be fair, when we say ‘simple’, we mean ‘uncomplicated’ — not unattractive! The 20th century saw a plethora of such watches hit the market. Generally available on leather straps and featuring two or three hands, these reliable wristwatches kept time during the classiest decades of the past 100 years. However, some were more innovative than others. Take this exquisite piece from Piaget, specialists in ultra-thin watchmaking: it’s as much akin to a piece of jewelry as it is to a more traditional wristwatch. Housed in a 23mm, yellow gold case with a fantastic, integrated 'woven' yellow gold bracelet, this Piaget features a striking onyx dial with a matching 'dauphine' handset, and Piaget's svelte Calibre 9P1 hand-winding movement within. Imagine the looks of curiosity — and envy — that you’ll stir up when rocking this beautiful Piaget at a cocktail party. With its eye-catching design, deep black dial, and awesome bracelet, this is a standout timepiece appropriate for virtually any wrist. While these beautiful Piaget pieces from the late 20th century went underappreciated for many years, we have recently seen a deserved surge in interest for these avant-garde designs. Catch this one before it’s gone! *Due to the design of this bracelet, sizing alterations may require custom work. Lead time after measurements are established is 4-6 weeks.*

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava
description: Patek Philippe is one of the few brands that knows how to execute simple perfection. Over the years, their dress-line Calatrava has evolved, but the look remains unmistakable and iconic, and its rich history provides the vintage enthusiast with a variety of choices in metals, sizes, and tiny details to obsess over. This particular example is of the fairer kind, a Reference 2545, (a sibling of the legendary Ref. 96 with a screw-down caseback and added water resistance) and is ideal for the collector who seeks a more minimal presence. Dating to roughly circa 1950's, it features a perfectly sized 32 mm solid 18K yellow gold case, with applied gold indicies and matching 'dauphine' handset. Powered the manual winding Calibre 12-400 BEAUTIFUL movement, it truly epitomizes what Patek Philippe is most known for- understated elegance and delicate finishing. This is one of the rarer vintage Pateks, and has the classic aesthetic we have come to know from the 96 and that has been passed down to dozens of references ever since. The combination of mid-century charm, modest proportions, classic aesthetics, and rare numbers make this one of the coolest vintage pieces available for sale. You won't see another one for a while. In other words- everything you need, nothing you don’t.

title: Cartier Ballon Bleu
description: The Ballon Bleu transformed Cartier's modern collection by proving that an entirely new design could become as recognizable as the Tank or the Santos. Introduced in 2007, its rounded case, floating crown guard, and fluid lines gave the maison a contemporary icon that remained unmistakably Cartier from every angle. This Reference W6920087 brings an added sense of warmth to the collection through its elegant stainless steel case and matching white alligator strap. Measuring a perfect 36.6mm, the case strikes a versatile balance on the wrist, while the matching strap—with its stainless steel deployant clasp—extends the watch's flowing silhouette seamlessly beyond the case. The focal point is its beautiful guilloche dial. Alive with subtle shifts in color, it provides a beautiful backdrop for Cartier's signature black Roman numerals, blued steel sword hands, and finely printed chemin-de-fer minute track. Framed by a smooth polished bezel, the dial is complemented by the collection's defining detail: a fluted crown set within the integrated crown guard and finished with Cartier's signature synthetic blue spinel cabochon. Powering the watch is Cartier's reliable quartz 690 caliber, delivering the convenience of quartz in a case whose proportions remain refined and elegant enough for daily wear. The Ballon Bleu occupies a unique place within Cartier's history. Rather than reinterpreting a historic design, it established a new visual language for the maison—one that has become every bit as recognizable as its earliest icons. In this beautiful configuration, paired with its strap and dial, the W6920087 perfectly captures Cartier's ability to blend fine jewelry and watchmaking into a single, enduring design.

title: Vulcain Multi-Scale Chronometre 'NOS' Chronograph
description: Vulcain is likely best known for its innovative Cricket alarm watch. While brands like Jaeger-LeCoultre developed its own wrist alarm, Vulcain is noteworthy for doing it first. Unveiled in 1947, the Cricket ranks as one of the most accurate and well-known of Vulcain's watches, and has been bestowed to almost every President since Truman. Yet despite this lineage, Vulcain also produced other wristwatches--many of them with complications such as chronographs. The brand's founder, Maurice Ditisheim, was himself an expert in the production of complicated movements for pocket-watches. So it's no surprise that his company--named after that divine master mechanic, the god Vulcan--would produce perhaps the most versatile of complications, the chronograph. Along with many other brands (from Hamilton to Rolex ), Vulcain utilized chronograph movements designed by famed èbauche manufacturer Valjoux. Valjoux--founded by Adolphe Nicole in 1844--specialized from the very beginning in the production of manually-wound chronograph movements. The manufacturer further changed the course of horological history by developing the first chronograph movement with a column wheel in the 1890s, a technology which would be featured in almost every chronograph until Landeron developed the cam in the late 1940s. The Vulcain chrono that we feature here is one of the most beautiful. Executed in 14K gold with a beautiful silver dial with twin registers, this manually wound beauty flaunts blue timing scales with faceted indexes, leaf hands, and recessed pushers. A unique articulating lug design integrates the strap directly into the case. Best of all, the caseback features a flip tab to open and reveal the stunning manually wound movement ticking within. This is a watch with history and personality, and deserves a place in your watchbox!

title: Patek Philippe Annual Calendar Moonphase
description: In 1991, the soon-to-be graduates at the Geneva School of Engineering were presented with their final project prior to receiving their diploma — simplify the perpetual calendar. Although the task was easier said than done, their work led to the inception of the annual calendar complication, patented by Patek in collaboration with the bright engineering minds at the GSE. Five years later, Patek debuted the Reference 5035 which marked the world’s first-ever annual calendar movement and finally bridged the gap between a triple date function and the formidable quantième perpétuel . This piece, a Reference 5146P-001, is housed in a beautifully proportioned 39mm platinum case with a sapphire crystal, signed crown, and a smooth polished bezel. It features a luminous sunburst grey dial with applied indices, recessed subsidiary registers indicating day and month, a moonphase aperture and date window at 6 o'clock, and a matching luminous 'feuille' handset. Powered by Patek Philippe's Calibre 315 S IRM QA LU automatic winding movement, it comes fitted to a signed black alligator strap with a signed platinum deployant clasp and includes its complete factory goodies. This piece packs pedigree, refinement, function and outstanding craftsmanship that can only be expected on Patek Philippe. Any old wristwatch can tell the time. Few truly define it.

title: Patek Philippe Nautilus Ladies Two-Tone
description: The Nautilus is without question one of the great horological icons of the 1970s, and one of the most in-demand timepiece models on the planet. Collectors and prospectors alike are clamoring to get their hands on Genta's second great luxury sports watch, and with the recent news of the discontinuation of the flagship reference 5711 in steel, this dramatic rise in popularity shows no signs of slowing down. This particular Nautilus is a ladies’ model, the Reference 4700/001. While later generations of this reference feature white date wheels, these first-gen examples are equipped with black date wheels that meld beautifully with the dial. Housed in a 27mm two tone case, this example features a champagne ‘Sigma’ dial with applied, gold indices, a lumed ‘pencil’ handset, and the aforementioned black date wheel. Powered by the Patek Philippe quartz Calibre E19 and paired to an integrated, two tone stainless steel and gold bracelet, it’s every bit as iconic as its larger, mechanical siblings. Plus, this piece has its original Extract from the Archives! The Nautilus has become a true piece of horological history; an icon of icons; and must be experienced to be understood. Just saying!

title: Patek Philippe Annual Calendar Moonphase
description: In 1991, the soon-to-be graduates at the Geneva School of Engineering were presented with their final project prior to receiving their diploma — simplify the perpetual calendar. It features a charming ivory white dial with applied indices, recessed subsidiary registers indicating day and month, a moonphase aperture and date window at 6 o'clock, and a matching luminous 'feuille' handset. Powered by Patek Philippe's Calibre 324 S IRM QA LU self-winding movement, it comes fitted to its signed black alligator leather strap with a signed 18k white gold deployant buckle. There’s no doubt the Nautilus and Aquanaut have gotten their time in the sun, and even vintage Patek Philippe in general continues to demand the attention of any savvy collector. But let us not forget the high-complication heavy-hitters hiding in plain sight in Patek’s modern catalogs!

title: Seiko Silverwave Diver
description: In the 1960s and 1970s, Seiko was undergoing a rebirth of sorts. The brand's position as official timer for the 1964 Summer Olympics, held in Tokyo, gave it exposure on a global scale. The following year, they launched what would become the first in a long line of dive watches. While many of Seiko's most famous dive pieces come from the 1970s, in the 1960s, the Silverwave line served as the progenitor to almost all modern Seiko divers. The Silverwave was the first Seiko to feature an inner rotating bezel, first automatic with a screwdown caseback for added waterproofing, and it was truly the brand's first attempt at dive watches more generally. Sadly, today, many have forgotten the importance of this family of watches. Until now! We are excited to showcase a beautiful representation of the Silverwave. This Seiko Sportsmatic Silverwave diver comes with its beautiful contrast inner bezel, 38mm case dimensions, and a stunning beads of rice signed bracelet sized up to a 7 inch wrist. A sunburst silver dial applique indexes, and a pointed handset round out the package. If you care about Seiko and its evolution of dive watches, this piece is an absolute must!

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava
description: Sometimes the simplest Patek Philippe watches reveal the most about what the manufacture does so well. Dating to the 2000s, this Reference 5115R is a beautifully traditional expression of the Patek Philippe dress watch, executed in 18K rose gold and measuring an elegant 35mm in diameter. At just 8mm thick, it has the slim proportions one wants from a watch of this kind, but there is considerably more going on here than first meets the eye. Most striking is the gorgeous Clous de Paris bezel, its intricate hobnail pattern creating a richly textured frame around the otherwise restrained dial. The white enamel dial is classically arranged with black Roman numerals, slender feuille-style hands, a chemin-de-fer minute track, and a beautifully proportioned subsidiary seconds register at 6:00. The combination of crisp black indications, white enamel, and warm rose gold feels quintessentially Patek Philippe. Inside is the manually wound Calibre 215 PS, with “PS” denoting petite seconde, or small seconds. The movement carries the historic Geneva Seal and offers approximately 44 hours of power reserve. There is something particularly appropriate about a hand-wound movement in a watch this traditional—the simple ritual of winding it is entirely in keeping with its old-school character. A scratch-resistant sapphire crystal protects the dial, while the watch comes fitted to a brown alligator leather strap with its original 18K rose gold Patek Philippe tang buckle. The Ref. 5115R is a dress-watch Patek at its most distilled: modestly sized, beautifully finished, and wonderfully traditional. And that Clous de Paris bezel gives an otherwise restrained watch just the right amount of textured flourish.

title: Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Diamonds
description: One name: Gerald Genta. The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak is perhaps Genta’s most memorable work, and in many ways changed the shape of the watch industry. The Royal Oak essentially created an entirely new category of 'luxury sport' timepieces, and with it came a new design language which inspired countless other manufactures. What's particularly delightful about the design of the Royal Oak is that it works brilliantly in a number of sizes and casing materials, from steel to carbon fiber or solid gold. This Royal Oak is a smaller model designed for the ladies market, but packs a ton of punch: Housed in a petite 26mm yellow gold case, it features a beautiful diamond-set bezel and dial. The diamond settings really do wonders to accentuate the geometry of the bezel and alongside the warmer tones of the champagne dial, this piece has an elegant, refined finish to it. The warmth of the material finishes and the industrial sophistication of the design of the Royal Oak couple to make one of the most compelling iterations available for sale. In good condition throughout, this small reference possesses all of the iconic features that the larger variants do - but just packing a little more punch.

When you hear the term ‘pilot’s watch,’ there’s a healthy chance that what comes to mind is a timepiece from the International Watch Company.... and that is because of the ancestors to this watch.
