Our longstanding relationship and shared passion for horological history and design have culminated in this unique offering. Each Accutron timepiece undergoes rigorous inspection and certification by expert watchmakers and is backed by the manufacture, ensuring unparalleled authenticity and quality.

title: Patek Philippe Mini Calatrava
description: The 'Holy Trinity' of watch brands: Audemars Piguet, Patek Philippe, and Vacheron Constantin. Perhaps the most celebrated of the three, Patek Philippe has an unrivaled reputation for crafting some of the most complicated — and some of the simplest, yet most beautiful — timekeepers the market has seen. Sports watches came later to Patek, as pressure from the new 'luxury sports watch' category introduced in the early 1970s forced the storied brand to evolve — but historically, classically-styled dress pieces is where the maison cut its teeth. This particular timepiece is a ladies' version of the famed Calatrava dress watch. Executed in beautiful yellow gold, it boasts a smooth bezel, a signed winding crown, a smooth bezel, long lugs, and a simple golden dial, minimalist printed indices, and a matching 'pencil' handset. The hallmarks on the case and lugs are so crisp and clean--- a testament to the quality of this example as a truly beautiful piece in sterling condition. Powered by a Patek Philippe hand-wound movement, it comes paired to a signed leather strap. Oozing with irreplaceable class, it's an ideal wrist companion for someone longing for a bit of midcentury elegance.

title: Patek Philippe Ellipse 'Chain-Link'
description: Few watches capture Patek Philippe’s particular brand of elegant eccentricity quite like the Golden Ellipse. Introduced in 1968, the Golden Ellipse broke decisively with the traditional round dress watch, its distinctive form occupying the space somewhere between a circle and a rectangle. Patek famously connected its proportions to the “golden ratio,” the mathematical equation long associated with harmonious design. The result became one of the manufacture’s defining shapes of the late 20th century, and a particularly compelling canvas for the smaller, jewelry-minded watches of the era. This 90s-era yellow gold Reference 4830J takes the idea somewhere especially chic. Measuring a wonderfully compact 26mm by 23mm, its softly rounded case frames a crisp white dial with oversized black Roman numerals and matching black hands. But the real action happens beyond the case. Fabulous sculptural “chain-link” lugs extend dramatically above and below, giving the diminutive watch considerably more presence on the wrist while blurring the distinction between watchmaking and jewelry design. The theme continues with the original Patek Philippe black alligator leather strap and remarkable signed yellow gold pin buckle, whose curving, open construction echoes the shape of the lugs. An additional brown alligator leather strap is included, offering an easy way to change the character of the watch. Inside is a Patek Philippe quartz movement, a fitting choice for the slender, design-driven watches the manufacture produced during this period. Better still, the caseback retains its original quartz sticker, a wonderfully nerdy detail and increasingly uncommon survivor that speaks to the watch’s preservation. Compact, sculptural and unmistakably Patek Philippe, this Golden Ellipse represents a side of the manufacture that collectors are increasingly rediscovering: less about complication and more about pure design. On the wrist, those extraordinary chain-link lugs make the 4830J feel almost like a piece of fine jewelry that happens to tell the time. This is a seriously stylish little watch.

title: Universal Genève Medico Compax
description: Universal Genève built its reputation on the chronograph. During the 1930s and ’40s, the manufacture developed an extraordinary assortment of purpose-built wrist chronographs, creating watches for pilots, motorists, athletes—and, in the case of the Medico-Compax, the medical profession. Dating to the 1940s, this Medico-Compax Reference 22517 is a particularly beautiful example. Its 37mm stainless steel case is generously sized for the period, with pump pushers and sharply defined lugs framing a wonderfully elaborate silver dial. Two snailed registers sit at 3:00 and 9:00, while applied Arabic numerals and elegant blued hands provide an appealing mixture of refinement and legibility. The defining feature, however, is the pulsations scale encircling the dial. Rather than a conventional tachymeter, the Medico-Compax was calibrated to allow a doctor to determine a patient’s heart rate quickly. Start the chronograph, count 15 heartbeats, stop it, and the central chronograph hand indicates the corresponding pulse rate directly on the scale. “GRADUÉ POUR 15 PULSATIONS” printed prominently along the perimeter makes the watch’s intended purpose delightfully explicit. Inside is a manually wound Universal Genève chronograph movement, continuing the manufacture’s celebrated tradition of producing sophisticated chronographs during one of its most important periods. With box and signed steel pin buckle, there is something especially appealing about complications created to solve highly specific problems, and the Medico-Compax may be one of the best examples. Its medical functionality is fascinating, but even removed from its original professional context, this is simply an exceptionally handsome vintage chronograph. At 36mm in steel, with its beautifully balanced two-register dial, blued hands, and wonderfully specialized pulsometer scale, this Reference 22517 represents Universal Genève doing what it did best: turning a serious instrument into an extraordinarily elegant wristwatch.

title: Omega Seamaster Aqua Terra 'Skyfall'
description: The Omega Seamaster Aqua Terra has always occupied an appealing middle ground: sporty enough to handle the water, refined enough to wear with tailoring, and refreshingly free of the overt tool-watch styling associated with most of the Seamaster family. This stainless steel example comes from one of the most desirable generations of the Aqua Terra, instantly recognizable by its blue vertical “Teak Concept” dial. Inspired by the wooden decking of luxury sailing yachts, the striped surface gives the dial considerable depth while applied indices, a framed date aperture at 3:00, and luminous hands keep everything crisp and highly legible. Measuring 41.5mm, the stainless steel case is paired with an integrated-style steel bracelet, giving the watch a substantial but decidedly polished presence on the wrist. Collectors have come to nickname this generation the “Skyfall” Aqua Terra, after Daniel Craig wore the smaller 38.5mm version as James Bond in the 2012 film, you guessed it, Skyfall . The association has only added to the appeal of a design that has since become something of a modern Omega classic. Particularly distinctive is the framed date window, a detail eliminated from later versions, along with the original vertically striped dial configuration. Inside is Omega’s automatic Co-Axial Calibre 8500, visible through the sapphire exhibition caseback. Developed in-house, the movement features Omega’s Co-Axial escapement, a 60-hour power reserve, and an independently adjustable hour hand—a particularly useful feature when traveling between time zones. Water resistance is rated to 150 meters, reinforcing the Aqua Terra’s ability to move comfortably between dress watch and sports watch territory. This example comes accompanied by its papers, warranty cards, and associated pamphlets. Bond connection aside, the appeal here is the watch itself. The blue-dial Aqua Terra combines some of Omega’s best early-21st-century design cues with a genuinely capable movement and everyday versatility, and this discontinued configuration has aged particularly well.

title: Patek Philippe Sculpture Two-Tone
description: Welcome to the wild side of Patek Philippe! Produced during the 1990s, the Sculpture belongs to a fascinating period when the manufacture was experimenting with unconventional cases, integrated bracelets, mixed metals, and a considerably more extroverted design language. Today, with neo-vintage Patek Philippe increasingly in the spotlight, the Sculpture suddenly looks remarkably prescient. This example combines stainless steel and 18K yellow gold in a substantial 38mm case with a smooth gold bezel and an integrated two-tone bracelet. The case is the real curiosity. Pronounced “ears” project from either side, inevitably recalling the Nautilus—and, in retrospect, the Aquanaut—but interpreted here in a much more flamboyant fashion. The bracelet continues the theme with sculptural links that make the entire watch feel like a single piece of industrial jewelry. Then there’s the black dial. Concentric geometric texturing radiates from its center, surrounded by applied gold Roman numerals and an almost architectural outer minute track. Tritium-filled feuille hands indicate the time, while a simple date aperture at 3:00 provides everyday practicality. Even the crown is wonderfully strange, with what appears to be deep blue lapis lazuli set into its end. Inside is Patek Philippe’s automatic Calibre 315, complete with quick-set date and gold winding rotor—a thoroughly serious movement inside one of the manufacture’s least conventional designs. The Sculpture was never produced in significant numbers, with total production across the various executions believed to have amounted to roughly 2,500 watches. That scarcity, combined with its very specific 1990s aesthetic, makes it particularly interesting today. This is primo neo-vintage Patek: rare, weird, luxurious, and completely removed from the restrained Calatrava idea of what a Patek Philippe should look like. Hot, hot, hot! Rare, rare, rare!

title: Tavannes Hermès Triple Register Chronograph
description: There are vintage chronographs that are compelling because of their movements, others because of their dials, and still others because of the name printed beneath 12 o’clock. This extraordinary 1940s Tavannes manages all three…and then adds Hermès to the equation. Tavannes was among Switzerland’s most significant watch manufacturers during the first half of the 20th century, producing sophisticated watches and movements while maintaining relationships with important retailers and luxury houses. This rare chronograph was made for Hermès, whose name appears discreetly beneath the Tavannes signature on its remarkable black gilt dial. And that dial is the star. Warm gilt printing contrasts beautifully against the glossy black surface, with large Arabic numerals, three subsidiary registers, an outer telemeter scale, and elegant golden feuille hands creating a wonderfully dense yet balanced composition. Decades of age have only added character, giving the watch exactly the sort of presence collectors seek in an untouched vintage chronograph. At 38mm, the stainless steel case is exceptionally large for a 1940s wristwatch. Its construction is equally interesting: a multi-part “clamshell” design developed to provide improved resistance to dust and moisture, with the movement effectively enclosed within the case structure. Inside is another major attraction: the manually wound Valjoux Calibre 71. The large 14-ligne, column-wheel chronograph movement is closely related to the celebrated Valjoux 72 architecture. It represents exactly the sort of high-grade movement one hopes to find inside a chronograph of this caliber. The combination is exceptional: 38mm steel clamshell case, Valjoux 71, black gilt dial, triple-register chronograph, AND Hermès provenance. It is difficult to imagine a much better recipe for a 1940s chronograph—and considerably harder to find another one.

title: Bulova Accutron 'Breguet' Red Fumé
description: In 1960, Bulova imagined the future of watchmaking—and that future hummed. The Accutron was one of the great technological leaps of the 20th century, replacing the traditional balance wheel with an electronically powered tuning fork. Developed under the direction of engineer Max Hetzel, the system delivered exceptional accuracy for its era and produced the faint, unmistakable hum that became an Accutron signature. Long before quartz reshaped the industry, Bulova had already introduced an entirely new way of keeping time. This 1973 example shows just how adventurous Accutron design became as the Space Age gave way to the 1970s. Housed in a wonderfully angular stainless steel cushion case, the watch is dominated by a fabulous red fumé dial that graduates from glowing crimson at its center to nearly black around the perimeter. Applied stylized “Breguet” Arabic numerals add an unexpectedly traditional flourish, while luminous hands and plots complete the wonderfully idiosyncratic combination. Inside is Bulova’s Calibre 218 tuning-fork movement, an evolution of the original Accutron technology that moved the time-setting crown from the caseback to the more conventional 4:00 position. Turn the watch over, and there’s another charming detail: a simple personal engraving on the caseback, adding a small piece of human history to an already distinctive vintage watch. There is something especially appealing about this particular Accutron. The cushion case, dramatic fumé color, and ornate numerals capture a moment when futuristic technology and flamboyant 1970s design could happily coexist on the same wrist. And yes, hold it to your ear. More than 50 years later, you can still hear the future humming away. ACCUTRON FACTORY CERTIFIED PRE-OWNED Analog:Shift is proud to be partnered with Accutron as the exclusive retailer for Factory Certified Pre-Owned timepieces. Our longstanding relationship and shared passion for horological history and design have culminated in this unique offering. Each Accutron timepiece undergoes rigorous inspection and certification by expert watchmakers and is backed by the manufacture, ensuring unparalleled authenticity and quality.

title: Vacheron Constantin 'Spillmann Calatrava'
description: The great dress watches of the 1950s often achieved their elegance with remarkably little: beautiful proportions, a superb movement, and a case whose details become more interesting the closer you look. This Vacheron & Constantin is an especially handsome example—and its case adds another important name to the story. Crafted in 18K yellow gold, the 34mm case was made by C.R. Spillmann & Co, the celebrated Geneva casemaker responsible for cases used by some of Switzerland’s most prestigious manufactures. Spillmann is particularly associated with exceptional complicated and waterproof cases for Rolex, and its work for Vacheron Constantin has become a point of considerable interest among vintage collectors. Here, the broad caseband flows into substantial, sharply formed lugs that curve downward around the wrist, giving the watch considerably more presence than its 35mm measurement might suggest. The two tone silvered satin dial is pure mid-century Geneva. Applied rose-gold triangular markers alternate with Arabic numerals at the cardinal positions, while slender matching baton hands indicate the time. A subsidiary seconds register at 6:00 provides just enough interruption to the otherwise beautifully spare composition. The simple rose-gold crown completes the case. Inside is the manually wound Vacheron Constantin Calibre 1001, an exceptionally thin movement perfectly suited to the restrained proportions of a classic dress watch. Between the Spillmann case, beautifully balanced dial architecture, warm rose gold, and hand-wound movement, this is the sort of vintage Vacheron that demonstrates why simplicity at the highest level is anything but simple.

title: Jaeger-LeCoultre Master Control Date 'Sector Dial'
description: There are anniversary watches that celebrate the past by reproducing it, and then there are those that understand what made the past so good in the first place. This Jaeger-LeCoultre Master Control Date belongs firmly in the latter camp. Introduced in 2017 to mark the 25th anniversary of the Master Control collection, this special edition looked to Jaeger-LeCoultre’s mid-century watches for inspiration. Its 39mm stainless steel case is paired with a beautifully restrained two-tone sector dial, combining a silvery central field with a circular brushed outer section divided by crisp black tracks. Oversized Arabic numerals at 6, 9, and 12 give the watch a slightly more casual character, while flashes of blue along the minute track provide an unexpectedly modern accent. The details are especially good. Skeletonized syringe-style hour and minute hands keep the dial open and airy, a slender central seconds hand adds another graphic element, and the framed date aperture at 3:00 is neatly incorporated into the sector layout. The result feels unmistakably vintage-inspired without tipping into reproduction territory. Inside is Jaeger-LeCoultre’s automatic Calibre 899/1, an appropriately refined movement from a manufacture whose reputation was built as much upon movement making as watchmaking. The watch is paired with a leather strap and deployant clasp and is accompanied by its original warranty card from the 2010s. Perhaps the greatest strength of this Master Control is its versatility. The sector dial has enough visual interest to distinguish it from the usual silver-dial dress watch, while the 39mm steel case makes it remarkably easy to wear. It’s a modern Jaeger-LeCoultre with its eyes firmly on the 1950s—and one of the most successful interpretations of the sector-dial revival.

title: IWC Pilot's Watch Chronograph
description: Few modern watches have translated the visual language of the cockpit quite as successfully as IWC’s Pilot’s Watch collection. By the 2010s, the manufacture had distilled decades of aviation-inspired watchmaking into something instantly recognizable: oversized Arabic numerals, stark black-and-white contrast, and instrumentation-style displays that favored function without sacrificing presence. This Pilot’s Watch Chronograph Reference IW377701 is a particularly handsome example. Its 43mm stainless steel case surrounds a matte black dial with luminous Arabic numerals and hands, the signature orientation triangle at 12:00, and three recessed chronograph registers. At 3:00, the day-and-date indication adds one of the watch’s most distinctive details: a vertical triple-date display whose stacked numerals recall the readouts of cockpit instruments and altimeters. Inside is IWC’s automatic Calibre 79320, a robust self-winding chronograph movement offering approximately 44 hours of power reserve. In keeping with the Pilot’s Watch’s functional origins, a soft-iron inner case provides additional protection against magnetic fields. Chronograph pushers flank the oversized crown, reinforcing the purposeful, instrument-like character of the design. This example comes fitted to a black alligator leather strap with a stainless steel pin buckle, a classic combination that nicely balances the substantial proportions of the case. The IW377701 comes from an especially appealing period in modern IWC design, before the Pilot’s Chronograph transitioned into the manufacture’s newer generation of movements and styling. At 43mm, it has the scale one expects from a proper aviation watch, while the monochromatic dial and beautifully organized display keep everything remarkably clean. It’s quintessential modern IWC: functional, handsome, and unmistakably descended from the instruments that inspired it. Wheel’s up!

title: Omega Seamaster Planet Ocean
description: There’s a particular kind of confidence that defined Omega’s dive watches in the early 2000s. Bigger. Bolder. Built like actual equipment. And few references capture that era better than the Omega Seamaster Planet Ocean Ref. 2209.50.00. Introduced as part of the first-generation Planet Ocean collection, the 2209.50.00 took the familiar Seamaster formula and pushed it into more serious territory. The case grew to 42mm, the water resistance jumped to an enormous 600 meters, and the overall design became sharper, cleaner, and unmistakably more purposeful. This wasn’t just a desk diver—it looked ready for saturation duty, whether you ever planned to leave dry land or not. The black dial remains one of Omega’s strongest modern designs: deeply legible, balanced, and free of unnecessary distraction. Broad arrow hands, oversized luminous markers, and the signature helium escape valve at 10 o’clock all reinforce the Planet Ocean’s professional dive credentials. But it’s the orange bezel that gives this reference its personality. Against the monochromatic steel case and black dial, the burst of color feels energetic without tipping into gimmick—a now-iconic detail that has aged exceptionally well. Inside beats the Co-Axial Caliber 2500, one of the movements that marked Omega’s technical turning point in the modern era. Automatic, chronometer-certified, and equipped with a 48-hour power reserve, it brought George Daniels’ Co-Axial escapement technology into everyday production and helped establish Omega’s contemporary identity. Paired with its stainless steel bracelet with diver extension clasp, the entire package wears with reassuring heft and unmistakable presence. This is the moment the Seamaster stopped trying to be elegant—and became undeniably cool instead.

title: Patek Philippe Annual Calendar
description: Some complications are impressive primarily because they are complicated. Patek Philippe’s Annual Calendar is different: it is genuinely useful. Introduced in 2010, the Reference 5205G brought a distinctly modern attitude to a complication Patek Philippe pioneered for the wrist in 1996. This white gold Reference 5205G-010 pairs that mechanical ingenuity with one of the most distinctive dial layouts in the modern Patek catalog. Measuring 40.2mm, the 18K white gold case is defined by its unusual skeletonized lugs, which visually separate the case from the strap and give the watch a lighter, more architectural profile. The two-tone slate grey is equally striking, with applied white gold markers and three beautifully integrated calendar apertures sweeping across its upper half. Day appears at 10:00, date at 12:00, and month at 2:00—a wonderfully intuitive arrangement that can be read almost instantaneously. At 6:00, Patek combines the moon-phase display with a 24-hour indication, adding considerable information without disrupting the dial’s symmetry. Inside is the automatic Calibre 324 S QA LU 24H/206, offering approximately 35 to 45 hours of power reserve. As an annual calendar, the mechanism automatically accounts for months containing 30 or 31 days, requiring manual correction only once each year at the end of February. It’s a wonderful complication put to remarkably practical use. This example is fitted to a signed grey Saffiano leather strap with an 18K white gold Patek Philippe pin buckle. The tonal combination of grey dial, white gold, and textured grey leather gives the watch a particularly contemporary character. Better still, it comes as an exceptional set, accompanied by its inner and outer boxes, Certificate of Origin, papers and pamphlets, original hangtags, and setting tool. Discontinued in 2018, the 5205G-010 represents an especially compelling period of modern Patek Philippe: mechanically sophisticated, slightly unconventional, and exceptionally elegant. Those three calendar apertures alone make it one of the great modern Patek dials.

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava
description: Patek Philippe has long been known for its complicated watchmaking, but following the stock market crash of 1929, fewer clients had the means to purchase these high-end timepieces. After securing a controlling interest in the firm, Jean and Charles Henri Stern decided to create a simple watch that would come in at a lower price point and appeal to the firm’s clientele. Using the principles espoused by the Bauhaus school and its minimalist, function-first philosophy, Patek conceived the Calatrava, taking its name from the Spanish military order established in the 12th century which had become the symbol of Patek Philippe. Since its debut in 1932, the Calatrava has become a byword for a simple, time-only dress watch — even from brands other than Patek itself. This piece, a Reference 6007G-010, isn’t your run-of-the-mill Calatrava. Debuted in 2023 in three individual colorways — red, blue and yellow — this particular Calatrava features an array of automotive-eqsque design cues that easily makes it the sportiest 'Trava in their modern lineup. Housed in a 40mm 18K white gold case, this piece features a polished bezel and case complemented by a sapphire crystal and a signed crown. The black luminous dial features a matching white gold handset and radially configured, luminous, white gold Arabic indices. Straying away from the traditional dressier aesthetics of the Calatrava model, the Patek Philippe design team elected to add sportier design notes with its center dial adorned with a 'carbon' finish and a red accented, checker-style, minute track. Outfitted to a signed black leather strap with a matching 'carbon' embossing, contrast red stitching and a spade-style 18K white gold pin buckle, this piece comes with all of its factory goodies including its inner box, out box, signed leather folio, books and Certificate of Origin dated 2024. Traditional Calatrava aesthetics were thrown out the window on this one — and we're here for it!

title: DOXA Sub 300T Sharkhunter
description: We aren't shy about our love of DOXA here at Analog:Shift. The original inspiration behind Analog:Shift was squarely centered on DOXA! In any flavor, any color, from the classic orange-dialed Professional to the stunning silver-dialed Searambler, we love 'em all. While perhaps not as well-known as the Blancpain Fifty-Fathoms or the Rolex Submariner, the DOXA Sub series played an integral role in the development of the modern diver's watch. The first generation of the model, introduced in 1967, brought innovations we now take for granted — a unidirectional bezel with the US Navy's no-decompression dive timing marks engraved; an expanding bracelet; brightly colored, hi-legibility dials; and an oversized luminous minute hand to name but a few. The DOXA 'Sharkhunter', though perhaps not as famous as its orange-dialed 'Professional' cousin, is among the most versatile of all the Sub colorways. But this is no ordinary vintage Sharkhunter. For avid SCUBA divers, it doesn't get much better than this! Housed in a 43mm cushion case with a unidirectional bezel, a recessed crown, and a mineral crystal that sits flush against the inner bezel’s edge — a tell-tale characteristic of a 300T case — this incredible piece features a matte-black dial with printed hour indices, an oversized minute hand, a 'dwarf' hour hand, and a date window at 3 o’clock. Beautifully patinated luminous material and well preserved printing make help this example stand out from the crowd. Powered by an automatic Swiss-made Caliber 58 movement and paired to its correct stainless steel 'beads-of-rice' bracelet with a DOXA-signed clasp, this Sharkhunter is ready for action. This example comes complete with its factory kit! Jacques Cousteau once said, “We must go and see for ourselves.” Take The Captain's advice and see what this exceptional vintage DOXA is all about!

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava
description: First presented in 1932 with the Reference 96, the Patek Philippe Calatrava is the benchmark for classic men’s dress watches. The groundbreaking reference set the stage for nearly every piece Patek has released since, and became the blueprint for other brand’s approaches to classy men’s timepieces. Heavily influenced by the Bauhaus design philosophy, the Calatrava was then considered extremely modern with its minimalist, less-is-more approach to watch design. The Calatrava 96 was also one of the first pieces the brand released after the Stern family purchased a majority share in Patek Philippe in the early '30s. In many respects, the 96 is emblematic of the Stern family’s contributions to Patek. The 96 was one of the earliest round wristwatches Patek ever made, and was also the very first serially-produced piece to receive its own reference. In the years since 1932, Patek has released dozens of Calatrava references, each with its own idiosyncrasies. Almost all share the underlying DNA of the 96, prioritizing subtle elegance above all else. This piece, a Reference 5227G-010, is the very image of the elegant Calatrava design but in a modern silhouette. With a highly comfortable 39mm 18K white gold case and measuring just 9mm thick, it’s an incredibly easy-wearing watch. The case features downturned lugs, a polished bezel, a sapphire crystal, a signed crown and an officer-style caseback that, when opened, reveals the maison’s Calibre 324 SC self-winding movement. Furnished with applied white gold indices, a ‘dot’ minute track, a matching dauphine handset, and a framed date window at 3 o’clock set against an black tone, the dial is an exercise of simplistic beauty. Outfitted to a signed alligator leather strap with an 18K white gold pin buckle, this piece is an exceptional example of the traditional Calatrava design and the maison’s artisanship. It also happens to come with its factory kit. Simply put, this Calatrava is everything you need in a dress watch, and nothing you don’t!

title: IWC Pilot's Chronograph
description: There is perhaps no more versatile complication than the chronograph. From race cars to rocket ships, boats to battlefields, you are likely to find a chronograph being employed to measure a plethora of tasks and times. From the Greek khrónos (“time”) and gráphō (“to write”), a chronograph is a watch that has the ability to record time, generally via the addition of small sub-counters that register minutes and hours. And what better use for a chronograph than within the confines of a pilot’s watch? IWC makes some of the finest pilot’s watches in the world, with a history stretching back to the early decades of the 20th century. This particular watch, the Pilot’s Chronograph IW377717 , features a 43mm stainless steel case with pump pushers, a signed screw-down crown, a sapphire crystal, IWC's Calibre 79320 automatic-winding chronograph movement with a day and date complication, and an excellent leather strap to match. This piece remains in outstanding, mint condition and comes with its warranty card dated 2019. Handsome, well sized and featuring a knockout movement, it would be tough to argue that this reference 377717 isn’t one of the best values in pilot’s chronographs available today.

title: IWC Portugieser 7 Day Automatic
description: Though the International Watch Company is most often associated with aviation, the manufacturer from Schaffhausen made its reputation with the Portuguese line, now its flagship and an opportunity for the brand to showcase its expertise in manufacturing complicated watches. The Portuguese line had its genesis in the 1930s, shortly before the Second World War. Two clients from Portugal tasked IWC's watchmakers with producing wristwatches that were as accurate as marine chronometers. In those days, the only way of achieving that goal was to take movements from pocket watches and put them in wristwatch cases. IWC used a 74 caliber movement from Hunter as the basis for the new line, christened Portuguese (or Portugieser) after the homeland of the clients who inspired it. Since the Hunter movement was a hefty 37mm alone, the Portuguese required a large case to match, a huge departure from the slim cases that typified wristwatches of the 1930s. In 1993, the brand's 125th anniversary, IWC introduced the Portuguese Reference 5441. Introduced in 2005, the Reference 5001 series (which we offer here), is the modern extension of the iconic Portuguese form. In keeping with its predecessors, the Reference 5001092 is imposing. Though the case is only 42.3mm in diameter the movement (the Calibre 50010, based on the legendary Calibre 5000) as well as the sapphire display case back make it quite substantial on the wrist. Yet this watch is not without touches of elegance (a nod to the ornamentations found on pocket watches in the golden age of railroad chronometers). From the feuille hands to the running seconds at 9 o'clock (not to mention the 7 day power reserve indicator, artfully-arranged on the dial), this watch is meant to be worn and admired. No blushing beauty, it won't slip unobtrusively under a cuff--but would you really want it to?

title: IWC Pilot's Chronograph
description: There is perhaps no more versatile complication than the chronograph. From race cars to rocket ships, boats to battlefields, you are likely to find a chronograph being employed to measure a plethora of tasks and times. From the Greek khrónos (“time”) and gráphō (“to write”), a chronograph is a watch that has the ability to record time, generally via the addition of small sub-counters that register minutes and hours. And what better use for a chronograph than within the confines of a pilot’s watch? IWC makes some of the finest pilot’s watches in the world, with a history stretching back to the early decades of the 20th century. This particular watch, the Pilot’s Chronograph IW377719, features a 43mm stainless steel case with pump pushers, a signed screw-down crown, a sapphire crystal, IWC's Calibre 79320 automatic-winding chronograph movement with a day and date complication, and an excellent multi link matching bracelet. This piece remains in outstanding, mint condition and comes with its warranty card dated 2018. Handsome, well sized and featuring a knockout movement, it would be tough to argue that this reference IW377719 isn’t one of the best values in pilot’s chronographs available today.

title: Omega Seamaster 300 Professional Co-Axial 'Casino Royale'
description: There are few modern dive watches as instantly recognizable as the Omega Seamaster Professional 300M. Introduced in the 1990s, it helped redefine Omega's sporting identity, combining professional diving capability with refined everyday wearability. Its distinctive wave dial, skeletonized hands, scalloped bezel, and helium escape valve have since become hallmarks of one of the most successful dive watch collections ever produced. This particular Seamaster Diver 300M, Ref. 2220.80.00, occupies a special place within that lineage. Introduced in 2006, it accompanied Daniel Craig's debut as James Bond in Casino Royale, marking the beginning of a new era for both the actor and the franchise. While Bond's association certainly added to its appeal, the watch stood on its own merits, representing one of the most technically significant evolutions of the Seamaster Professional. Housed in a 41mm stainless steel case and paired with the collection's signature multi-link bracelet, it retains all of the visual cues collectors love while introducing one of Omega's most important technical advancements: the Co-Axial escapement. At its heart beats the self-winding Omega Calibre 2500, the brand's first widely produced Co-Axial movement. Developed from George Daniels' revolutionary escapement design, it reduced friction within the movement, improving long-term reliability and extending service intervals. As one of the earliest production watches to feature this groundbreaking technology, the Ref. 2220.80.00 represents a pivotal chapter in Omega's modern history. The rich blue wave-pattern dial is paired with a matching unidirectional dive bezel, while oversized luminous hour markers, 'skeletonized' hands, and a date display at three o'clock ensure exceptional legibility in any environment. Protected by a domed sapphire crystal and water-resistant to 300 meters, the watch remains every bit the professional dive instrument its name suggests. Fitted to its original stainless steel bracelet with a foldover clasp and diver's extension, this Seamaster embodies everything that has made the collection a modern classic. Whether appreciated as the watch that introduced Daniel Craig's Bond or simply as one of the finest everyday dive watches Omega has ever produced, the Reference 2220.80.00 continues to strike a rare balance between technical innovation, timeless design, and cinematic history.

title: IWC Portofino
description: The Portofino line has long been an overlooked corner of the IWC catalog. Inspired by classic 1960s models, modern Portofino watches combine tried-and-true characteristics of favorite mid-century timepieces with excellent modern movements, handsome dial designs, and a wide array of strap choices. Their chronographs in particular provide a welcome, dressier alternative to the popular, sportier choices prevalent in today’s market. The particular IWC Portofino we have here is a beautiful contemporary reference. Housed in a 39mm stainless steel case with a sapphire crystal, a signed crown, and a polished bezel, it features a satin black dial with applied indices, a matching ‘feuille’ handset, and a date display at 3 o'clock. Powered by the IWC's Caliber 30110 automatic winding movement, it comes paired to a signed black leather strap with a signed steel deployant clasp. The Portofino line is an excellent option if you are looking for a dressier option from IWC — and if the chronograph isn't your cup of tea, this simpler time & date variant may just be the thing for you. Furthermore, simply swap out the strap for something in a more casual leather, and you've got a piece that make for an easy-wearing everyday experience. Either way, you can’t go wrong!

title: Cartier Roadster
description: Some watches arrive ahead of their time. Introduced at the dawn of the 21st century, the Cartier Roadster broke from the maison's traditional playbook, pairing Cartier's unmistakable elegance with the muscular stance of a modern sports watch. Inspired by the streamlined curves of 1950s European sports cars, its tonneau-shaped case, flowing bracelet, and distinctive magnified date window made it one of the brand's boldest contemporary designs. Long appreciated by collectors, the Roadster enjoyed a remarkable resurgence in 2026, when Cartier reintroduced the collection to widespread acclaim. The revival underscored what enthusiasts had known all along: the Roadster's sculptural design had aged exceptionally well, feeling every bit as fresh today as when it first debuted. This Reference W62025V3 features the collection's versatile 37mm x 44mm stainless steel case, topped by a scratch-resistant sapphire crystal with the Roadster's signature integrated Cyclops magnifier over the date display. The silver sunray dial showcases bold, radial black Roman numerals surrounding an inner railroad minute track, while luminescent blued sword-shaped hands provide excellent legibility in classic Cartier fashion. A reliable automatic winding movement ticks within to ensure everyday wearing convenience. Fitted to its original stainless steel bracelet with double deployant clasp, the Roadster also incorporates Cartier's ingenious quick-change system, allowing the bracelet or strap to be swapped in seconds without tools—a feature that was years ahead of its time and remains one of the collection's defining innovations. The Roadster occupies a unique place within Cartier's storied catalog. Sportier than a Tank, more unconventional than a Santos, yet unmistakably Cartier in every detail, it represents one of the maison's most distinctive modern designs. With the renewed enthusiasm surrounding the collection, there has rarely been a better moment to rediscover one of Cartier's most charismatic creations.

title: Patek Philippe Annual Calendar Moonphase
description: In 1991, the soon-to-be graduates at the Geneva School of Engineering were presented with their final project prior to receiving their diploma — to simplify the perpetual calendar. Although the task was easier said than done, their work led to the inception of the annual calendar complication, patented by Patek Philippe in collaboration with the bright engineering minds at the GSE. Five years later, Patek debuted the Reference 5035, a watch powered by the world’s first-ever annual calendar movement and one that finally bridged the gap between a triple-date function and the formidable quantième perpétuel . This slightly later annual calendar, a Reference 5146J-010 , is housed in a beautifully proportioned 39mm 18K yellow gold case with a sapphire crystal, signed crown, and a smooth, polished bezel. It features a luminous, sunburst anthracite-toned dial with applied indices, recessed subsidiary registers indicating day and month, a moonphase aperture and date window at 6 o'clock, and a matching luminous 'feuille' handset. Powered by Patek Philippe's Calibre 315 self-winding movement, it comes complete with a signed alligator leather strap and its signed 18K yellow gold deployant buckle. This piece packs pedigree, elegance, function and outstanding craftsmanship — exactly what you'd expect from a Patek Philippe!

title: Patek Philippe Tonneau Perpetual Calendar
description: A perpetual calendar is like a small computer on your wrist. Think of it this way: Imagine a watch that keeps track of not only the time, but also the date, the day of the week, and the month, tells you whether it’s a leap year or not, and what the current phase of the moon is. Oh, and one more thing — imagine it does all of this mechanically, using springs and gears, and that you only have to adjust it once every century or so. Crazy, right? Patek Philippe has been making such timepieces since the Second World War, and continues to make some of the most superlative quantieme perpetuelles on the market. This particular example, a Reference 5040P from the 2000s, is a spectacularly elegant model in an offbeat, tonneau-shaped case that remains understated despite its highly complicated nature. Magnifique! Housed in a 35mm platinum case with a signed crown, a sapphire crystal, and a smooth bezel, it features a silver dial with applied, white gold ‘Breguet’ numerals, a matching ‘Breguet’ handset, and an outer ‘railroad’ minute track. Calendar indications include a month and leap-year sundial at 3 o’clock, a date and moonphase aperture at 6 o’clock, and a day and 24-hour sundial at 9 o’clock, all of which is powered by the automatic Patek Philippe Calibre 240 Q. (The magnificent movement architecture, you’ll be delighted to know, is viewable via a transparent sapphire caseback.) Paired to a signed, black alligator leather strap with a signed, platinum deployant clasp, this magnificent QP is a sophisticated masterwork of haute horlogerie — in other words, it’s precisely the type of watch you want from as storied and important a watchmaker as Patek Philippe!

title: Patek Philippe Annual Calendar Moonphase
description: The Annual Calendar is a complication invented by Patek Philippe. While it plays second fiddle to the perpetual calendar in the minds of most collectors, the reality is that the construction of the annual calendar mechanism is equally challenging, and in some cases, requires even more components. Launched in 1996, the Reference 5035 was Patek's first Annual Calendar model and set the bar for all that followed — including those from competitors. This particular example, a Reference 5396/1G-010, is housed in a beautifully proportioned 38.5mm white gold case with a sapphire crystal, a signed crown, and a polished bezel. It features a crisp satin silver dial with applied white gold indices, a matching 'dauphine' handset, date, day of the week, month, and moonphase apertures, and a 24hr indicator at the 6 o'clock position. Powered by Patek Philippe's Caliber 324 S QA LU 24H automatic winding movement, it comes paired to a matching white gold Patek Philippe multi-link 'brick' bracelet with a signed locking clasp. This piece packs pedigree, refinement, function, and outstanding craftsmanship that can only be expected on Patek Philippe. Delightfully, it's also accompanied by its factory goodies including its Certificate of Origin dating to March, 2015. Any old wristwatch can tell the time. Few truly define it.

title: Audemars Piguet Royal Oak 'Yves Klein'
description: A product of the 1970s, a decade brimming with imaginative creativity across all facets of design, the Audemars Piguet Royal Oak pioneered a new category — the ‘luxury sport’ watch. Legend has it that the entire Royal Oak design was sketched by Gérald Genta in a single day! Initially launched in stainless steel in 1972, the RO went on to inspire countless other manufactures and remains relevant to this very day. What's particularly delightful about the design of the Royal Oak is that it works brilliantly in a number of sizes and casing materials, from steel to carbon fiber or solid gold. This example, a Reference 14790ST, features a lovely steel construction with its signature octagonal-shaped case, correct unsigned steel crown, sapphire crystal and comes fitted to the classic integrated, multi-link bracelet equipped with a signed locking deployant clasp. The real star of the show is the dial, made as a rarer alternative branded 'Yves Klein' for its striking blue hued dial. Yves Klein was a famous French designer who used this complexion often in his designs. Coveted among collectors as a particularly rare and desirable configuration, these pieces are collector favorites. The dial remains in exceptional condition showing a light, even patina throughout. Featuring applied indices, a matching handset and a hovering logo at 12 o’clock, the dial is exquisitely simple and beautifully balanced. Powered by an automatic movement, this is a vibe we’ll quite happily keep from the 20th century.

title: Roger Dubuis Hommage Bi-Retrograde Perpetual Calendar
description: There was a brief moment when Roger Dubuis represented the future of traditional watchmaking. Founded in 1995 by the former Patek Philippe watchmaker whose name appears on the dial, the manufacture set out to build complicated wristwatches to the highest standards of Geneva's classical tradition. Before bold skeletonized cases and architectural designs came to define the brand, Roger Dubuis earned its reputation through beautifully proportioned watches like the Hommage collection—pieces whose technical ambition was matched only by the quality of their execution. This Hommage Bi-Retrograde Perpetual Calendar, Reference H37 57710, stands among the finest examples of that early philosophy. Crafted in 18K white gold, the classically sized case frames a striking black dial whose complexity is organized with remarkable clarity. Twin retrograde displays sweep dramatically across the upper and lower halves of the dial, indicating the date and day of the week, while the month, leap-year cycle, moonphase, and perpetual calendar indications are arranged in a layout that feels both technically sophisticated and surprisingly intuitive. The Bulletin d'Observatoire script pays tribute to the great observatory chronometers of the twentieth century, underscoring the collection's deep roots in Genevan watchmaking. Powering the watch is an automatic Roger Dubuis manufacture calibre finished to the exacting standards that defined the brand's formative years. Geneva stripes, beautifully beveled bridges, polished steelwork, and meticulous hand-finishing are all on display through the sapphire caseback, a reminder that these early Roger Dubuis references were conceived as modern haute horlogerie in the purest sense. The watch is fitted to a black alligator leather strap secured by a fascinating signed 18K white gold deployant clasp. An exceptional suite of accessories accompanies the watch: the original inner and outer presentation boxes, Certificate of Origin, period papers and pamphlets, service records, leather travel pouch, hang tags, calendar corrector, the original buckle, and an additional caseback. Complete examples of early Roger Dubuis complicated references are becoming increasingly difficult to source, making this an especially compelling offering. As collectors continue to rediscover the earliest years of Roger Dubuis, watches like the Hommage Bi-Retrograde Perpetual Calendar have emerged as defining references. They represent a unique chapter in modern independent watchmaking—one where traditional Genevan craftsmanship, inventive complications, and uncompromising finishing came together to create some of the most accomplished wristwatches of their generation.

title: Patek Philippe Perpetual Calendar Moonphase Chronograph
description: There are watches that define a category, and then there are watches that define a manufacture. For Patek Philippe, the Reference 3970 belongs firmly in the latter camp. Introduced in 1986 as the successor to the legendary Reference 2499, it carried the maison's perpetual calendar chronograph into the modern era while preserving everything collectors admired about its predecessor. Produced for nearly two decades in relatively limited numbers, the 3970 has become one of the cornerstones of modern Patek Philippe collecting—a reference that seamlessly bridges traditional haute horlogerie and contemporary wearability. This Reference 3970E is crafted in 18K yellow gold and measures a beautifully judged 37mm, a size that remains as refined today as when it debuted. The silver dial is a triumph of organization. Twin apertures display the day and month beneath 12 o'clock, while the leap-year cycle, 24-hour indication, chronograph registers, date, and moonphase are arranged with remarkable clarity despite the extraordinary complexity beneath the surface. Applied faceted hour markers and elegant sword-shaped hands complete a design that feels both technically sophisticated and visually effortless. Powering the watch is Patek Philippe's celebrated manually wound perpetual calendar chronograph calibre, extensively re-engineered from the legendary Lemania base and finished to the uncompromising standards that define the manufacture. Through the sapphire caseback, collectors are rewarded with exquisitely beveled bridges, Geneva stripes, polished steelwork, and impeccable hand-finishing throughout—a movement that remains among the finest ever fitted to a serially produced wristwatch. The watch is fitted to a rich brown leather strap secured by a signed 18K yellow gold Patek Philippe buckle. It is accompanied by its original inner and outer presentation boxes, leather document folio, Certificate of Origin, period pamphlets, and setting tool. Such complete examples have become increasingly difficult to source, adding further appeal to one of the manufacture's most celebrated references. The 3970 occupies a singular place in Patek Philippe's history. For many collectors, it represents the final perpetual calendar chronograph before the manufacture embraced a more contemporary approach to case proportions and movement architecture. Its restrained dimensions, manually wound calibre, and classically balanced dial have only grown more compelling with time. Nearly four decades after its introduction, the Reference 3970 remains not simply one of Patek Philippe's defining creations, but one of the great complicated wristwatches of the modern era.

title: Omega Seamaster Diver 300M 'James Bond 50th Anniversary'
description: Few fictional characters have influenced wristwatch culture as profoundly as James Bond. Since GoldenEye in 1995, Omega's Seamaster has become inseparable from cinema's most famous secret agent, appearing on the wrists of Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig across nearly three decades of films. To celebrate the franchise's golden anniversary in 2012, Omega produced one of the collection's most thoughtfully executed commemorative editions, and not just for 007 superfans. This Seamaster Diver 300M "James Bond 50th Anniversary" transforms the familiar Diver 300M into something uniquely collectible without compromising the watch's everyday appeal. Its glossy black dial is engraved with a repeating diagonal pattern of miniature 007 logos, a detail that only gradually reveals itself as the light shifts across the surface. A single diamond replaces the hour marker at seven o'clock—a subtle reference to Bond's famous agent designation—while the red "50" on the black ceramic dive bezel commemorates half a century of the world's longest-running film franchise. The 36mm stainless steel case retains every hallmark of the modern Seamaster Professional: the signature twisted lyre lugs, helium escape valve at ten o'clock, unidirectional ceramic timing bezel, and robust 300-meter water resistance. Turn the watch over, however, and the celebration continues. Visible through the sapphire caseback is Omega's Co-Axial Calibre 2507, distinguished by a custom rotor shaped like the iconic spiraled gun barrel sequence that has introduced every Bond film since Dr. No. Even the rotor's central hub has been styled to resemble the base of a cartridge, demonstrating just how deeply Omega embraced the theme. The watch remains every bit the professional dive instrument its name suggests. Omega's dual-color Super-LumiNova display uses green illumination for the minute hand and bezel pip. In contrast, the remaining hands and markers glow blue, allowing elapsed dive time to be distinguished instantly in low-light conditions. Presented on its original stainless steel bracelet (w/ divers extension) with a signed deployant clasp, this example is accompanied by its original document folio, warranty card, and period papers and pamphlets. Special editions like this one often rely on obvious branding, but the best examples reward closer inspection. The James Bond 50th Anniversary Seamaster succeeds because every commemorative detail is woven into the design. More than a decade after its introduction, it remains one of the most distinctive and most intelligently executed Bond watches Omega has ever produced.

title: Patek Philippe Neptune
description: The Patek Philippe Nautilus may dominate conversations about the maison's sports watches, but it wasn't the only answer Patek Philippe offered in the 1990s. Introduced in 1996 alongside the Aquanaut, the Neptune represented a different interpretation of the luxury sports watch. Rather than borrowing Gérald Genta's porthole-inspired architecture, the Neptune forged its own identity through a rounded case, sculpted crown guards, a distinctive fluted bezel, and one of the most intricate integrated bracelets Patek Philippe has ever produced. Overshadowed for years by its more famous siblings, it has quietly become one of the manufacture's most intriguing modern references. This Reference 5080/1A features a 36mm stainless steel case with integrated crown guards, a signed crown, sapphire crystal, and the collection's signature fluted bezel. Its black dial strikes a balance between elegance and sportiness, pairing applied quadrant Roman numerals with polished baton markers, luminous feuille hands, a central chemin de fer minute track, and a framed date aperture at three o'clock. Powering the watch is Patek Philippe's self-winding Calibre 315, a movement renowned for its slim profile, reliability, and refined finishing. Completing the package is the beautifully engineered integrated stainless steel bracelet, secured by a signed deployant clasp whose construction is every bit as impressive as the case itself. The Neptune occupies a fascinating chapter in Patek Philippe's history. Produced for only a relatively brief period and never achieving the widespread recognition of the Nautilus or Aquanaut, it has become a favorite among collectors who appreciate the road less traveled. Distinctive, beautifully made, and unmistakably Patek Philippe, the Reference 5080/1A serves as a reminder that some of the manufacture's most rewarding designs have always lived just outside the spotlight.

title: Bulova Accutron 'Mickey Mouse'
description: By the 1970s, Bulova's revolutionary Accutron movement had already proven itself everywhere from aircraft cockpits to NASA instrumentation. Having established its technological credentials, the company was free to have a little fun. This 1974 Bulova Accutron "Mickey Mouse" (dial code N4 - 1974) pairs one of the most innovative electronic movements of the twentieth century with one of the world's most recognizable characters. It's an unlikely combination that works remarkably well. Housed in a distinctive gold-plated asymmetrical case, the dial sits slightly lower within the broad brushed bezel, giving the watch a graphic, almost architectural appearance that feels unmistakably of its era. Of course, the dial steals the show. Mickey Mouse has appeared on countless watches since his debut in the 1930s, but few examples are as charming as this. His outstretched arms serve as the hour and minute hands, while the framed date window at three o'clock is cleverly integrated into the composition. What could have been little more than licensed merchandise instead becomes a wonderfully executed piece of industrial design. Inside beats Bulova's celebrated Accutron Calibre 218 tuning fork movement. Rather than relying on a traditional balance wheel, it uses an electronically driven tuning fork vibrating at 360 hertz to regulate time. The result is the movement's signature smooth sweep of the seconds hand and the unmistakable electronic hum that has fascinated collectors for generations. Completing the package is the signed crown, correctly bearing the Accutron tuning fork emblem. Vintage Mickey Mouse watches have become a collecting category all their own, but few combine genuine horological significance with such playful character. This Accutron represents both worlds at once: a watch powered by one of the most important electronic movements ever produced, wrapped around one of the most enduring icons of popular culture. It's a reminder that some of the most memorable designs are the ones that refuse to take themselves too seriously. Our longstanding relationship and shared passion for horological history and design have culminated in this unique offering. Each Accutron timepiece undergoes rigorous inspection and certification by expert watchmakers and is backed by the manufacture, ensuring unparalleled authenticity and quality.

title: Patek Philippe World Time Ladies 'New York Edition'
description: There’s an infinite amount of romance being able to tell the time anywhere in the world. The advent of transcontinental and transatlantic jet travel made it possible for a person to sip an espresso in the Bar Della Pace in the morning and still make an 8 o’clock reservation at Lutèce that same evening. But nearly a hundred years earlier, to meet the demands prompted by the establishment of railway time in the 1860s, watchmakers such as Hamilton and Elgin developed railroad pocket chronometers that included a third hand to indicate an additional timezone. This set the framework of what was to come. In the 1930s and 1940s, manufactures such as Vacheron Constantin and Patek Philippe produced “world time” pocket watches: Using a special dial layout designed by Louis Cottier, these showed the time across the globe’s different time zones simultaneously. In the 1950s, the advent (and immediacy) of jet travel — and the frequency at which transatlantic and transcontinental flights occurred — made it necessary for travelers to have a wristwatch that could display multiple time zones at once. The Patek Philippe Reference 7130R-012 New York Limited Edition is a modern reimagining of just such a watch. Rendered here in 18K rose gold, it features a 36mm case with a sapphire crystal, a signed crown, a stunning diamond-set bezel, and a sapphire exhibition caseback framing the maison’s self-winding Calibre 240 HU micro-rotor movement. The dial features an outer city disc with blue printing; a bi-color hour ring with silver denoting daytime and a contrasting dark blue tone signifying night; applied rose gold 'dart' indices; a classic Patek Philippe World Time handset; and a stunning inner blue dial displaying a rendering of the New York City skyline. These features function harmoniously with a push of a rectangular pusher positioned at 10 o’clock. Paired with a signed blue alligator leather strap with a signed 18K rose gold deployant buckle, this piece is an accurate representation of the maison's ability to elevate a classic complication. Furthermore, it comes with its factory goodies and signed Certificate of Origin dated November, 2017. There’s a traveler’s watch, and then there’s a traveler’s watch — this 7130R is the latter.

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava
description: First presented in 1932 with the Reference 96, the Patek Philippe Calatrava is the benchmark for classic men’s dress watches. The groundbreaking reference set the stage for nearly every piece Patek has released since, and became the blueprint for other brands’ approaches to classy men’s timepieces. Heavily influenced by the Bauhaus design philosophy, the Calatrava was then considered extremely modern with its minimalist, ‘less is more’ approach to watch design. Over the years, the dressy Calatrava has evolved, but the look remains unmistakable and iconic, and its rich history provides the vintage and pre-owned enthusiast with a variety of choices in metals, sizes, and tiny details to obsess over. This piece, a Reference 6007G, isn’t your run-of-the-mill Calatrava. Having debuted in 2023 in three individual colorways — red, blue and yellow — it features an array of automotive-eqsque design cues that easily makes it the sportiest 'Trava in their modern lineup. Housed in a 40mm 18K white gold case, it boasts a polished bezel and case complemented by a sapphire crystal and a signed crown. The black luminous dial features a matching white gold handset and radially configured, luminous, white gold Arabic indices. Straying away from the traditional dressier aesthetics of the Calatrava model, the Patek Philippe design team elected to add sportier design notes with its center dial adorned with a 'carbon' finish and a red-accented, checker-style minute track. Outfitted to a signed black leather strap with a matching 'carbon' embossing, contrasting red stitching and a spade-style 18K white gold pin buckle, this piece is powered by the Patek Philippe cal. 26-330 S C automatic movement and comes with its Certificate of Origin dated February, 2025 Traditional Calatrava aesthetics were thrown out the window on this one — and we're here for it!

title: Universal Genève Tri-Compax 'Eric Clapton'
description: Eric Clapton's guitar playing is legendary, and his taste in watches is no less distinguished. The bluesman was once the owner of a platinum Patek Philippe perpetual calendar chronograph that sold at Christie's for $12 million, but long before that, photographs taken during his years with Cream captured him wearing another remarkable chronograph — one that would become closely associated with his name. Collectors now refer to the watch — a Universal Genève Tri-Compax — as the "Clapton." The association has helped make the watch one of Universal Genève's most recognizable chronographs, but the Tri-Compax is only one chapter in a history that stretches back to the earliest days of the wristwatch. Founded in Le Locle in 1894, Universal Genève established a reputation for producing high-quality watches and developing its own movements. The acquisition of movement designer and complications specialist Louis-Édouard Berthoud in 1897 further strengthened the company's expertise in complicated watchmaking. By the 1930s, U.G. had introduced the Compax family of chronographs, which quickly earned a following among Europe's watch-buying elite. The Tri-Compax, introduced in the 1940s, was the most elaborate expression of the line. In addition to a chronograph, it combined a full calendar — day, date and month — with a moon-phase display. Despite the amount of information packed onto its dial, the watch is remarkably balanced and legible. Its three chronograph registers sit neatly among applied hour markers and luminous plots, producing a design that is both technically ambitious and unusually restrained. In its early years, the Tri-Compax was offered in precious metals and gold-plated cases, attracting notable wearers including President Harry Truman. Later examples, however, gave the model an entirely different character. Steel cases, sporty proportions, and distinctive "panda" dials transformed the Tri-Compax into one of the era's most compelling chronographs — and ultimately helped secure its place among vintage-watch icons. The most famous of these later watches may be the example associated with Clapton. Introduced in 1967, the so-called "Eric Clapton" Tri-Compax is distinguished by its steel case, 'panda' dial, and external tachymeter scale. Inside is Universal Genève's Caliber 281, a chronograph movement with an integrated calendar mechanism and an important place in the company's history. For Clapton, the watch was simply a striking piece of equipment worn during the height of Cream's fame. For collectors, it has become something more: a tangible link between one of rock's most influential guitarists and one of the great chronographs of the 20th century. This example, with its screw-down caseback, signed crown, pump pushers, clean white dial, black tachymeter bezel, luminous tritium plots, four subdials, dual calendar apertures, and luminous 'baton' handset, features honest wear indicating a life well-loved on its previous owner's wrist. Paired to a signed black alligator leather strap with tone-on-tone stitching and a signed stainless steel pin buckle, this classic hand-wound chronograph is ready to embrace its second life with an enthusiastic new owner. (Just don't imagine that strapping it on will instantly allow you to nail the solo from Crossroads !)
