It is equal parts technical achievement, everyday companion, and elegant dress watch—proof that Patek Philippe’s greatest complications are often those designed not only to impress but to be worn. For collectors seeking one of the manufacture’s most complete modern references, few watches combine innovation, practicality, and refinement as effortlessly as the Annual Calendar Flyback Chronograph.

title: A.Lange & Söhne 1815
description: There are dress watches, and then there are A. Lange & Söhne dress watches. Revived in the early 1990s under the leadership of Walter Lange, the great-grandson of founder Ferdinand Adolph Lange, A. Lange & Söhne quickly reestablished itself as one of the world's premier watchmakers. Rather than chasing trends, the reborn manufacture drew inspiration from its rich Saxon heritage, emphasizing mechanical excellence, restrained design, and a level of finishing that rivaled anything produced in Switzerland. Few collections embody those values more completely than the 1815. Named for the birth year of Ferdinand Adolph Lange himself, the 1815 is a celebration of traditional German watchmaking. Its design draws heavily from historic pocket watches produced in Glashütte during the nineteenth century, combining crisp 'Arabic' numerals, a 'railway-style' minute track, blued steel hands, and a subsidiary seconds display into a layout that feels both timeless and unmistakably Lange. This particular Ref. 206.025 elevates the formula even further. Crafted in platinum, its 35.9mm case possesses a reassuring heft while maintaining the elegant proportions that have made early 1815 references so beloved among collectors. The satin silver dial is beautifully restrained, allowing the black printed numerals, subsidiary seconds register, and blued lance hands to take center stage. Equally noteworthy is its signed platinum beads-of-rice bracelet, a configuration seldom encountered today. Seen primarily on early examples from the mid-1990s and early 2000s, the bracelet lends the watch a distinctly period-correct character while underscoring its status as one of the earliest generations of the modern Lange renaissance. Fluid, substantial, and beautifully integrated, it transforms an already exceptional dress watch into something altogether more uncommon. Turn the watch over and the manually wound Calibre L941.1 reveals itself through the sapphire display back. Featuring the hallmarks of modern Lange watchmaking—including a hand-engraved balance cock, untreated German silver bridges, gold chatons, and blued screws—it remains one of the most beautiful time-only movements ever produced. Produced in small numbers and rarely encountered with its original platinum bracelet, this early 1815 represents Lange at its purest: mechanically exceptional, aesthetically restrained, and built to a standard few manufacturers have ever achieved.

title: Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Offshore 'End of Days'
description: Audemars Piguet, the vaunted manufacture from Les Brassus, wasn't doing so well at the end of the 1960s. Their horological prowess aside, times were changing, customer tastes were evolving, and AP was stuck firmly in a very traditional past. Fortunately for us, their executives recognized this, and bet it all on the launch of an avant-garde timepiece the likes of which the world had never seen. Utilizing the talents of a designer named Gerald Genta, AP planned from the beginning to make their new watch, dubbed the Royal Oak, a contradiction to tradition, and it became the world's first luxury sports watch — made in stainless steel, no less. The gamble paid off: Genta became a household name, and the watch world clamored to get their hands on the Royal Oak’s cutting-edge design, which featured a sharply angled watch with integrated bracelet, micro- tapisserie dial, and ultra-thin movement. In 1993, the Royal Oak line expanded to include the Offshore Chronograph, which has driven the bulk of sales for Audemars in the past few decades. Debatably, the Offshore is responsible for carrying AP into the 21st century and ushering it into the powerhouse position in which it exists today. This particular Royal Oak Offshore was designed for Arnold Schwarzenegger’s devil-fighting, grizzled cop character in the 1999 feature film End of Days , which probably explains its swagger! Housed in a black PVD 42mm case (in fact the very first AP with a black coated case), it utilizes the Jaeger-LeCoultre-based Calibre 2226/2840 movement. Featuring a triple-register chronograph layout with running seconds, 30-minute and 12-hour counters; rounded baton hands; Arabic indices; an outer tachymeter scale; and plenty of lume, it comes paired to its original double-layered fabric strap with Velcro closure. Limited to 500 pieces, this example comes with its inner and outer box set, warranty booklet, and 'birthday' pamphlet. If Y2K were a watch, this would be it!

title: Omega Tank 'Stingray'
description: The 1930s were a remarkable period for watch design. Freed from the constraints of traditional round pocket-watch conversions, manufacturers embraced bold geometric forms, streamlined architecture, and the emerging Art Deco aesthetic. Omega was among the leaders of this movement, producing wristwatches that were every bit as sophisticated as the era's finest automobiles, skyscrapers, and ocean liners. This exceptional Omega dress watch is a striking survivor from that golden age. Crafted in rarely seen 18K yellow gold, the watch is housed within a dramatic "Stingray" case, a style named for its sweeping flared sides that create a sense of movement and visual tension across the wrist. Measuring an impressive 39mm by 26mm, the case possesses extraordinary presence for its era, earning its reputation as a jumbo model while remaining elegant and perfectly proportioned. The unrestored silvered dial is equally captivating. Nearly a century after its creation, it retains remarkable luster and clarity, showcasing a distinctive half-sector design that perfectly captures the precision and graphic sophistication of the Art Deco period. Bold black indices radiate outward from the central chapter ring, while the subsidiary seconds register at six o'clock adds balance and visual depth. The blued steel hands provide a subtle flash of color and reinforce the watch's refined character. What makes watches like this so appealing is their ability to bridge the worlds of horology, architecture, and industrial design. Every surface, angle, and proportion has been carefully considered, resulting in a watch that feels as much like a miniature sculpture as a timekeeping instrument. Today, vintage Omega collectors often focus on the brand's later sports models, but pieces such as this remind us of the manufacture's extraordinary design achievements during the interwar years. Rarely encountered in 18k gold, fitted with a beautifully preserved original dial, and housed in one of Omega's most distinctive case designs, this Stingray represents a wonderful expression of pre-war elegance and craftsmanship.

title: Cartier Baignoire
description: Ladies' watches, unfortunately, don’t get the attention they deserve. At Analog:Shift, we're always down to curate a selection of timepieces that provide equally engaging options for ladies as the more common men’s pieces. No watch better captures this philosophy than the Cartier Baignoire . This example, a Reference WGBA0042-4194 features a beautiful case shape, with its soft curves and oblong ellipse aesthetic. It’s rather unique with its silvered dial finish. This is the high jewelry side of Cartier showing through! This watch is anything but boring, and provides an incredible host of details to obsess over. This piece features an iridescent dial with a stamped hour track that loses the minute track of most of the older variants. The piece is powered by a very period appropriate quartz movement. It is in excellent condition and awaits its next custodian’s wrist. We love a little variety, and it’s pieces like this Cartier Baignoire that'll surely add some spice to any watch collection!

title: Hamilton Odyssee 2001
description: The late 19th and early 20th centuries were without question the golden age of American watchmaking. The implementation of mass production and interchangeable parts assured American supremacy. Brands such as Gruen, Elgin, and Hamilton vied against the Swiss to dominate the watch industry—and Hamilton, in particular, was at the top of its game. In particular, the development of railroad chronometers gave the manufacture a reputation for accuracy and dependability, in an age where those qualities were vital in a watch. But Hamilton’s production did not rest on railroad chronometers alone: throughout the 1920s and 1930s, and on into World War II, Hamilton released a dizzying array of designs. The brand's aesthetics got more adventurous and polarizing through midcentury and into the 1970s. In 1966, Hamilton was asked to create a prop for the iconic film "2001: A Space Odyssey" by Stanley Kubrick. In 1969, Hamilton did a commemorative edition of the model, changing the name on the dial to the French spelling of Odyssey "Odyssee" to avoid copyright issues. This watch took its mission seriously, embracing the futuristic, otherworldly space climate of the movie's subject line and running with it to generate one of the most exciting watch designs to come from the era. In many ways, this piece predated the space craze of cushion case pieces of the 1970s and comes with an exciting story behind it for lovers of film history. Snag this beauty before someone else does!

title: Boucheron 'Clous de Paris' Dress Watch
description: What watch should the Elvis lover buy? We’d wager it would look something like the Boucheron! Manufacturing watches and jewelry in Paris since 1858, Boucheron has always taken an out of the box approach to watch design. This particular piece features an 18K yellow gold rectangular case with a Cloud de Paris vaulted bezel, and a trap that integrates directly into the case. The striking glint of the hobnail bezel is extremely characteristic of the Vegas styling of mid to late century designs. The case is filled with a hobnail dial with minimalist, applique indexes and a simple handset. The entire case and dial follows the same motif and the result is something truly beautiful and unique. Powering this beauty is a manually wound movement shaped to fit the rectangular case. As a whole, this piece has a playful undertone that reminds us of the nostalgia of a bygone era. Set on a more austere lizzard watch strap, and paired with a matching pin buckle, this piece may be bright and striking, but it still features the attention to detail that speaks to the high jewelry piece that it is. The perfect choice for a particular collector— you know who you are!

title: Breguet Classique Perpetual Calender
description: In the world of luxury watches, there’s often a tug of war between price and complication. The more sophisticated, intricate, and elaborate a movement is, the higher up the monetary ladder a watch will climb. Only the most respected high-horology names even venture to attempt the most complicated movements. Today’s watch is an anomaly in this convention. No, this piece isn’t made by a little-known boutique manufacturer — it’s made by Breguet, one of the most revered brands in horological history. No, this piece isn’t a simple time-only dress watch — it’s a perpetual calendar executed in an extra-slim package. And yet, this watch trades for significantly less than many watches with a similar complication. In short, it’s proof positive that if you know where to look, you can still find outsized value in the watch world. A Breguet Classique Perpetual Calendar, its 39mm diameter makes it perfect for contemporary proportions. Housed in an 18K yellow gold case with a stepped bezel, a signed crown, straight lugs, and a sapphire crystal, it features a white guilloché dial with an outer minute track in black, a blued steel ‘Breguet’ handset, a power reserve indicator between 10 and 11 o’clock, a moonphase display between 1 and 2 o’clock, a central month display, a day indicator at 4 o’clock, a date indicator at 6 o’clock, and a leap year indicator at 8 o’clock. Powered by a self-winding micro rotor off center movement, it comes paired to a unique signed, factory-issued alligator leather strap with an 18K yellow gold deployant buckle. If you’re on the hunt for an elegant, complicated calendar watch from a company with several hundred years of watchmaking history, look no further than this beautiful Classique Reference 5327!

title: Cartier Cle de Cartier
description: Ladies' watches , unfortunately, don’t get the attention they deserve. It has seemingly been long assumed that women will be content with shoddily-designed timepieces devoid of soul, providing of course that they are pink and have loads of precious stones set on them. We know this to be nonsense - a lady’s watch shouldn't be any less considered than a man’s, and we seek out examples of watches done right, regardless of intended gender. At Analog:Shift, we are excited to curate a selection of timepieces that provide equally engaging options for ladies as the more common men’s pieces. Take this Cle de Cartier for example. This example, a Reference 3867, features a beautiful cushion case shape, with its soft curves. This watch is anything but boring, and provides an incredible host of details to obsess over. In spite of the unique design, this piece still preserves many of the details of classic Cartier we would hope to see: a Roman numeral and guilloché dial, blued steel hands, petite Cartier logo, blue sapphire crown (in this case, a unique shape), and more all serve as a reminder that this piece is backed by a name with an unrivaled history for fine jewelry making, and yes, watchmaking too. Fantastic. This watch is powered by an automatic winding movement and dates to the 2010s. It is in excellent condition and awaits its next custodian’s wrist!

title: Cartier Baignoire
description: Ladies' watches, unfortunately, don’t get the attention they deserve. It has seemingly been long assumed that women will be content with shoddily-designed timepieces devoid of soul, providing of course that they are pink and have loads of precious stones set on them. We know this to be nonsense — a lady’s watch shouldn't be any less considered than a man’s, and we seek out examples of watches done right, regardless of intended gender. At Analog:Shift HQ, we are excited to curate a selection of timepieces that provide equally engaging options for ladies as the more common men’s pieces. No watch better captures this philosophy than the Cartier Baignoire. This example, a Reference W15045D8-1954 , features a beautiful case shape, with its soft curves and oblong 'ellipse' aesthetic. Paired with a beautiful 18K yellow gold bracelet with an equally distinct link profile, this watch is anything but boring, and provides an incredible host of details to obsess over.It measures in at a comfy 22mm x 31mm and wears a bit broader thanks to the bracelet integration. In spite of the unique design, this piece still preserves many of the details of classic Cartier we would hope to see: a 'Roman' numeral dial, blued steel hands, petite Cartier logo, and more all serve as a reminder that this piece is backed by a name with an unrivaled history for fine jewelry making, and yes, watchmaking too. A Baignoire on a leather strap is a solid choice for any occasion. However, a Baignoire on an integrated bracelet is seemingly more our style!

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava Weekly Calendar
description: There is unusual for Patek Philippe—and then there’s the Reference 5212A-001. At a glance, it reads like a classic Calatrava: clean lines, restrained proportions, and that unmistakable sense of balance that Patek Philippe has spent nearly two centuries perfecting. But look closer, and the 5212A seriousness begins to relax—in the best possible way. Introduced in 2019, this reference brings together a rarely seen complication: the weekly calendar. Alongside the traditional day and date, it tracks the week number, displayed via a central hand against an outer track that corresponds to the months. It’s the kind of function that feels almost academic—until you realize how elegantly it’s been executed. The dial remains airy, legible, and quietly dynamic, a small miracle given the amount of information on display. Then there’s the typography. In a move that feels almost subversive for a brand so rooted in tradition, Patek based the dial text on hand-drawn numerals from the design phase. The result is subtly irregular—each character just slightly different, lending the watch a human touch that’s rare at this level of watchmaking. It’s idiosyncratic, charming, and entirely intentional. Housed in a 40mm stainless steel case—still something of a novelty in Patek’s complicated lineup—the 5212A features stepped lugs, a polished bezel, and a silver opaline dial with blackened gold indices and dauphine hands. Inside, the Caliber 26-330 SC C J SE powers the display with quiet precision, paired to a tan topstitched calfskin strap that leans into its understated personality. This particular Ref. 5212A also includes the original inner and outer boxes, leather folder, and pamphlets. It’s thoughtful. A little eccentric. Deeply considered. Perfectly charming. It proves that even Patek can loosen its tie—just enough to make things interesting.

title: A. Lange & Söhne Lange 1815 Rattrapante Chronograph
description: Born in 1815, Ferdinand Adolph Lange received a rigorous education at the hands of nurses and governesses. At 15 he became a student at the Saxon Technical school in Dresden. Following that, he pursued training under Johann Christian Friedrich Gutkaes, Sr, royal clockmaker to the King of Saxony. In 1846 he and his brother-in-law formed A. Lange & Söhne. Lange’s use of precision tools and instruments allowed the manufacture to attain a level of precision that was heretofore unknown in mass-produced watches. After his death in 1878, his sons Richard and Emil would carry on his legacy. However, the Soviet occupation of East Germany at the end of the Second World War saw an end to A. Lange & Söhne. But after Reunification in the 1990s, the manufacture would make its triumphant return. At the helm of the company would be another Lange, Ferdinand’s great-grandson Walter. The 1815 family honors this watchmaking legacy. Simple and elegant, it’s a careful distillation of Saxon watchmaking and design — adorned with just enough decoration to be beautiful, its otherwise minimalist look mixes Bauhaus principles with classical aesthetics. But this particular watch is no ordinary, run-of-the-mill 1815 — if there is such a thing to begin with! What we have here is a split second chronograph; featuring a 41.2mm 950 platinum case with a sapphire crystal, a signed crown, square pushers, a polished bezel, and a satin silver dial with recessed sub registers, printed black 'Arabic' numerals and a matching blued-steel 'lance' handset. Limited to just 200 examples, this incredible split second piece is powered by the mammoth Calibre L101.2. The stunning movement has over 350 parts, each hand finished, and represents the pinnacle of complicated movement construction. This piece comes fitted to a signed black alligator strap with a matching platinum pin buckle. There’s nothing wrong with a classic dress watch from a member of the “Holy Trinity.” But for a modern stunner, strap on this incredible, classically-inspired chronograph — which is complete with its factory goodies — and feel the awesome horological power of the Lange dynasty!

title: Omega Seamaster 300 Professional 'Goldeneye'
description: "For England, James?" "For England, Alec." James Bond has worn many different watches in film and literature, ranging from Hamilton, Seiko, and even Gruen, to Rolex. But for the modern generation, Omega has been the Bond watch. For Pierce Brosnan's debut as James Bond in Goldeneye, he wore a blue Seamaster Professional. Seeing as Goldeneye is a product of the mid-nineties, the example he wore was quartz. Fortunately the watch nerds in the room, Omega also made this automatic version - featuring the iconic blue wave pattern on the dial that characterized this generation of "Bond Seamasters" and perfectly patinated luminescent material. While ours doesn't come equipped with any special modifications from Q-Branch, it does come with all the hallmarks of a luxurious yet rugged timepiece worthy of the world's favorite secret agent. This piece features a 41mm stainless steel case, the noteworthy 300 meter water resistance rating, and lovely blue dial characteristic of the Reference 2531.80.00. This piece is perfect parts neo vintage and contemporary, giving you the best of both worlds. Whether you drink your Martini's shaken or stirred, this is an essential watch for any Bond enthusiast. ...Walther PPK not included, but this piece does come with its box, warranty card, and hangtags!

title: Bulova Accutron 218 Dress Model
description: Not every revolution announces itself with a bang. Sometimes, it just hums. When Bulova introduced the Accutron in 1960, it fundamentally changed the way a watch could keep time. Instead of relying on a traditional balance wheel, the Accutron employed a tiny electronic tuning fork vibrating at 360 hertz, producing the now-famous soft hum that became its signature. Accurate to within a minute a month, it was one of the most advanced wristwatches of its era and a genuine glimpse into the future. This example is a classic Accutron 218 "Dress" model from the early 1970s, showcasing the clean, modern aesthetic that made the collection so appealing. Housed in a stainless steel asymmetrical case, it features the characteristic crown tucked discreetly at 4 o'clock—a defining feature of the 218 movement family. The silver sunburst dial is wonderfully restrained, punctuated by applied black-accented baton indices, a vivid red seconds hand, and the applied tuning fork emblem at 6 o'clock, a quiet reminder that this is no ordinary mechanical watch. Inside beats the legendary Bulova Calibre 218 tuning fork movement, whose electronically driven mechanism occupies a fascinating chapter between the age of traditional mechanical watchmaking and the arrival of quartz. It remains one of the most innovative movements ever fitted to a wristwatch and, thanks to its distinctive technology, one of the most enjoyable to own. The Spaceview may receive most of the attention, but these standard Accutron models are where the design really shines. Clean, architectural, and unmistakably American, they capture the optimistic spirit of the Space Age without blasting it. More than fifty years later, they remain one of vintage watchmaking's smartest and most affordable technological icons.

title: Omega Seamaster 300 Professional Co-Axial Black Black
description: The Seamaster 300 was Omega's response to the Rolex Submariner upon its introduction in 1957. Featuring a robust steel case with a 300-meter depth rating, a rotating bezel graduated with dive-timing scales, and a metal bracelet with diver's expansion links, the early Seamaster 300 was not only functional a diver that would go on to see use in Her Majesty's Navy, but is arguably some of the handsomest sports watch designs of the past century. As it evolved, the Omega Seamaster 300 went on to see numerous evolutionary changes, with nearly innumerable variants in a variety of materials and colorways produced in the past 60 years. This fact alone has made the Seamaster Professional line (as it came to be known) so desirable to a large portion of the collector community — simply because they don't all look exactly the same . One of the watershed design motifs began in the 1990s with the introduction of blue and black “wave” dials popularized by Pierce Brosnan's 007 in the 1996 Bond film Goldeneye . This design language lives on well after the 90s ended in both modern James Bond-themed limited editions and in the core collection. This particular piece however, is a completely blacked-out, time-only alternative to your traditional steel variant. It features the now-classic twisted-lug case in all-black ceramic sized at 43.5mm with a helium escape valve at 10:00, a scalloped bezel with a matte black ceramic insert, a signed crown, and a luminous black ceramic wave dial with a matching 'skeletonized-sword' handset. Fitted to an excellent signed black rubber strap with a signed, black ceramic pin buckle, this piece is powered by Omega's Calibre 8806 Master Chronometer automatic movement, which can be viewed through its sapphire caseback. True to the first 300 Professional from nearly 30 years prior, it’s a watch that nevertheless possesses "all of the usual refinements," with a tactical, stealthy twist.

title: Bulova Two-Tone Champion
description: The 1970s was a golden age for creative industrial design, with watchmaking being particularly fertile ground for innovation. Oversized cases, bright colors, strange complications — the confluence of the hippie movement with new sporting and leisure activities resulted in specialist timepieces whose fun-loving designs are finding new life today as beloved vintage goods. This particular funky ‘70s timepiece is from beloved American-founded brand Bulova. Housed in a 40mm x 36mm two tone stainless steel electroplated yellow gold geometric case with a brilliant multi-link two tone bracelet with a signed blade clasp, an acrylic crystal, a signed crown, and a softly vaulted flat bezel. It features a cool two tone dial execution with a date function at 3 o'clock. Powered by the automatic Bulova Caliber 11AOACB movement providing a signature sweep second action and a not-so-common for the era quick setting date function with about 40 hours of power reserve, this humble Bulova is a prime example of creative early ‘70s watch design that nevertheless remains moderately inconspicuous. Try it on for size and see what we mean!

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava
description: First presented in 1932 with the Reference 96, the Patek Philippe Calatrava is the benchmark for classic men’s dress watches. The groundbreaking reference set the stage for nearly every piece Patek has released since, and became the blueprint for other brands’ approaches to classy men’s timepieces. Heavily influenced by the Bauhaus design philosophy, the Calatrava was then considered extremely modern with its minimalist, ‘less is more’ approach to watch design. Over the years, the dressy Calatrava has evolved, but the look remains unmistakable and iconic, and its rich history provides the vintage and pre-owned enthusiast with a variety of choices in metals, sizes, and tiny details to obsess over. This particular example, a Reference 3796, is a delight for male collectors seeking a more minimal presence or for a lady who enjoys a beautiful mid-sized, hand-wound watch. Dating to circa the 1990s, it features a perfectly sized 31mm 18K rose gold case with a smooth bezel, a signed crown, and a sapphire crystal. Its silvered dial with applied gold 'wedge' indices, an outer gold 'dot' minute track, a gold 'dauphine' handset, and a subtle sub-seconds display above 6 o'clock is the picture of pared-back style. Powered the manually wound Calibre 215 movement and paired to a red alligator leather strap with a rose gold pin buckle, it truly epitomizes what Patek Philippe is most known for — understated elegance and delicate finishing. This reference is essentially a direct modernized replica of the 96 that made the Calatrava a famous watch. Don't sleep on one of the last-generation Calatrava references with true midcentury looks!

title: Bulova Two-Tone Day Date
description: The 1970s was a golden age for creative industrial design, with watchmaking being particularly fertile ground for innovation. Oversized cases, bright colors, strange complications — the confluence of the hippie movement with new sporting and leisure activities resulted in specialist timepieces whose fun-loving designs are finding new life today as beloved vintage goods. This particular funky ‘70s timepiece is from beloved American-founded brand Bulova. Housed in a 36mm two tone stainless steel cushion case with an integrated multi-link bracelet and a signed blade clasp, an acrylic crystal, a signed crown, and a softly fluted bezel. It features a cool - patterned champagne dial with a framed day date function. Powered by the automatic Bulova Caliber 11BSACB movement providing a signature sweep second action and a not-so-common for the era instant setting date function, this humble Bulova is a prime example of creative ‘70s watch design that nevertheless remains moderately inconspicuous. Try it on for size and see what we mean!

title: A. Lange & Söhne Lange 1 Tourbillon Perpetual Calendar
description: What you’re looking at is a variation of perhaps the most important wristwatch of the last 30 years. The Lange 1 is without question the manufacturer’s flagship model, and the big date function is its hallmark. Though found in watches like the Zeitwerk or the Langematik Sax-O-Mat, it’s in the Lange 1 that it’s shown to the greatest effect. Alongside other details such as asymmetrical sub-dials depicting the hours and sub-seconds, and the A. Lange & Söhne signature with its famous ampersand, it shows a clarity of vision that is wholly Lange. The Lange 1 has seen many variations, and this is perhaps the most impressive. At first glance, instantly recognizable as a Lange 1, this piece also flaunts a perpetual calendar display neatly incorporated to the existing design DNA, and a tourbillon hidden discreetly behind the dial. Sized 42mm in rose gold, this Reference 720.032 is the result of tucking as much complication as possible into the framework of the Lange 1 design language. It's a brilliantly complicated and beautiful movement, and showcases the success of Lange's movement design to preserve the aesthetic of their collections. If you're looking for the most complicated Lange 1 on the market but want to maintain a discreet low profile, this is the perfect watch for you. The tourbillon hides on the caseback, but the opulence and quality of this piece is visible from across the room. A masterpiece of the highest order, this watch is truly something special in all its Teutonic splendor.

title: Cartier Ballon Bleu Diamonds
description: No, it’s not a Tank. And yes, it deserves your attention! While Parisian jeweler to the stars Cartier may be best known in horological circles for its famed Tank watch, the French firm produced — and continues to produce — numerous other models that deserve equal billing for their unique and sumptuous designs. Launched in 2007, the Ballon Bleu is an adventurous take on the Cartier aesthetic — which is of course itself already unique within the greater watchmaking world. Featuring an opulent, round case and a bubble winding crown, the Ballon Bleu provides a captivating housing for the maison’s world famous combination of Arabic numerals and thin sword hands. This particular Ballon Bleu, a decorated automatic variant, comes in with a 36mm, diamond-set stainless steel case with a sapphire crystal, a 'guarded' sapphire cabochon crown, and a crisp silver dial set with 21 brilliant cut diamonds. The bezel is decorated with 54 diamonds. Powered by an automatic movement, it comes paired to an integrated, stainless steel 'H-link' bracelet with a hidden deployant clasp. With everyone clamoring for the Tank and the Santos, why not spring for something more subtle — but certainly no less splendid — in the form of the Ballon Bleu? You won’t regret it!

title: Patek Philippe Complications Chronograph
description: Patek Philippe has long set the standard for complicated watchmaking, producing some of the finest chronographs ever created. From the legendary references of the 1940s and 1950s to today’s in-house masterpieces, the Geneva manufacture has consistently demonstrated that true luxury lies not in excess, but in impeccable design, flawless execution, and mechanical excellence. The Reference 5172G-010 is perhaps the purest expression of that philosophy. Introduced as the evolution of the celebrated 5170, it combines thoroughly modern proportions with unmistakable vintage-inspired details, creating one of the most compelling manually wound chronographs in Patek Philippe’s current collection. Its 41mm 18K white gold case is beautifully proportioned, featuring elegant three-tier stepped lugs, a polished stepped bezel, and tasti tondi (Italian for round pushers) pump pushers that pay homage to the maison’s revered mid-century chronographs. The rose gilt dial is where the 5172G truly comes alive. Applied white gold 'Arabic' numerals with luminous accents, blued steel 'syringe' hands, twin recessed registers, and a tachymeter scale evoke the look and feel of Patek Philippe’s most celebrated vintage references while remaining unmistakably contemporary. Every element has been thoughtfully considered, resulting in a dial that is both remarkably legible and effortlessly elegant. Visible through the sapphire exhibition caseback is the exceptional Caliber CH 29-535 PS, Patek Philippe’s fully in-house, manually wound chronograph movement. Widely regarded as one of the finest traditional chronograph calibers in production, it combines six patented chronograph innovations with exquisite hand-finishing, a classic column-wheel architecture, and the tactile satisfaction that only a manually wound chronograph can provide. Accompanying the watch is a true collector-grade suite of accessories, including its inner and outer presentation boxes, Certificate of Origin, warranty card, warranty booklet, instruction manuals and pamphlets, and the original signed white gold buckle. Among modern Patek Philippe chronographs, the 5172G occupies a particularly special place. It captures everything enthusiasts admire about the manufacture’s golden age—warm dial tones, syringe hands, stepped architecture, and traditional chronograph mechanics—while benefiting from the engineering, reliability, and finishing of a contemporary masterpiece. For collectors seeking a modern Patek that wears like tomorrow’s vintage classic, few references are more complete than the 5172G-010.

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava
description: Few watches define classic dress watch design as completely as the Patek Philippe Calatrava. Introduced in 1932 during one of the most challenging economic periods in modern history, the Calatrava represented a new direction for the Geneva manufacture. Under the stewardship of Jean and Charles Henri Stern, Patek Philippe created a watch guided by the principles of Bauhaus design—clean, functional, and devoid of unnecessary ornamentation. Named after the medieval Order of Calatrava, whose cross remains the maison's emblem, it has since become the benchmark against which virtually every time-only dress watch is measured. This Reference 6119G-001 reinterprets that enduring formula for the modern collector. Crafted in 18K white gold, its 39mm case strikes a contemporary balance while preserving the elegance that has defined the Calatrava for generations. The signature Clous de Paris hobnail bezel adds subtle texture and depth, framing a vertically satin-brushed anthracite dial appointed with applied white gold hour markers, dauphine hands, a subsidiary seconds display at six o'clock, and a crisp railroad minute track. The result is unmistakably Patek Philippe—understated, impeccably proportioned, and effortlessly refined. Visible through the sapphire exhibition caseback is the hand-wound Caliber 30-255 PS, a thoroughly modern movement offering exceptional finishing, outstanding accuracy, and an impressive 65-hour power reserve. The watch is paired with its original black alligator leather strap and signed 18K white gold pin buckle. Completing the package is an exceptional suite of original accessories, including the inner and outer presentation boxes, hang tags, warranty cards, instruction booklets and pamphlets, Certificate of Origin, and the original signed buckle—a true collector-grade full set. More than ninety years after its introduction, the Calatrava remains the purest expression of Patek Philippe's philosophy: timeless design, uncompromising craftsmanship, and mechanical excellence. Few watches are as enduring or as essential as a proper Calatrava.

title: Hamilton 'Sherwood'
description: The late 1930s marked one of Hamilton’s most celebrated periods, when the Lancaster, Pennsylvania manufacturer was producing some of America’s finest Art Deco wristwatches. While the brand had earned its reputation supplying precision railroad timekeepers, it also embraced the era’s modernist aesthetic, creating elegant rectangular dress watches that rivaled anything coming from Switzerland. The Sherwood is a quintessential example. Crafted in solid 14-karat yellow gold, its slender rectangular case is defined by graceful stepped sides and clean architectural lines that capture the sophistication of prewar American design. The silvered dial features applied gold Arabic numerals, blued Art Deco chapter rings, elegant leaf hands, and a beautifully proportioned subsidiary seconds register at six o’clock. Like so many Hamiltons of the era, the Sherwood strikes a remarkable balance between ornamentation and restraint, making it as wearable today as it was nearly ninety years ago. Powering the watch is a hand-wound Hamilton mechanical movement, reflecting the exceptional craftsmanship that made the company one of America’s premier watchmakers. Every detail, from the crisp typography to the finely executed case, speaks to an era when Hamilton was producing watches to the highest standards of American manufacturing. Adding another layer of charm is the engraved caseback, which reads: “J. Horacek Jr. Atlanta 3-31-39” Presentation engravings like this offer a tangible connection to the watch’s original owner, transforming it from a beautiful vintage timepiece into a personal artifact of American history. Whether commemorating a milestone, graduation, anniversary, or professional achievement, these inscriptions tell stories that have traveled alongside the watch for generations. Elegant, historically significant, and unmistakably Art Deco, the Hamilton Sherwood represents the golden age of American watchmaking—a period when Hamilton’s dress watches were every bit as accomplished as the railroad timepieces that made the brand famous. Few vintage watches capture the romance of prewar design quite so effortlessly.

title: Hamilton 'Masonic' Brock
description: By the first half of the 20th century, Hamilton had become synonymous with American precision. From its headquarters in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, the company built its reputation on exceptionally accurate railroad watches before expanding into elegant wristwatches that reflected the optimism and sophistication of the Art Deco era. While Hamilton's railroad chronometers cemented the brand's legacy, its dress watches proved that technical excellence and beautiful design could exist in equal measure. The Brock is a wonderful example of this philosophy. Crafted in 14-karat yellow gold, its slim rectangular case embraces the clean geometry that defined the period while remaining unmistakably American in character. A silvered dial is adorned with applied gold Breguet numerals, a finely detailed railroad minute track, elegant gold hands, and a subsidiary seconds register at six o'clock. The result is a watch that feels both refined and purposeful, balancing decorative flourishes with Hamilton's longstanding commitment to legibility. What truly sets this example apart, however, is its remarkable provenance. The caseback is beautifully engraved: "Presented to J. W. Simpson – 1946 – Doric Lodge No. 132 – Portland, Ore." Accompanying the inscription is the iconic Square and Compasses, the universally recognized emblem of Freemasonry. More than a simple presentation engraving, it transforms this Hamilton into a tangible piece of personal history—one that commemorates a milestone within one of America's oldest fraternal organizations. Watches like this were often presented in recognition of years of service, leadership, or distinguished membership, making each example a one-of-a-kind artifact with a story that extends well beyond the watch itself. Vintage Hamiltons are cherished for their enduring quality and timeless design. However, those bearing such deeply personal engravings offer something rarer still: a direct connection to the individual who first wore them. It is precisely the sort of provenance that reminds us a great vintage watch is more than a machine. It is a witness to a life well lived.

title: Bulova Accutron Canadian Railroad
description: Few watches illustrate the technological optimism of the 1960s and 1970s quite like the Bulova Accutron. Introduced in 1960, the Accutron revolutionized timekeeping with its electronically driven tuning fork movement, offering unprecedented accuracy years before quartz would transform the industry. The unmistakable hum of its movement and perfectly smooth sweeping seconds hand became hallmarks of one of the most important wristwatches of the twentieth century. This exceptional Railroad Approved R.R. 218-0 is among the most distinctive Accutrons produced. Designed to meet the demanding standards of the Canadian railroads, it features a crisp white dial with oversized black Arabic numerals, an inner 24-hour military track, and a date aperture at 3 o'clock. Most notably, the dial replaces the traditional 12 with a bold "0" at the top of the hour—a unique requirement of Canadian railroad specifications that immediately distinguishes this model from its American counterparts. Bold black hands and a vibrant orange sweep seconds hand ensure outstanding legibility at a glance. Inside beats Bulova's celebrated Caliber 218-0 tuning fork movement. Rather than relying on a conventional balance wheel, the movement uses an electronically driven tuning fork vibrating at 360 Hz to power the watch. The result is the signature humming sound and fluid, uninterrupted sweep of the seconds hand that made the Accutron one of the most advanced timepieces of its era. Completing the watch is a vintage gold-tone expansion bracelet fitted with a charming "Stop / Perpetual Calendar" window insert—a wonderfully nostalgic accessory popular throughout the late 1960s and 1970s. Originally designed to hold a miniature sliding paper or metal perpetual calendar, it provided a clever analog reference for the date before the age of digital devices. While collectors often gravitate toward the Spaceview, Railroad Approved Accutrons represent another fascinating chapter in Bulova's history. Purpose-built for professionals whose work demanded precision and reliability, they combine historic significance with unmistakable mid-century industrial design. Add in the period expansion bracelet and perpetual calendar insert, and this example becomes an especially evocative time capsule from one of the most innovative decades in watchmaking.

title: Bulova Accutron Direct Read
description: The 1970s imagined the future differently. It wasn’t round dials and sweeping hands—it was digital displays, integrated bracelets, and bold geometric cases that looked as though they had arrived from tomorrow. Long before LED and LCD watches took over, Bulova pioneered its own vision of the digital age with the remarkable Accutron Direct Read. Produced in 1973, as confirmed by its N3 date code, this striking example features a commanding 42mm gold-plated case with an integrated bracelet and signed deployant clasp. Rather than a conventional dial, the watch displays the time through a horizontal viewing aperture. Hours jump instantaneously while minutes and seconds advance via rotating numbered discs, creating the illusion of a digital display despite being entirely mechanical. The result is one of the most distinctive and conversation-starting time displays of the decade. Powering the watch is Bulova’s ingenious Caliber 2186 Accutron movement, an evolution of the company’s legendary tuning-fork technology. Instead of traditional hands, the movement drives a series of rotating discs that reveal the hours, minutes, and seconds through carefully shaped windows. The system combines the smooth precision of the Accutron with a display unlike anything else on the market at the time, earning the model the nickname of a “Driver’s Watch” thanks to its easily readable, in-line display. The Direct Read perfectly captures an era when watchmakers weren’t afraid to challenge convention. While brands like Hamilton experimented with LEDs and Girard-Perregaux explored quartz, Bulova charted its own path by marrying its revolutionary Accutron technology with one of the most imaginative displays ever fitted to a wristwatch. Today, the Direct Read remains a cult favorite among collectors—not only for its unmistakably futuristic styling, but because it represents one of the last great innovations of the mechanical-electronic age before quartz forever changed the industry.

title: Bulova Skystar World Time
description: Let’s be straight here - we feel like Bulova doesn’t get enough credit. Before the quartz era, Bulova had a reputation like no other. Obsessed with precision, Bulova went above and beyond; they built their own observatories to determine universal time and developed the concept of interchangeable parts to watchmaking. They were also responsible for the Accutron, the worlds first electronic movement, the same movement powered that every other device for NASA's Apollo missions outside the wrist-worn Omega Speedmasters. Even Bulova's advertising was innovative. In 1926, they produced the first radio ad and went on to run the first television commercial in 1941. For decades, America truly ran on Bulova time. Their spotless reputation extended to tool watches, where they produced tough-as-nails pieces for military and civilians alike, including the legendary A-11 and A-17 pilot’s watches in the 40’s and 50’s, and a line of fun and functional chronographs dive watches in the 60’s and 70’s. These models, including the Snorkel and Oceanographer, combined good looks, rugged movements, and Bulova’s cheeky 666 foot depth rating into one badass package. What we have here is something a bit out of the ordinary for Bulova-- a lesser known model that doesn't receive nearly the attention of some of the other more famous lines in Bulova's archive. A Skystar World Time, this model Reference 761 features a classic diver profile with rotating world time bezel affixed atop the white dial display. With a very 70s appropriate cushion case and integrated lugless strap, this model is topped off with a day date functionality. If you're a lover of all things mechanical, perhaps you're a traveler with a bent for the occasional dive, this is the perfect vintage piece for you.

title: Seiko Diver 'Captain Willard'
description: "I love the smell of napalm in the morning." That delightfully morose soundbite isn't the only memorable takeaway from the Vietnam War epic Apocalypse Now . For dive watch enthusiasts, the film holds another: Martin Sheen's use of a Seiko 6105-8119 on screen in his portrayal of Captain Willard. While Hollywood's prominent use of timepieces in film is well documented (and generally done for paid product placement), there are only a few films that really "got it right" in regards to the watches used on screen. The reason Apocalypse Now stands out as a winner? Because the Seiko 6105 truly was a common choice of GIs during the conflict, in a way starting an entire trend for budget-priced, oversized steel tool watches that they would purchase when they returned stateside. As our founder James Lamdin said, "These were big, bold pieces meant for hard use on the wrists by people who knew how to use them." As a diver's tool, the 6105 is a worthy instrument in all regards: Developed by Seiko in the late 1960s, the large case boasted 150 meters of water resistance, a bi-directional bezel for use in dive timing, and copious swathes of luminescent material for visibility in low light and underwater. Utilized extensively by soldiers and frogmen, the 6105 developed a reputation as a no-nonsense timepiece for use in the field, a reputation that has lasted to this day and undoubtedly inspired countless dive watches — including more than a few homage reissues from Seiko itself! — in the subsequent decades. This timepiece, a Reference 6105-8110, was produced alongside the 6105-8000 and features most of the classic hallmarks we adore about the ‘Captain Willard’ — including the characteristic 44mm asymmetric case. The -8000 was designed with a more traditional tonneau case design and slimmer proportions — and is the reason we’ve dubbed it the ‘Skinny Willard’, despite its already substantial 41mm width. This stunning example features an incredibly strong case with factory finishing, a signed crown at 4 o’clock, a Hardlex crystal and a lovely, fully-graduated bezel insert. Its black dial features a set of luminous, applied indices and matching handset with ‘stoplight’ seconds hand. Powered by the venerable Seiko Calibre 6105 automatic movement with date function read via a framed date window at 3 o’clock. As the successor to the 62MAS the 6105-8110 helped establish the design language for the brand’s most iconic dive watches, and is one of the most overlooked Seiko models of the period. We hope you'll scoop this up, wear it with pride, and help change that!

title: Hamilton Khaki Field 'First Edition'
description: You can’t get much more democratic — or more iconic — than a GI field watch. Produced for the U.S. Military beginning in the 1960s, Hamilton’s no-nonsense field watches were built to be issued, worn hard, and replaced without sentiment. They were tools first: matte dials, luminous Arabic numerals, hacking seconds, and cases sized for function over flash. Many were pushed to their limits in real-world conditions, their scars earned honestly. The reference 9219 marks a pivotal moment. It’s widely considered the first civilian-market model to feature the “Khaki” name boldly printed on the dial — effectively the birth of Hamilton’s official Khaki collection. Think of it as a continuation of the military contract, refined for everyday life. The formula remained intact: compact steel case, highly legible dial, and a bombproof manual-wind ETA movement inside. The differences? Additional dial text, a simplified screw caseback, and removable spring bars replacing fixed military bars. In other words, the soul stayed the same. With its sub-$1K accessibility, spartan proportions, and pure utilitarian aesthetic, this is the watch equivalent of a white T-shirt and fatigues — timeless, adaptable, and perpetually in style. Field-tested heritage. Civilian freedom. The original Khaki.

title: Cartier Pasha De Cartier Two-Tone
description: There is more to Cartier than the Tank. Much more. While Parisian jeweler to the stars Cartier may be best known in horological circles for its famed Tank watch, the French firm produced — and continues to produce — numerous other watch models that deserve equal billing for their unique and sumptuous designs. The Pasha is one such silhouette. Launched in 1985, it was supposedly inspired by the lines of a one-off commission from 1932 for the Pasha of Marrakesh that featured a screw-down, waterproof cap over the crown. None other than famed watch designer Gérald Genta was the one who revived the design in the 1980s, launching yet another winning collection for the famed Parisian jeweler and watchmaker. This piece, a Reference W2PA0008 , dates to 2023 and features a 35mm two tone stainless steel and rose gold case with a sapphire crystal; a concave, gold bezel; cabochon blue crown, crown protector; and a stunning silver guilloché dial featuring blue accents and a classic kite handset. Outfitted on a multi-link two tone rose gold and stainless steel bracelet with a hidden deployant clasp, this piece has all the Pasha design hallmarks that have had collectors coming back for more for years. Everyone knows the Tank. This is an opportunity to thoroughly enjoy its equally compelling sibling!

title: Cartier Ballon Bleu
description: No, it’s not a Tank. And yes, it deserves your attention! While Parisian jeweler to the stars Cartier may be best known in horological circles for its famed Tank watch, the French firm produced — and continues to produce — numerous other models that deserve equal billing for their unique and sumptuous designs. Launched in 2007, the Ballon Bleu is an adventurous take on the Cariter aesthetic — which is of course itself already unique within the greater watchmaking world. Featuring an opulent, round case and a ‘bubble’ winding crown, the Ballon Bleu provides a captivating housing for the maison’s world famous combination of Roman numerals and thin blue sword hands. This Ballon Bleu, a Reference W69012Z4 , is housed in a 42mm stainless steel case with a sapphire crystal and a guarded sapphire cabochon crown. It features a silver dial with printed black 'Roman' indices, a blued-steel 'sword' handset, and an inner minute track. Powered by an automatic movement, it comes paired to an integrated multi-link stainless steel bracelet with a deployant. With everyone clamoring for the Tank and the Santos, why not spring for something different — and splendid — in the form of the Ballon Bleu?

title: Patek Philippe Aquanaut
description: The Patek Philippe Aquanaut may be one of the most important modern luxury sport watches on the market. The Reference 5060J, launched in 1996 for the 20th anniversary of the Nautilus, was a sort of transitional watch. Borrowing features from the Nautilus but doing away with the famed case “ears” of that porthole-inspired model and adding lugs, it provided the basis for the Reference 5060A in 1997, the first model actually bearing the Aquanaut name. The Aquanaut would go on to form the basis of a full collection of luxury sports watches that provided the entry point into the Patek Philippe catalog. This piece, a Reference 5167/1A-001, dates to 2009 and features a 40mm stainless steel case with a satin-finished bezel, sapphire crystal, a signed screw-down crown and a water resistance rating up to 120 meters. On the dial you'll find all of the signature Aquanaut features present — offered in an ombre anthracite tone that fades to black towards the edges, 'hobnail' texturing, luminous Arabic indices, a matching luminous handset and a date indicator at 3 o’clock. In excellent condition throughout and fitted to a Patek Philippe signed, integrated rubber strap with steel deployant, this piece is accompanied by its inner and outer box set, paperwork, and its Certificate of Origin. Additionally, it comes with a Patek Philippe, stainless steel bracelet if you're into that sort of thing! With more presence on the wrist compared to its older siblings, the 5167 remains one of most highly-coveted steel sport watches on the market. Try it on and you'll see why!

title: Cartier Tank Francaise
description: What do General Pershing, Muhammed Ali, and Jackie Kennedy all have in common? Entrer Le Tank! It is among the most iconic designs in horological history — the Cartier Tank, transcending the passing fancies of trend and remaining as elegant as it ever was. However, there are many iterations of the famed wristwatch from Cartier, including slightly different takes such as the Tank Francaise. The Tank Francaise retains much of the elegant lines of Louis Cartier’s early-20th century design, with just a few minor changes and the option for a bracelet. This particular example, dates to circa the 2000s and features a 25mm stainless steel case with a matching bracelet, a sapphire crystal, Cartier's signature sapphire cabochon crown, a beautiful crisp white dial with printed 'Roman' indices and matching blued-steel 'sword' handset, a date window and a reliable quartz movement within. The Tank is a long-established classic from the likes of a legendary brand. Why not spring for a more modern version with a twist?

title: Cartier Ballon Bleu
description: Few contemporary watches have become as synonymous with Cartier as the Ballon Bleu. Introduced in 2007, it quickly established itself as one of the maison's modern classics, reimagining Cartier's unmistakable design language through softer curves and fluid proportions. Elegant yet contemporary, the Ballon Bleu proved that Cartier could create a new icon without relying on the angular silhouettes of the Tank or Santos. Its defining feature is the ingenious crown design, in which the signature blue sapphire cabochon appears to float within an integrated protective arch that subtly interrupts the Roman-numeral minute track. Combined with the rounded case and gently domed crystal, the result is a watch that feels sculptural from every angle while remaining unmistakably Cartier. This Ref. W69010Z4 is presented in the collection's highly wearable 28mm stainless steel case, fitted with a scratch-resistant sapphire crystal and the Ballon Bleu's distinctive sapphire cabochon crown. The silver guilloché-style dial showcases Cartier's signature black 'Roman' numerals, blued steel 'sword' hands, and a finely printed chemin de fer minute track, creating a timeless display that has become one of the maison's enduring hallmarks. Powered by a reliable quartz movement, it is fitted to its original integrated stainless steel bracelet with a concealed double-folding clasp, giving the watch the seamless appearance and exceptional comfort that define the Ballon Bleu collection. The Ballon Bleu has become a favorite of royalty (Catherine, Princess of Wales!), actors, and collectors alike for good reason. Graceful without feeling delicate and instantly recognizable without being ostentatious, it represents Cartier at its most modern. For those seeking an everyday luxury watch with enduring style, few contemporary designs have proven as universally appealing.

title: Jaeger-LeCoultre Mini Duoplan
description: We admittedly have a thing for Reversos. Whether classic or contemporary, the Reverso has become a staple in the collections of many men (and women) of discerning taste. That said, the Reverso is far from the only great watch JLC made. This Duoplan is exactly what we mean. Introduced in 1925, the JLC Duoplan movement was revolutionary for the watch industry. It simultaneously was supremely small and thin, and also highly accurate. In a world where these two objectives are often in a tug of war with one another, the Duoplan helped accelerate the advancement of the watchmaking industry as a whole. This particular backwinding Duoplan exploits this mechanical advantage to its fullest. A tiny little dress piece, this 16mm rose gold piece features a lovely patinated salmon dial with Arabic numerals, a two tone dial finish, and blued steel hands for a pop of color. This piece is topped off with petite lugs sticking off the block center case. Tiny on the wrist but mighty in its history, this piece bears an important part of JLC's history and the history of ultra-thin watchmaking in general. As lovers of history, watchmaking, and JLC, this piece is an ideal milestone in the world of horology and we are happy to offer it for sale here in the shop.

title: Jules Jurgensen Diver
description: The history of watchmaking under the Jurgensen name goes all the way back to the 1700s to the family's progenitor, Jorgen Jurgensen, a runaway farm boy who became the apprentice to (and later, the business partner of) a heralded watchmaker in Locle, Switzerland. Jorgen's son, Urban, followed in his father's footsteps, studying below some of the best watchmakers of the era in Switzerland, Paris and London. By the time Jules was born in 1808, the family name was enmeshed with clock and watchmaking. Jules furthered the prestige by designing and achieving patents that became benchmarks of style and function for pocket watches, so much so that they were incorporated into many American pocket watches right through to the late 1800s. The Jurgensen name continued to resonate throughout Europe well into the mid-1900s, despite having been sold to an American company in the late 1930s. By 1960, the brand had lost much of it's production capabilities and were using more Swiss contract parts to produce their timepieces. But what the brand never lost sight of was building unique and interesting timepieces capable of stirring all walks of enthusiasts. This particular piece, likely from the 1970s, caught our eye immediately. Most overt is the incredible 36mm cushion case with wide flanks and a rotating bezel, but the grey dial is really the star of the show. The dial, sporting the storied Jules Jurgensen name, bears an inner chapter ring with beautifully patinaed indices. With the inclusion of a date function at 3:00, this one is a head-turner that is sure to be a pleasure to wear on the regular.

title: Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Quantième Annuel
description: Few watches have shaped modern collecting quite like the Audemars Piguet Royal Oak. When Gérald Genta unveiled its revolutionary octagonal bezel, exposed white gold screws, and integrated bracelet in 1972, the Royal Oak forever changed the notion of what a luxury sports watch could be. More than five decades later, it remains one of the most influential designs in horological history. Among the countless Royal Oak references produced over the years, the Quantième Annuel Ref. 25920 occupies a particularly special place. Introduced in the late 1990s, it remains the only Royal Oak ever equipped with an Annual Calendar complication, making it one of the collection's most distinctive and collectible variants. Designed to automatically distinguish between 30- and 31-day months, the Annual Calendar requires correction just once a year at the end of February, offering a remarkable blend of technical sophistication and everyday practicality. This Reference 25920BA is crafted entirely in 18K yellow gold, with the Royal Oak's iconic 36mm case and integrated bracelet offering proportions that feel both timeless and remarkably contemporary. The warm gold beautifully complements the rich dark blue Grande Tapisserie dial, whose textured surface serves as the backdrop for one of Audemars Piguet's most inventive calendar displays. A centrally mounted red arrow-tipped hand traces the pointer date around the outer chapter ring, while an off-center rotating month register at 6 o'clock introduces an unexpected touch of asymmetry that gives the watch its unmistakable character. Bright white luminous hour markers and hands maintain the Royal Oak's sporting DNA while preserving excellent legibility. Inside beats an Audemars Piguet's self-winding Caliber 2225/2814, a beautifully finished movement that seamlessly integrates the Annual Calendar complication into one of the manufacture's most celebrated collections. The combination of elegant engineering and intuitive usability makes the Reference 25920 one of the most practical and complicated Royal Oaks ever produced. Rare, technically fascinating, and unlike any other Royal Oak ever made, the Ref. 25920BA represents a remarkable chapter in Audemars Piguet's history. For collectors seeking something beyond the familiar perpetual calendars and chronographs, it offers the perfect intersection of Gérald Genta's iconic design, precious-metal craftsmanship, and one of modern watchmaking's most ingenious complications.

title: Patek Philippe Annual Calendar
description: Few complications have had as much influence on modern watchmaking as the Annual Calendar. Introduced by Patek Philippe in 1996, the complication bridged the gap between simple calendar watches and the lofty perpetual calendar, offering remarkable practicality while requiring adjustment just once per year, at the end of February. It was a genuine innovation—one so significant that Patek patented the mechanism and created an entirely new category of complication. The Ref. 5396 traces its lineage directly to that groundbreaking first-generation Ref. 5035, refining the concept into one of the most elegant and enduring Annual Calendars in the manufacture's catalog. Its balanced display, classical proportions, and exceptional legibility have made it a favorite among collectors who appreciate complications designed for everyday use. This Ref. 5396G-011 is housed in a beautifully proportioned 38.5mm white gold case featuring a sapphire crystal, signed crown, and polished bezel. The silver opaline dial is a study in understated sophistication, fitted with applied white gold hour markers, dauphine hands, twin apertures for the day and month, a pointer date display, moonphase indication, and a 24-hour display integrated within the subsidiary register at 6 o'clock. Despite the wealth of information presented, the dial remains remarkably clean and harmonious—a hallmark of Patek Philippe's finest calendar watches. Powering the watch is the automatic Caliber 324 S QA LU 24H, visible through the sapphire caseback and finished to the exacting standards that have defined the manufacture for generations. It is paired with a signed black alligator strap and a matching white gold pin buckle. The beauty of the Annual Calendar lies in its balance. Complex enough to fascinate, practical enough to wear every day, and elegant enough to accompany any occasion, the Ref. 5396 represents Patek Philippe at its most thoughtful—transforming the passage of days, months, and lunar cycles into something both useful and beautiful. Some watches tell time. The best remind us how thoughtfully it passes.

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava
description: First presented in 1932 with the Reference 96, the Patek Philippe Calatrava is the benchmark for classic men’s dress watches. The groundbreaking reference set the stage for nearly every piece Patek has released since, and became the blueprint for other brand’s approaches to classy men’s timepieces. Heavily influenced by the Bauhaus design philosophy, the Calatrava was then considered extremely modern with its minimalist, less-is-more approach to watch design. The Calatrava 96 was also one of the first pieces the brand released after the Stern family purchased a majority share in Patek Philippe in the early 30s. In many respects, the 96 is emblematic of the Stern family’s contributions to Patek. The 96 was one of the earliest round watches Patek ever made, and was also the very first serially produced piece to receive its own reference. In the years since 1932, Patek has released dozens of Calatrava references, each with its own idiosyncrasies. Almost all share the underlying DNA of the 96, prioritizing subtle elegance above all else. This piece, a Reference 5227G-001, is the very image of the elegant Calatrava design, but in a modern silhouette. With a nearly perfect 39mm 18K white gold case and its 9mm case thickness, it’s an incredibly easy-wearing watch. The case features downturned lugs, a polished bezel, a sapphire crystal, a signed crown and an officer-style caseback that when opened, reveals the maison’s Calibre 315 / 190 self-winding movement. Furnished with applied white gold indices, a ‘dot’ minute track, a matching dauphine handset and a framed date window at 3 o’clock set against an ivory tone, the dial is an exercise of simplistic beauty. Outfitted to a signed black alligator leather strap with an 18K white gold pin buckle, this piece is an exceptional example of the traditional Calatrava design and the maison’s artisanship. Simply put, this Calatrava is everything you need, and nothing you don’t.

title: Patek Philippe Annual Calendar Moonphase
description: In 1991, the soon-to-be graduates at the Geneva School of Engineering were presented with their final project prior to receiving their diploma — simplify the perpetual calendar. Although the task was easier said than done, their work led to the inception of the annual calendar complication, patented by Patek in collaboration with the bright engineering minds at the GSE. Five years later, Patek debuted the Reference 5035 which marked the world’s first-ever annual calendar movement and finally bridged the gap between a triple date function and the formidable quantième perpétuel . This piece transports us forward to the present day and is a handsome modern interpretation of the Patek Philippe Complications Annual Calendar. Designated as a Reference 5205R-011, this lovely timepiece features a 40mm 18k rose gold case with sculpted, hollowed lugs, a concave bezel, and polished finish. The brown sector dial features a set of applied rose gold indices and presents a set of day-date-month apertures at 12 o’clock, a subsidiary pointer-date dial with a moon phase display and a ‘dauphine’ handset. This subtle olive green color is one of the most unique on the market, and definitely adds a lovely personality to the right outfit. T he back side features an exhibition back providing a window to admire the self-winding movement and its 21k gold winding rotor adorned with the hallmark Patek Philippe seal . It comes fitted to a signed alligator strap with a matching 18K rose gold pin buckle. This piece is also accompanied by its box set, leather folio, books, and Certificate of Origin. There’s no doubt the Nautilus and Aquanaut have gotten their time in the sun, and even vintage Patek Philippe in general continues to demand the attention of any savvy collector. But let us not pass over the high-complication heavy-hitters hiding in plain sight in Patek’s modern catalog!

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava
description: For a brand so closely associated with tradition, Patek Philippe occasionally produces a watch that reminds us it has one eye firmly on the future. The Calatrava has served as the cornerstone of the Patek Philippe collection since 1932. Created during the economic uncertainty of the Great Depression, it distilled the manufacture's values into their purest form: elegance, restraint, and impeccable proportion. Nearly a century later, it remains the benchmark against which all dress watches are measured. Which is precisely why the Reference 6007G-001 feels so unexpected. Introduced in 2023 as part of a trio of boldly accented Calatravas, the 6007G-001 takes one of watchmaking's most traditional designs and injects it with a dose of contemporary energy. While the case and overall architecture remain unmistakably Calatrava, the details tell a different story—one that feels inspired by performance, precision, and modern design. Housed in a 40mm 18K white gold case, the watch combines polished surfaces and classical proportions with a striking dial unlike anything else in the Calatrava family. The ebony-black center features a carbon-pattern motif, surrounded by a circular satin-brushed outer track that creates depth and visual texture. Bright yellow accents energize the composition, highlighting the minute track, central seconds hand, and applied 'Arabic' numerals. The effect is dynamic without becoming loud—a difficult balance that Patek manages with remarkable confidence. White gold hands and luminous markers ensure excellent legibility, while the sporty dial treatment gives the watch a distinctly contemporary character rarely seen from the Genevan manufacture. Inside beats the automatic Caliber 26-330 S C, visible through the sapphire caseback and finished to the exacting standards collectors expect from Patek Philippe. Traditional craftsmanship remains at the heart of the watch, even as the aesthetics venture into new territory. The watch is fitted to a black calfskin strap embossed with a carbon-style texture and accented by vibrant yellow stitching, secured by a signed 18K white gold pin buckle. Accompanied by its inner and outer boxes, signed leather folio with papers/pamplets and Certificate of Origin, this Reference 6007G-001 represents one of the most distinctive and youthful Calatravas produced in recent years. The Calatrava may have defined the dress watch. The 6007G-010 proves it doesn't have to live in the past, because even icons occasionally benefit from a shot of adrenaline.

title: Cartier Ronde Solo de Cartier
description: While Cartier is forever associated with the Tank, the maison has long understood that true elegance isn't confined to a single shape. For those who appreciate Cartier's unmistakable design language but prefer the timeless appeal of a round watch, the Ronde de Cartier offers a compelling alternative. Drawing inspiration from early 20th-century dress watches, the Ronde distills Cartier's signature aesthetic into its purest form. Roman numerals, blued steel sword hands, a chemin de fer minute track, and the iconic sapphire cabochon crown are all present, proving that a Cartier can be instantly recognizable without its famous rectangular silhouette. This Ronde Solo de Cartier is housed in an elegant 36mm yellow-gold case (with a steel case back) that strikes the perfect balance between dress-watch refinement and everyday versatility. Beneath its sapphire crystal is a satin-silver dial featuring oversized black Roman numerals, an inner railroad-minute track with a discreet 24-hour scale, a date display at 3 o'clock, and Cartier's signature blued-steel hands. Slim, refined, and effortlessly legible, it embodies the restrained sophistication that has defined the maison for more than a century. Powered by a reliable quartz movement, it is paired with a signed black alligator leather strap and a matching yellow gold pin buckle. Accompanied by its original warranty card, this example is ready to be worn and enjoyed. For collectors who appreciate Cartier's rich design heritage but want something beyond the Tank or Santos, the Ronde Solo is one of the maison's quiet successes. Understated, impeccably proportioned, and unmistakably Cartier, it is a watch that feels equally at home beneath a cuff or worn every day.

title: Piaget Oval Onyx 'Belt' Dress Watch
description: Few maisons embraced jewelry and watchmaking as seamlessly as Piaget. During the 1970s and '80s, while much of Swiss watchmaking wrestled with the Quartz Crisis, Piaget charted its own course, creating some of the era's most glamorous and unmistakably sophisticated timepieces. Stone dials, impossibly slim movements, sculptural gold bracelets, and fashion-forward silhouettes became the brand's calling cards, earning Piaget a devoted following among tastemakers such as Elizabeth Taylor, Jackie Kennedy, and Andy Warhol. This elegant Reference 9802 D perfectly captures that golden era. Its polished yellow gold oval case frames a deep black natural onyx dial — a hallmark of Piaget's design language and one of the maison's most enduring signatures. Free of hour markers and distractions, the glossy stone surface allows the faceted yellow gold dauphine hands and discreet Piaget signature to float effortlessly across the dial, creating a study in minimalist luxury. Measuring approximately 27mm, the watch wears with remarkable elegance thanks to its elongated proportions and ultra-thin manually wound movement. A petite cabochon-set crown and a sapphire crystal preserve the refined profile, while the true showpiece is the original black alligator-leather bracelet. Designed like a fine belt, it is punctuated by polished yellow gold oval links that echo the shape of the case itself, blurring the line between wristwatch and jewelry in classic Piaget fashion. The result is less a traditional wristwatch than a wearable piece of design. Chic, understated, and unmistakably French in spirit despite its Swiss origins, it embodies an era when Piaget proved that the most luxurious watches had their own unique personality. They offered up impeccable proportions, extraordinary materials, and effortless style. Vintage Piaget is hotter than hot for collectors drawn to stone dials, back in vogue vintage 80s, or the enduring appeal of jewelry watches. Few pieces capture the maison's aesthetic quite as beautifully as this one.

title: Benrus Type II Class A
description: Few military-issued watches have earned the cult status of the Benrus Type II. Developed to meet the exacting MIL-W-50717 specification issued by the U.S. government in the early 1970s, it was purpose-built for America's most demanding military personnel, including Navy SEALs, Army Special Forces, and other elite units operating in some of the harshest environments imaginable. Following its success supplying field and pilot's watches throughout the Vietnam War, Benrus was selected to manufacture the Type I and Type II—two purpose-built dive watches sharing the same rugged 43mm asymmetrical parkerized steel case, automatic movement, fixed-bar construction, and 1,200-foot depth rating. While the sterile-dial Type I has become the more widely recognized design, the Type II's highly legible Arabic-numeral dial with 24-hour military time offers even greater at-a-glance readability, making it a favorite among service members in the field. Produced in relatively small numbers, the Type II Class A represents the highest military specification assigned to the series. Its matte, non-reflective finish, bidirectional bezel, oversized crown, and uncompromising functionality embody everything a true military tool watch should be. Every design decision served a purpose, with nothing added for decoration and nothing included that wasn't mission critical. Dating to 1976, this example represents one of the last generations of American-made mechanical military watches issued before quartz technology reshaped military procurement. More than fifty years later, the Benrus Type II remains one of the purest expressions of functional watchmaking ever created—a genuine military instrument whose influence can still be seen in modern tool watches today. Scarce, historically significant, and remarkably wearable, it stands among the most desirable vintage military watches available to collectors.

title: Benrus Type 1 MIL SPEC Reissue
description: Military watches occupy a unique place in the history of tool watches. Every detail exists for a reason. There are no polished flourishes, unnecessary complications, or decorative excesses—only clarity, durability, and reliability. Few watches embody that philosophy better than the Benrus Type I. Originally developed in the early 1970s to meet the U.S. military's demanding MIL-W-50717 specification, the Type I was produced for elite military personnel, including special operations units and combat divers. Its sterile dial, asymmetrical bead-blasted case, oversized luminous markers, and highly legible baton hands made it one of the purest expressions of military watch design ever issued. Today, surviving originals are among the most coveted American military watches ever produced. This faithful 2020 Benrus reissue captures the spirit of the original while benefiting from modern manufacturing. Measuring 39.5mm in its signature matte-finished stainless steel case, it retains the instantly recognizable sterile dial, bidirectional timing bezel, and fixed-bar construction that defined the military-issued model. Powered by a modern automatic movement and built to contemporary standards, it offers all the character of the original without the compromises of a fifty-year-old service watch. Produced in November 2020, this example remains in excellent condition and is accompanied by its original canvas travel pouch, additional strap, tags, and factory pamphlets.
