Whether you're drawn to military history, purposeful design, or simply one of the cleanest dive watch aesthetics ever created, the Benrus Type I remains an enduring icon—proof that sometimes the most compelling design is also the most utilitarian.

title: Omega 'Jumbo' Curvex
description: Mid century was a remarkable period for watch design. Freed from the constraints of traditional round pocket-watch conversions, manufacturers embraced bold geometric forms, streamlined architecture, and the emerging Art Deco aesthetic. Omega was among the leaders of this movement, producing wristwatches that were every bit as sophisticated as the era's finest automobiles, skyscrapers, and ocean liners. This exceptional Omega dress watch is a striking survivor from that golden age. Crafted in stainless steel, the watch is housed within a dramatic Curvex curved case, a style named for its sweeping flared sides that create a sense of movement and visual tension across the wrist. Measuring an impressive 22mm x 44mm, the case possesses extraordinary presence for its era, earning its reputation as a jumbo model while remaining elegant and perfectly proportioned. On wrists today, this watch wears very well with its curved profile conforming to even smaller wrists. The beautiful charcoal dial is equally captivating. Nearly a century after its creation, it retains remarkable luster and clarity, showcasing a distinctive sector design that perfectly captures the precision and graphic sophistication of the Art Deco period. Bold gilt indices radiate outward from the central frame, while the subsidiary seconds register at six o'clock adds balance and visual depth. What makes watches like this so appealing is their ability to bridge the worlds of horology, architecture, and industrial design. Every surface, angle, and proportion has been carefully considered, resulting in a watch that feels as much like a miniature sculpture as a timekeeping instrument. Today, vintage Omega collectors often focus on the brand's later sports models, but pieces such as this remind us of the manufacture's extraordinary design achievements during the interwar years. This Curvex represents a wonderful expression of pre-war elegance and craftsmanship.

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava
description: First presented in 1932 with the Reference 96, the Patek Philippe Calatrava is the benchmark for classic men’s dress watches. Though it wouldn't attain the "Calatrava" designation until the 1980s, this groundbreaking reference set the stage for nearly every piece Patek has released since, and became the blueprint for other brands’ approaches to classy men’s timepieces. Heavily influenced by the Bauhaus design philosophy, the Calatrava was then considered extremely modern with its minimalist, ‘less is more’ approach to watch design. Over the years, this dressy collection has evolved, but the look remains unmistakable and iconic, and its rich history provides the vintage and pre-owned enthusiast with a variety of choices in metals, sizes, and tiny details to obsess over. In 1951, for example, Patek Philippe debuted the Reference 2508: A 35mm hand-wound dress watch in a waterproof, screw-down case from Taubert, it's among the most wearable of the vintage Calatrava models — and certainly among the most lovely. With roughly 1,000 pieces produced in yellow gold and far fewer in rose — not to mention just a handful known in stainless steel — it's also incredibly rare. This particular example, a Reference 2508J, dates to the early 1950s. Housed in a 35mm yellow gold case with a correct, unsigned crown, a smooth bezel, and an acrylic crystal, it features a beautifully brushed midcase with clear hallmarks and a 10-sided screw-down caseback. Its silver dial is balanced and lovely: Featuring an outer 1/5th-seconds track, applied yellow gold 'triangle' and 'pyramid' indices, a matching gold 'dauphine' handset, and a blued steel central seconds hand, it boasts the perfect mix of Bauhaus-inspired simplicity and slightly more modern proportions. Inside this exquisitely preserved piece and covered with a dust cover beats the Patek Philippe Calibre 27 SC, a hand-wound movement adjusted to five positions (plus heat, cold, and isochronism) and covered in handsome Geneva striping. Paired to a signed brown alligator-pattern leather strap from Analog:Shift with a signed yellow gold pin buckle, it is, quite frankly, the platonic ideal of a midcentury dress watch. While references such as the 2508 and 2509 long flew under the radar, the market is finally catching up and realizing just how special these watches truly are. Once you strap this incredible example to your wrist, you're bound to come to the same realization.

title: Patek Philippe Gondolo
description: Not every timepiece from the world’s greatest watchmaker fits neatly into the mold of an overarching theme or collection. While we love a simple Calatrava, a sporty Aquanaut, or a complicated perpetual calendar as much as the next guy, the oddball, more overlooked and usually limited-production shaped watches made by the maison in second half of the 20th century are often some of the most innovative and charming in the brand’s oeuvre . The Gondolo collection in particular has an interesting history rooted, not in Geneva, but Rio de Janeiro. Patek enjoyed a fruitful partnership with the Brazilian retailer, Gondolo & Labouriau, for almost 60 years — from that, the Gondolo collection was born. Veering away from the traditional aesthetics of round-cased watches, the Gondolo contains a wide variety of complications in tonneau-shaped cases that explore a more adventurous side of Patek Phillipe’s watchmaking. Take this ladies’ Gondolo ref. 4866/1J-001 , for example. Housed in a 25mm square 18K yellow gold case with a sapphire crystal and a signed crown, it features a beautiful black dial with Roman cardinal indexes, and a simply marvelous multi link yellow gold bracelet integrating directly into the watch at the lugs. The profile continues up into the multi stepped bezel with rounded scrolled motif set into its surface. Powered by the Patek Philippe Calibre E-15 quartz movement, this stunning, no-fuss Patek Philippe Gondolo is the perfect dress watch companion for an elegant, formal evening. Once you see it in person, we know you won’t be able to resist its charms!

title: Vacheron Constantin Overseas
description: The Holy Trinity of watch brands: Rolex, Patek Philippe, and Vacheron Constantin. Far less understood than either of its respected compatriots, Vacheron Constantin has a legacy of producing some of the very finest high horology complications in history — and some of the loveliest. Sports watches came later to VC, as pressure from the new 'luxury sports watch' category introduced in the early 1970s forced the storied brand to evolve. Its entry arrived in the form of the Reference 222, whose design language would form the inspiration for the current Overseas collection. The Overseas — which competes with other watches such as the Patek Philippe Nautilus, Audemars Piguet Royal Oak, IWC Ingenieur, and Piaget Polo in the 'luxury sports watch' category — often finds itself favored by collectors who value a certain je ne sais quoi in their watches. After all, this is one of few 1970s icons not designed by the famed Gérald Genta! This particular example, an Overseas Reference 42040J, is sized at 37mm — the perfect diameter for a wide range of wrist sizes. Dating to the late 1990s, this early execution features an 18k yellow gold case with an integrated-style bracelet, a notched bezel, a date complication, and a beautiful silver guilloché 'sigma' dial with applied 'wedge' indices, luminous tritium plots, and a luminous 'sword' handset. Powered by the Vacheron Constantin Calibre 1310 automatic movement — a highly modified version of the Girard-Perregaux Caliber 3100 that measures roughly 3mm thick — the Ref. 42040J is wondrously slim, clocking in at just 8.5mm. Elegant and emblematic of neo-vintage 1990s design codes, it's an ideal city-slicking watch for the discerning collector.

title: A. Lange & Söhne Saxonia Automatic
description: A. Lange & Söhne has always approached watchmaking differently. From Ferdinand Adolph Lange’s early pursuit of precision in 19th-century Glashütte to the brand’s remarkable revival in the 1990s under Walter Lange, the manufacture has consistently balanced technical rigor with an unmistakable sense of refinement. Today, Lange sits in rarefied territory — equally admired for its engineering and its design language. While collectors often gravitate toward icons like the Lange 1 or Datograph, there’s something particularly compelling about the quieter corners of the catalog — and particularly, that occupied by the Saxonia. Introduced as a study in restraint, the Saxonia strips away excess and focuses on proportion, finishing, and balance. This ladies' Reference 840.032 from the 2010s takes that philosophy and softens it with just the right amount of luminosity. Housed in a 37mm 18K rose gold case, it wears with remarkable elegance thanks to its slim profile and gently curved lugs. The diamond-set bezel — featuring 68 brilliant-cut stones — adds brilliance without overwhelming the design, framing a luminous white mother-of-pearl dial that shifts beautifully in changing light. Applied pink gold indices and slender alpha hands maintain the clean architectural clarity that Lange does so well, while the restrained dial layout keeps the focus exactly where it should be: on material, proportion, and finish. Turn the watch over, and the self-winding Caliber L086.4 reminds you this is still very much a Lange product. Glashütte striping, gold chatons , blued screws, and a three-quarter plate are all present and accounted for, delivering 72 hours of power reserve with unmistakable Saxon precision. Paired with a signed burgundy alligator strap with a signed rose gold pin buckle, this Saxonia is proof that understatement, when executed at this level, can be utterly captivating.

title: Gerald Genta Octagonal 'Donald Duck'
description: Gerald Genta. If you have explored this hobby long enough to find yourself here, browsing our website, chances are you have come across his name. Perhaps the only watch designer known by name to more than a handful of horological scholars, Gerald Genta's most groundbreaking and iconic designs need no introduction... Moreover, cartoon watches have a special place in the watch world. What started in the early 1930s as something of a marketing ploy, has evolved into a staple of the industry - from $20 quartz pieces and beyond... The watch that we have here combines two great names in the watch and pop culture worlds. Gerald Genta and Donald Duck. With a stylized 18K yellow gold and stainless steel octagonal case, this watch has a seemingly endless number of interesting features, including a octagonal faceted sapphire crystal, a 'Mother of Pearl" dial, "T-bar" lugs with a pale blue alligator strap, and everyone's favorite duck front and center with his hands to tell the time. This watch checks all the boxes for an interesting, off the beaten path watch and all at an accessible price point!

title: Patek Philippe Annual Calendar
description: In 1991, the soon-to-be graduates at the Geneva School of Engineering were presented with their final project prior to receiving their diploma — simplify the perpetual calendar. Although the task was easier said than done, their work led to the inception of the annual calendar complication, patented by Patek in collaboration with the bright engineering minds at the GSE. Five years later, Patek debuted the Reference 5035 which marked the world’s first-ever annual calendar movement and finally bridged the gap between a triple date function and the formidable quantième perpétuel . This piece transports us forward to the present day and is a handsome modern interpretation of the Patek Philippe Complications Annual Calendar. Designated as a Reference 5205R-010 , this lovely timepiece features a 40mm 18K rose gold case with sculpted, hollowed lugs, a concave bezel, and polished finish. The black 'sector' dial features a set of applied rose gold indices and presents a set of day-date-month apertures at 12 o’clock, a subsidiary pointer-date dial with a moon phase display and a ‘dauphine’ handset. This dial color is one of the most striking combinations with the case on the market, and definitely adds a lovely personality to the right outfit. T he back side of the piece features an exhibition back providing a window to admire the self-winding Calibre 324 movement and its 21K gold winding rotor adorned with the hallmark Patek Philippe seal . It comes fitted to a signed alligator strap with a matching 18K rose gold pin buckle. This piece is also accompanied by its box set, leather folio, and even hangtags. There’s no doubt the Nautilus and Aquanaut have gotten their time in the sun, and even vintage Patek Philippe in general continues to demand the attention of any savvy collector. But let us not pass over the high-complication heavy-hitters hiding in plain sight in Patek’s modern catalog!

title: Franck Muller Cintrée Curvex Color Dreams
description: In the world of haute horlogerie , where time is not just measured, but celebrated , Franck Muller stands as an overlooked luminary. Established in 1991, the brand's vision was clear: to create timepieces that transcend the mundane, leaning on expressions of individuality and above all, elevating timekeeping to an art form. Franck Muller is renowned for its vibrant and visually captivating dials. The Color Dreams collection, for instance, showcases an array of bright hues, with each dial resembling a miniature canvas where said colors dance harmoniously. Each watch exudes an avant garde design language that balances the classical and the whimsical , bringing a much-needed, playful approach to modern horology. This particular Franck Muller Cintrée Curvex Reference 1750 S6, dating to the early 2000s, is a standout example of the firm's adaption of its signature silhouette to ladies' wrists. Measuring 25mm x 35mm in a white gold tonneau case, it features a curved sapphire crystal, a signed crown, and an absolutely wild, deep blue guilloche dial with stylized 'shadow' indices, multi-colored, stylized 'Arabic' indices, a feuillie handset, and a sub-seconds display above 6 o'clock. Powered by a hand-wound and highly decorated version of the ETA/Peseux Calibre 7001, it comes fitted to one of our Saffiano leather straps with a signed white gold pin buckle. Though the brand's early-2000s heyday may have passed, its wares from that era remain incredibly compelling — not to mention excellent bargains. For someone on the hunt for a fun and funky everyday watch, this Reference 1750 S6 presents the perfect option.

title: Breguet Classique Complications Tourbillon Perpetual Calendar
description: The impact of 18th/19th-century watchmaker Abraham-Louis Breguet upon the watch industry is difficult to encapsulate in just a handful of sentences — developer of the tourbillon as well as the souscription business model, his name is associated with countless innovations that reverberate throughout the horological world to this day. Though modern wristwatches are somewhat far removed from Breguet's original pocket watches fit for royalty, the French-Swiss master craftsman's design language endures in references such as the 3755PR/1E/9V6, a perpetual calendar with a tourbillon and a skeletonized dial. Housed within the marque's Classique Complications sub-collection, it's quite simply an astounding feat of horology. Launched at Baselworld 2005, the 3755PR/1E/9V6 represents the creative apotheosis of early Swatch Group-era Breguet, with the Hayeks intent on conveying A.L. Breguet's importance through inspired use of the tourbillon. Housed in a 40mm platinum case, this example features the coin-edge caseband found in many Breguet references combined with a smooth bezel, signed crown, and sapphire crystal. The dial's use of ample negative space makes it easy to view the rose gold, hand-wound Calibre 558QPSQ beneath. An incredibly complicated movement, the 558QPSQ includes not only main time-telling functionality, but also a one-minute tourbillon and a perpetual calendar with retrograde date function. Hand-skeletonized and engraved, the 3755PR/1E/9V6 was produced in extremely limited numbers. That this example comes not only with its correct black alligator strap with platinum deployant clasp — but also its inner and outer boxes, papers and pamphlets, and certificate of origin dating to 2008 — makes it a highly rare bird, indeed. For dedicated Breguet collectors or for those who simply value complicated watchmaking at its finest, this is a piece that's difficult to top.

title: Vacheron Constantin Overseas
description: When Vacheron Constantin introduced the Overseas in 1996, it marked a new chapter for one of watchmaking's oldest manufactures. Designed by Jörg Hysek, the collection drew subtle inspiration from the brand's Maltese Cross emblem while embracing the growing demand for refined luxury sports watches. Rather than imitating its contemporaries, the Overseas established its own identity through sculptural casework, an integrated bracelet, and the understated elegance that has long defined Vacheron Constantin. This particular Reference 42050J represents one of the earliest expressions of that vision. Crafted entirely in 18K yellow gold, the 35mm case offers proportions that feel remarkably current, while the integrated bracelet flows seamlessly into the case, creating a design that wears as a single, cohesive piece. The distinctive notched bezel, inspired by the Maltese Cross, lends the watch its unmistakable character without overpowering its clean lines. The rich blue dial provides a striking contrast against the warmth of the yellow gold. Applied gold hour markers and matching hands maintain exceptional legibility, while the framed date aperture at three o'clock introduces a welcome touch of practicality. The dial is refreshingly restrained, allowing its vibrant color and elegant proportions to speak for themselves. Powering the watch is Vacheron Constantin's automatic Calibre 1310, a reliable self-winding movement that perfectly complements the Overseas' philosophy of everyday luxury. Completing the package is the original 18K yellow gold bracelet with its signed double deployant clasp, one of the defining elements of the collection and a testament to Vacheron Constantin's attention to detail. Produced during the inaugural years of the Overseas collection, the Ref. 42050 occupies an important place in the model's history. It captures a moment when Vacheron Constantin reimagined the luxury sports watch through its own distinctly Genevan lens, creating a design that remains elegant, wearable, and increasingly collectible. For enthusiasts seeking an early Overseas in full yellow gold, few references capture the spirit of the collection more beautifully.

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava
description: For a brand so closely associated with tradition, Patek Philippe occasionally reminds us that it knows how to have a little fun. The Calatrava has been the foundation of the Patek Philippe collection since 1932. Conceived during the Great Depression as a simpler, more accessible alternative to the manufacture's complicated watches, it became the definitive expression of the dress watch. Guided by Bauhaus principles and a philosophy of functional elegance, the Calatrava established a design language that continues to influence watchmaking nearly a century later. Which is precisely why the Reference 6007G-011 is so intriguing. While unmistakably a Calatrava, this modern interpretation pushes the collection into unfamiliar territory. Introduced in 2023 alongside sister references featuring red and yellow accents, the 6007G-011 brings a distinctly contemporary energy to one of watchmaking's most traditional canvases. The result is arguably the sportiest Calatrava in the current catalog. Housed in a 40mm 18K white gold case, the watch pairs its polished surfaces and classic round profile with a surprisingly dynamic dial. The black ebony-toned center features a carbon-pattern motif that contrasts against a circular satin-brushed outer track, while electric blue accents animate the minute scale, seconds hand, and applied 'Arabic' numerals. White gold markers and hands filled with luminous material provide exceptional legibility, lending the watch an almost instrument-like character. Inside beats the automatic Caliber 26-330 S C, visible through the sapphire caseback and finished to the exacting standards one expects from Patek Philippe. While the movement remains thoroughly traditional, the watch surrounding it feels refreshingly contemporary. Fitted to a black calfskin strap embossed with a carbon-style texture and accented by blue stitching, the package is completed by an 18K white gold pin buckle. Accompanied by its inner and outer boxes, signed leather folio, books, and Certificate of Origin, this example offers the full ownership experience. The Calatrava may have started life as the ultimate dress watch. The 6007G-011 proves it can still surprise us. This reference is what happens when Patek Philippe loosens its tie, but never compromises its standards.

title: Patek Philippe Tonneau Perpetual Calendar
description: Some watches define a complication. Others redefine the watch itself. For decades, the Reference 3940 has stood as Patek Philippe's quintessential perpetual calendar, a masterpiece of proportion and mechanical elegance that helped usher traditional Swiss watchmaking into the modern era. Introduced during the height of the Quartz Crisis in 1985, it demonstrated that craftsmanship, innovation, and timeless design still had a place in haute horlogerie . The Ref. 5940, introduced a generation later, took that celebrated formula in a bold new direction. Rather than housing its legendary perpetual calendar movement in a traditional round case, Patek Philippe opted for a softly curved tonneau-shaped case that recalls the elegant shapes of Art Deco watches. Crafted in 18k yellow gold, the 5940J possesses a wonderfully architectural presence on the wrist, offering a distinctive alternative to its round-cased sibling while retaining every bit of its mechanical pedigree. The silver-white dial is unmistakably Patek Philippe. Applied Breguet numerals lend warmth and character, while the beautifully balanced perpetual calendar displays the day, month, leap year, date, and moonphase with exceptional clarity. Despite the immense amount of information on display, the dial never feels crowded, a testament to Patek Philippe's unparalleled talent for visual restraint. Beneath the solid gold case beats the legendary self-winding Calibre 240 Q. Powered by an off-center 22K gold micro-rotor, the movement remains one of the finest automatic perpetual calendar calibres ever produced. Slim, elegant, and exquisitely finished, it perfectly complements the refined proportions of the watch while showcasing the level of craftsmanship that has defined Patek Philippe for generations. Paired with a brown alligator leather strap and crafted as a true Grand Complication, the Ref. 5940J occupies a fascinating place within the modern Patek Philippe catalog. It offers all of the technical brilliance of the celebrated Ref. 3940, wrapped in a case that is more distinctive, more architectural, and arguably even more elegant. For collectors who appreciate perpetual calendars but seek something beyond the expected, the 5940 remains one of Patek Philippe's most compelling modern creations. Sophisticated without being ostentatious, familiar yet refreshingly uncommon, it is a watch that quietly rewards those who know exactly what they're looking at.

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava
description: For a brand so closely associated with tradition, Patek Philippe occasionally produces a watch that reminds us it has one eye firmly on the future. The Calatrava has served as the cornerstone of the Patek Philippe collection since 1932. Created during the economic uncertainty of the Great Depression, it distilled the manufacture's values into their purest form: elegance, restraint, and impeccable proportion. Nearly a century later, it remains the benchmark against which all dress watches are measured. Which is precisely why the Reference 6007G-001 feels so unexpected. Introduced in 2023 as part of a trio of boldly accented Calatravas, the 6007G-001 takes one of watchmaking's most traditional designs and injects it with a dose of contemporary energy. While the case and overall architecture remain unmistakably Calatrava, the details tell a different story—one that feels inspired by performance, precision, and modern design. Housed in a 40mm 18K white gold case, the watch combines polished surfaces and classical proportions with a striking dial unlike anything else in the Calatrava family. The ebony-black center features a carbon-pattern motif, surrounded by a circular satin-brushed outer track that creates depth and visual texture. Bright yellow accents energize the composition, highlighting the minute track, central seconds hand, and applied 'Arabic' numerals. The effect is dynamic without becoming loud—a difficult balance that Patek manages with remarkable confidence. White gold hands and luminous markers ensure excellent legibility, while the sporty dial treatment gives the watch a distinctly contemporary character rarely seen from the Genevan manufacture. Inside beats the automatic Caliber 26-330 S C, visible through the sapphire caseback and finished to the exacting standards collectors expect from Patek Philippe. Traditional craftsmanship remains at the heart of the watch, even as the aesthetics venture into new territory. The watch is fitted to a black calfskin strap embossed with a carbon-style texture and accented by vibrant yellow stitching, secured by a signed 18K white gold pin buckle. Accompanied by its signed leather folio and Certificate of Origin, this Reference 6007G-001 represents one of the most distinctive and youthful Calatravas produced in recent years. The Calatrava may have defined the dress watch. The 6007G-010 proves it doesn't have to live in the past, because even icons occasionally benefit from a shot of adrenaline.

title: Patek Philippe Chronograph
description: Patek Philippe has sat atop the horological mountain for going on two centuries, having earned near-universal acclaim for their proficiencies in designing, engineering, and manufacturing some of the most exquisite timepieces the world has ever seen. The celebrated maison has a tradition of creating watches that transcend generations. Leaning on the pillars of timeless design, refinement, and mechanical ingenuity, there’s arguably no other manufacture that does it better. One of the most legendary of complications for Patek Philippe is the chronograph. Manually wound chronographs are some of the most difficult to produce properly. After the discontinuation of the 1463 in the mid 20th century, Patek had no dedicated manually wound chronograph in the collections. Then, in 1998, the brand presented the reference 5070. Modern in proportions at 42mm, and utilizing a much smaller movement (a buildout of the Lemania 2310), Patek filled the extra dial space with added scales around the perimeter of the broad dial. The 5070 was bold in its proportions, and the market didn’t initially fall for it. Over time, however, the small production numbers, and perfect sizing by modern standards allowed the watch to go on to enjoy one of the most legendary collecting statuses in the neo-vintage Patek marketplace. This particular 5070 is the beautiful rose gold iteration, bearing a gray/ silver dial with matching rose gold indexes, and tone on tone hands for added legibility. This iteration was produced for about 4 years from 2003-2007. A true collector’s gem, for lovers of collectible Patek, this is a holy grail.

title: Patek Philippe Chronograph
description: Patek Philippe has sat atop the horological mountain for going on two centuries, having earned near-universal acclaim for their proficiencies in designing, engineering, and manufacturing some of the most exquisite timepieces the world has ever seen. The celebrated maison has a tradition of creating watches that transcend generations. Leaning on the pillars of timeless design, refinement, and mechanical ingenuity, there’s arguably no other manufacture that does it better. One of the most legendary of complications for Patek Philippe is the chronograph. Manually wound chronographs are some of the most difficult to produce properly. After the discontinuation of the 1463 in the mid 20th century, Patek had no dedicated manually wound chronograph in the collections. Then, in 1998, the brand presented the reference 5070. Modern in proportions at 42mm, and utilizing a much smaller movement (a buildout of the Lemania 2310), Patek filled the extra dial space with added scales around the perimeter of the broad dial. The 5070 was bold in its proportions, and the market didn’t initially fall for it. Over time, however, the small production numbers, and perfect sizing by modern standards allowed the watch to go on to enjoy one of the most legendary collecting statuses in the neo-vintage Patek marketplace. This particular 5070 is the beautiful white gold iteration, bearing a silver dial with blackened indexes, and hands for added legibility. This iteration was produced for about 6 years from 2001-2007. A true collector’s gem, for lovers of collectible Patek, this is a holy grail.

title: Patek Philippe Chronograph
description: Patek Philippe has sat atop the horological mountain for going on two centuries, having earned near-universal acclaim for their proficiencies in designing, engineering, and manufacturing some of the most exquisite timepieces the world has ever seen. The celebrated maison has a tradition of creating watches that transcend generations. Leaning on the pillars of timeless design, refinement, and mechanical ingenuity, there’s arguably no other manufacture that does it better. One of the most legendary of complications for Patek Philippe is the chronograph. Manually wound chronographs are some of the most difficult to produce properly. After the discontinuation of the 1463 in the mid 20th century, Patek had no dedicated manually wound chronograph in the collections. Then, in 1998, the brand presented the reference 5070. Modern in proportions at 42mm, and utilizing a much smaller movement (a buildout of the Lemania 2310), Patek filled the extra dial space with added scales around the perimeter of the broad dial. The 5070 was bold in its proportions, and the market didn’t initially fall for it. Over time, however, the small production numbers, and perfect sizing by modern standards allowed the watch to go on to enjoy one of the most legendary collecting statuses in the neo-vintage Patek marketplace. This particular 5070 is one of the most rare, the first iteration of the production family, made for roughly three years in yellow gold with a black dial and gilt details. A true collector’s gem, for lovers of collectible Patek, this is a holy grail.

title: Franck Muller Cintrée Curvex Jumping Hour
description: Few watchmakers embraced the exuberance of the late twentieth century quite like Franck Muller. At a time when much of Swiss watchmaking was rediscovering its past, Muller looked forward, combining traditional complications with bold case designs, expressive typography, and an unmistakable sense of theatricality. His watches quickly became symbols of modern haute horlogerie, proving that serious watchmaking could also be playful. Among the manufacture's most iconic creations is the Cintrée Curvex. Introduced in the early 1990s, its gracefully curved tonneau-shaped case became the defining silhouette of the brand and remains one of the most recognizable case designs in contemporary watchmaking. This particular Cintrée Curvex, Ref. 7500 SC, showcases one of Franck Muller's favorite complications: the jumping hour. Rather than employing a traditional hour hand, the watch displays the current hour through a discreet aperture that instantaneously advances at the top of each hour, while a centrally mounted minute hand sweeps across the dial in conventional fashion. The result is both mechanically fascinating and delightfully unconventional, transforming the simple act of reading the time into a uniquely engaging experience. Crafted in 18K pink gold, the elegantly curved 32.5mm by 28.5mm case sits beautifully on the wrist, its sculptural profile accentuated by polished surfaces and flowing lines. The silvered dial provides a refined backdrop for the jumping-hour display, balancing classical watchmaking with the playful spirit that has long defined the brand. Inside beats an automatic mechanical movement, combining everyday practicality with the charm of one of horology's oldest and most captivating complications. Completing the watch is a brown alligator strap fitted with its original 18k pink gold Franck Muller buckle, a fitting companion to the warmth of the case. Produced during the manufacture's formative years, this Cintrée Curvex Jumping Hour captures the creative confidence that made Franck Muller one of the most influential independent watchmakers of his generation. Elegant, technically intriguing, and instantly recognizable, it remains a wonderful reminder that some of the most memorable watches are those willing to tell time a little differently.

title: Daniel Roth Master Perpetual Calendar
description: Few names command as much reverence among collectors of independent watchmaking as Daniel Roth. Long before the modern renaissance of artisanal horology, Roth left the security of Switzerland's great manufactures to establish his own atelier in 1988, becoming one of the first contemporary watchmakers to build a brand around his own name. Drawing upon his experience at Jaeger-LeCoultre, Audemars Piguet, and, most famously, Breguet, he created watches that blended classical aesthetics with uncompromising mechanical ambition. Among his most celebrated creations is the Daniel Roth Perpetual Calendar. Introduced in the early 1990s, it represents a remarkable collaboration between two of the era's greatest watchmaking minds: Daniel Roth and Philippe Dufour. Seeking to develop the world's first instantaneous perpetual calendar, the pair would go on to design its foundation before extensively reengineering it to fit Roth's signature double-ellipse case. While the immense energy demands ultimately prevented the fully instantaneous display they envisioned, the resulting watch remains one of the most fascinating perpetual calendars of its generation and an important chapter in the history of independent watchmaking. This particular example, a Reference 118.X.040, is an especially desirable early execution in 18k yellow gold. Measuring 35mm by 38mm, the distinctive double-ellipse case remains unlike anything else in watchmaking, striking a perfect balance between classical elegance and modern originality. Its sophisticated grey dial is framed by a hand-finished guilloché chapter ring with Roman numerals, while the perpetual calendar displays are thoughtfully arranged to preserve both symmetry and legibility. The combination of warm yellow gold and cool grey gives the watch a quietly distinguished presence that feels every bit as compelling today as it did three decades ago. Visible through the caseback is the automatic Calibre DR114, meticulously modified for Daniel Roth and finished in keeping with the standards that defined the brand's early production. Completing the watch is a leather strap fitted with its original 18k yellow gold Daniel Roth buckle. Produced in exceptionally small numbers during the manufacture's formative years, this piece occupies a special place in the history of modern independent watchmaking. It is not merely an exceptional perpetual calendar, but the product of a rare collaboration between Daniel Roth and Philippe Dufour, two figures whose influence continues to shape haute horlogerie today. For collectors, opportunities to acquire one of these early masterpieces are few and far between.

title: A. Lange & Söhne Lange 1 Moonphase
description: The Lange 1 is one of the defining watches of modern haute horlogerie. Introduced in 1994 as part of A. Lange & Söhne's celebrated revival, its asymmetrical dial, outsize date, and unmistakably Saxon aesthetic challenged conventional notions of dress-watch design. More than three decades later, it remains the manufacture's signature creation and one of the most recognizable timepieces in contemporary watchmaking. The Lange 1 Moonphase takes that iconic design and adds one of the manufacture's most poetic complications. At first glance, the familiar off-center layout appears unchanged. Look closer and the moonphase reveals itself as something entirely unique. Rather than presenting the moon against a static sky, Lange integrates a day/night indication directly into the celestial display. As the hours pass, the moon travels across a rotating disc that shifts from a bright daytime blue to a deep midnight sky populated by 383 individually rendered stars. It is an elegant solution that combines technical ingenuity with remarkable visual beauty. This particular Reference 192.025 is crafted in 950 platinum, a metal prized not only for its rarity but for its remarkable presence on the wrist. Measuring 38.5mm in diameter, the case pairs beautifully with a rhodium-colored solid silver dial, whose cool tones perfectly complement the platinum case. The familiar Lange 1 architecture remains beautifully balanced, with the oversized date, power reserve indicator, off-center time display, and moonphase each occupying their own distinct space without ever feeling crowded. Powering the watch is the manually wound Calibre L121.3, visible through the sapphire display back. Comprising 438 meticulously finished components, the movement offers a 72-hour power reserve while showcasing the hallmarks of modern Lange watchmaking: untreated German silver bridges, screwed gold chatons, blued screws, and the manufacture's signature hand-engraved balance cock. The moonphase itself is no less impressive, requiring correction by just one day after 122.6 years of continuous operation. Fitted to a black alligator strap with a platinum prong buckle, the Lange 1 Moonphase Ref. 192.025 is a masterclass in restrained complexity. It demonstrates A. Lange & Söhne's unique ability to combine mechanical innovation, impeccable finishing, and timeless design into a watch that is as intellectually satisfying as it is beautiful. Few modern dress watches communicate that philosophy more completely.

title: Omega Seamaster 'Jacques Mayol'
description: Few names are more closely associated with the spirit of the Seamaster than Jacques Mayol. A pioneer of competitive freediving and the first person to descend to a depth of 100 meters on a single breath, Mayol redefined what was thought possible beneath the surface. His extraordinary career, immortalized in Luc Besson's movie The Big Blue, embodied a quieter, more introspective relationship with the sea than traditional scuba diving. Omega celebrated that legacy in 1996 with this limited-edition Seamaster, a tribute to one of the ocean's greatest ambassadors. Limited to just 3,000 pieces worldwide, this example, Reference 2553.41.00, is numbered 1332. Measuring 36mm in stainless steel, it captures the proportions and restrained elegance that defined the Seamaster Professional before the trend toward larger dive watches. The deep green dial immediately distinguishes it from the standard collection, lending the watch a unique character while subtly evoking the colors of the sea. Powered by an automatic Omega movement and protected by a screw-down crown and caseback, the watch offers the robust engineering collectors expect from the Seamaster line. The familiar unidirectional dive bezel, luminous hands and markers, and integrated stainless steel bracelet combine everyday versatility with genuine underwater capability. Beyond its technical merits, the Jacques Mayol edition represents an important moment in Omega's history. Rather than commemorating an anniversary or cinematic partnership, it honors a man whose passion for the ocean perfectly reflected the Seamaster's enduring identity. Today, these limited editions remain among the most distinctive and collectible references from the 1990s, appealing to enthusiasts who appreciate their uncommon dial colors and compelling backstories. Accompanied by its original International Warranty card and instruction manual, this numbered Jacques Mayol Limited Edition is a complete and increasingly desirable example of one of Omega's most thoughtful commemorative Seamasters. Elegant, capable, and steeped in maritime history, it is a fitting tribute to a true legend of the deep.

title: Omega Seamaster Dive Chronograph
description: The Seamaster Professional has always been more than just Omega's dive watch. Throughout the 1990s, it evolved into one of the brand's most versatile platforms, serving everyone from professional divers to racing enthusiasts and, of course, a certain British secret agent. While the time-only models became icons in their own right, the chronograph variants offered an extra measure of mechanical complexity without sacrificing the collection's unmistakable identity. This particular Seamaster Professional Chronograph, Reference 2298.80.00, takes that formula one step further by embracing one of the decade's most advanced materials: titanium. Measuring 41.5mm, the case and matching bracelet are crafted entirely from the lightweight metal, giving the watch a distinctly modern feel while dramatically reducing weight compared to its stainless steel counterparts. The result is a robust professional dive watch that wears with remarkable comfort. The familiar blue wave dial is joined by a matching blue dive bezel, creating one of Omega's most recognizable color combinations. Large luminous hour markers, skeletonized hands, and bold chronograph registers ensure exceptional legibility, while the date display at three o'clock and helium escape valve at ten o'clock reinforce the watch's professional diving credentials. Despite its impressive specification sheet, the design remains balanced and unmistakably Omega. Powering the watch is the self-winding Omega Calibre 1164, a COSC-certified chronometer offering chronograph functionality, a date display, and a 44-hour power reserve. Protected beneath a domed sapphire crystal and water-resistant to 300 meters, it remains every bit as capable today as when it left the factory. Fitted to its original titanium bracelet with a foldover clasp and diver's extension, this Seamaster Professional Chronograph is accompanied by its original warranty card and instruction manual, an increasingly desirable addition for collectors of neo-vintage Omega. Together, they reinforce the watch's provenance while completing an already compelling package. Capturing an exciting moment in Omega's history, when cutting-edge materials, professional tool-watch engineering, and unmistakable 1990s design came together, it remains one of the era's most appealing modern classics. Rugged enough for the ocean, refined enough for everyday wear, it is every bit the Seamaster its name promises.

title: Bvlgari Two-Tone Stepped Case by Gérald Genta
description: The 1970s marked a fascinating chapter in Bvlgari's history. Long before the Octo became the brand's contemporary design icon, the Roman jeweler looked to one of the twentieth century's greatest watch designers, Gérald Genta, to help define its emerging identity in watchmaking. The result was a series of elegant, architecturally inspired creations that blended Italian style with Swiss craftsmanship, still refreshingly modern today. This remarkable two-tone Bulgari is one of those designs. Attributed to Gérald Genta and dating to the mid-1970s, the watch embodies his unmistakable talent for transforming simple geometry into something memorable. Measuring 27mm by 30mm, its stepped case is crafted in 18k white and yellow gold, with alternating tones that emphasize the layered architecture of the bezel. The effect is sculptural without ever feeling excessive, a hallmark of Genta's best work, like the Royal Oak or Nautilus. The minimalist black dial provides the perfect counterpoint to the richly detailed case. Slender gilt baton markers radiate outward between oversized numerals at twelve and six, while the absence of unnecessary text or decoration allows the design to speak for itself. It is a study in proportion, contrast, and restraint. Powering the watch is a manually wound movement that preserves the slim profile collectors prize in pieces from this era. Completing the package is its original black lizard strap secured by the original 18K gold Bulgari buckle. The case itself remains especially well preserved, retaining its original caseback sticker and crisp hallmarks. Produced at a pivotal moment in Bulgari's history, when fine jewelry, industrial design, and haute horlogerie began to converge, this uncommon timepiece captures the creative confidence that would eventually lead to some of the most influential watch designs of the modern era. Elegant, architectural, and unmistakably Gérald Genta, it is a hidden gem from one of watchmaking's most inspired creative partnerships.

title: Cartier Crash 'Bond Street London'
description: If Cartier is regarded as the master of watch design, the Crash is Cartier’s masterwork. One of the most collectible watches on the planet, it exudes an aura of mystery and legend unlike any other. Since the introduction of the Crash in 1967, the elusive watch has enjoyed a special place in Cartier’s catalog as an object both extremely rare and highly coveted. Until just a few years ago, its true story was unknown. Dozens of legends emerged explaining the origins of this almost mythical design: Some claimed that it was inspired by the paintings of Salvador Dali, a brilliant Spanish surrealist artist known for his eclectic paintings of melting timepieces with distorted, asymmetrical case shapes. Others suggested that the Crash was actually influenced by a destroyed Cartier Maxi Oval, tragically devastated by a fatal car fire. Unfortunately for the more imaginative among us, the truth is quite a bit less exciting. The granddaughter of Jean-Jacques Cartier, Francesca Cartier Breckell, revealed that Jean-Jacques and famous designer Rupert Emerson wanted to modernize a Cartier design to suit the emerging psychedelic era of fashion and culture. The result was the Cartier Crash, a modified Maxi Oval. With its asymmetrical, whimsical case design, flowing lines, and elegant incongruity, it has since become a cultural fascination. The mystery of the Crash certainly added a zero or two to the price tag, but at the end of the day, with soaring demand, Cartier had only made a few hundred total pieces — indeed, the Crash was always designed to be a rare gem for the distinguished few. A number of celebrities have owned one, including Jay-Z, Kanye West, Timothée Chalamet, and Elton John. This particular reference, a WGCH0050-4549 , is especially desirable. In 2019, to celebrate the re-opening of the New Bond Street Cartier boutique, Cartier presented limited edition Cartier Crashes. A year later, the platinum limited production example we have here followed. The general belief is that Cartier is delivering only one Crash per month, making these an extreme rarity . This piece features a 38mm x 25.5mm platinum case with a custom-cut sapphire crystal made specifically for the intentionally misshapen case of the Crash. Fitted with Cartier's defining red cabochon crown signifying the platinum material, this piece houses a silvery dial with stylized Roman numerals and a blued-steel 'sword' handset. A signed, gray leather strap with tone-on-tone stitching and matching deployant clasp, which itself is malformed to play on the crash motif, complement the case tones beautifully. Powered by the manually-wound Calibre 1917 MC, this London Boutique Edition Crash comes complete with its factory kit. With slightly updated case proportions blended with the Crash's unique design and elegant aura, this timepiece was made for the modern day Cartier aficionado. Own the ultimate collector’s Cartier, today!

title: Patek Philippe Nautilus Chronograph
description: The Patek Philippe Nautilus is without question one of the great horological icons of the 1970s, and has in recent years once again become one of the most in-demand wristwatch models on the planet. Collectors and prospectors alike have clamored to get their hands on Genta's second great act in luxury sports watch design, and since the legendary stainless steel, time-and-date, Reference 5711 rode off into the sunset in 2021, demand has never been higher. Interestingly enough, most of the demand for Nautilus models are centered around non-complicated models, something we can't fully wrap our heads around when considering the capabilities and expertise in high horology from Patek Philippe. This example, a Reference 5980/1A-001 , resides in the complications camp, boasting a flyback chronograph complication with a mono-counter display. Wrapped in a much-adored stainless steel case as the “A” suggests in its reference designation, this Nautilus features a three-part stainless case spanning 40.5mm in diameter. Displaying a masterful blend of satin and polish finishings throughout, this piece offers a signed screw-down crown, angular chronograph pushers that parallel the case flank, articulating end-links, sapphire crystal and of course, the model’s signature ‘eared’ silhouette. Its dial is finished in a beautiful blue fumé with hallmark horizontal texturing - affectionately referred to as the 'Garage Door' by some collectors. The dial features applied luminous indices, a matching luminous handset, a date window at 3 o’clock and a mono-counter 'bullseye' chronograph register at 6 o’clock, equipped with stacked minute and hour counter hands. Its Calibre CH 28-520 C flyback chronograph movement utilizes a column wheel mechanism and vertical clutch system for dead-on accuracy rating attested by the manufacture , as well as by our measure. This Nautilus makes for a pretty epic daily driver capable of just about anything you can throw at it! Fitted to an integrated stainless steel bracelet which cohesively follows the case taper and culminates with a signed locking clasp, this comes accompanied by its inner and box set, leather folio, and Certificate of Origin dated April 2012. A stainless steel complicated Nautilus — does it get any better than that?

title: Gruen Curvex 'Count'
description: One of the most famous curved wristwatch is without a doubt the Gruen Curvex, which was introduced in 1935 and almost single-handedly saw Gruen through the Great Depression. Thanks to strategic partnerships with Swiss companies like Rolex and movement manufacturer Aegler, Gruen had enjoyed success with its doctor’s watch, the Techni-Quadron (which Rolex marketed as the Prince in Europe and the British Empire). But the brand also earned a reputation for innovation in aesthetics. Throughout the 1920s, Gruen experimented with different movement and watch designs, including the Quadron, which housed a tonneau-shaped movement in a rectangular case. But after the Wall Street Crash of 1929, the U.S. watch industry took a massive hit. Sales of watches went down from five million to only 800,000 a year. Gruen, which was once ranked in the top tier of the watch industry, found itself selling watches at lower price points. Despite the economic setbacks and political changeovers, the brand was poised for a comeback—which came in the form of this watch, the Curvex. Gruen had actually applied for a patent for a curved movement in 1929, through its Bienne-based agent, Emile Frey. It was granted to Frey in 1932, but assigned to Gruen. Accordingly, the movement designers at the Precision Factory set to work designing what would become a revolutionary watch movement: the Calibre 311. The Curvex that we offer here features the Calibre 370. The 36 hr power reserve movement has a unique scalloping to its profile that matches the case. This particular Curvex, the ‘Count’, dates to circa 1940s. Made from 10K filled gold case, the case has aged to a lovely tone. At its time, this watch was the peak of fashion and trend, but today, it constitutes a wonderful heritage callback to a bygone era. This beautiful piece features a stunning 'Breguet' dial and handset, and is in exceptional condition for its age. The piece features scalloping on the vertical brancards that carries through the full design visually partitioning the piece into three main segments. There's no other watch that looks like this. Own a piece of horological history with this Gruen!

title: A. Lange & Söhne Lange 1815 Flyback Chronograph
description: Born in 1815, Ferdinand Adolph Lange received a rigorous education at the hands of nurses and governesses. At 15 he became a student at the Saxon Technical school in Dresden. Following that, he pursued training under Johann Christian Friedrich Gutkaes, Sr, royal clockmaker to the King of Saxony. In 1846 he and his brother-in-law formed A. Lange & Söhne. Lange’s use of precision tools and instruments allowed the manufacture to attain a level of precision that was heretofore unknown in mass-produced watches. After his death in 1878, his sons Richard and Emil would carry on his legacy. However, the Soviet occupation of East Germany at the end of the Second World War saw an end to A. Lange & Söhne. But after Reunification in the 1990s, the manufacture would make its triumphant return. At the helm of the company would be another Lange, Ferdinand’s great-grandson Walter. The model 1815 honors this watchmaking legacy. Simple and elegant, it’s a careful distillation of Saxon watchmaking and design — adorned with just enough decoration to be beautiful, its otherwise minimalist look mixes Bauhaus principles with classical aesthetics. But this particular watch is no ordinary, run-of-the-mill 1815 — if there is such a thing to begin with! What we have here is a flyback chronograph; featuring a 39.5mm rose gold case with a sapphire crystal, a signed crown, square pushers, a polished bezel, and a deep gloss black dial with recessed contrast silver sub registers, printed 'Arabic' numerals and a matching rose gold 'lance' handset. This piece comes fitted to a signed brown alligator strap with a signed rose gold pin buckle, and packs Lange's hand-cranking Calibre L951.0 flyback chronograph movement within - and is thankfully visible through a sapphire display caseback. There’s nothing wrong with a classic dress watch from a member of the “Holy Trinity.” But for a modern stunner, virtually any Lange can step up to delight. This one is no different.

title: Patek Philippe Nautilus
description: The Nautilus is without question one of the great horological icons of the 1970s, and one of the most in-demand timepiece models on the planet. Collectors and prospectors alike are clamoring to get their hands on Genta's second great luxury sports watch, and with the recent news of the discontinuation of the flagship reference 5711 in steel, this dramatic rise in popularity shows no signs of slowing down. This midsize Nautilus, a Reference 3800/001, embodies all of the porthole-inspired character of its larger siblings. This piece is presented in an elegant 37mm stainless steel monobloc case with matching integrated bracelet, an automatic winding Calibre 335SC movement, and a stunning blue gradient 'teak Sigma' dial with beautifully patinated tritium luminous indices and matching handset. Perhaps best of all for a watch of this era, this piece comes with its complete kit. A Patek Philippe Nautilus — in any of its variations — is a very special thing. But we'd be lying if we said we didn't have a real affinity for the often overlooked midsize models such as this one!

title: Universal Genève Unisonic 'Tiffany & Co.'
description: By now, Universal Genève should be well known in the watch collecting community. The brand attained a reputation in its heyday for well-constructed, aesthetically-appealing designs, typified in the Compax and Polerouter models. Yet even with its commitment to aesthetic excellence, Universal Genève was no stranger to mechanical innovation. Bulova's introduction of the Accutron 218 movement in 1965 intrigued and impressed brands and consumers alike, and Universal Genève sought to implement this new technology a decade before the Quartz Revolution changed the watchmaking game forever. The Unisonic was the result — a stunning and innovative timepiece that merged UG's attentive Swiss design language with future-forward American movement, a marriage artfully denoted by the unique UG/Accutron logo printed on the watch's dial. (Cool, right?) This particular Unisonic from the 1960s-1970s is crisp and clean — a prime example of the model. Housed in a highly wearable, brushed solid 18K yellow gold case, it features an acrylic crystal, a signed crown, and a clean, champagne tritium dial with printed Roman numerals, a day-date display, and a matching stick handset. It has developed a lovely warm patina with age, and has the quality of the watch you feel you've always owned. In outstanding overall condition and powered by an Accutron movement, it comes matched one of our Analog:Shift Saffiano straps. But wait — there's more . In addition to the Accutron logo and the Universal Genève wordmark, you'll likely have noticed yet another wordmark: That's right — this particular Unisonic was retailed by none other than Tiffany & Co., making it the type of rare, double-signed beauty that drives collectors absolutely mad. Coupling the elegance of Universal Genève with true technological innovation — plus a co-sign from an icon in Jewelry — this is a piece of horological history, a relic from that transitional period between the introduction of the tuning fork and the Quartz Revolution. Check this one out!

title: Patek Philippe Neptune
description: Patek Philippe made a fantastic, stainless steel sports watch and we're not talking about the Aquanaut or the Nautilus. The Patek Philippe Neptune has been long under-appreciated since its debut in 1996 along with the Aquanaut. Both pieces served as alternatives to the popular Nautilus and were meant to inject some life and energy to the the maison's sports watch collection. The Neptune in its multiple iterations stood on its own unique design language with its round case equipped with crown guards, svelte proportions and an excellent, multi-link integrated bracelet. This piece, a Reference 5080/1A-001, features a 37mm stainless steel case with signature crown guards, signed crown, sapphire crystal and a stunning fluted bezel with polished hour markers. The black dial features applied, quadrant Roman indices; a date indicator at 3 o'clock, luminous 'feuille' handset and a central chemin de fer minute track. Powered by a self-winding Patek Philippe Calibre 315 SC movement, this piece features a stainless steel integrated bracelet with matching finishing and a signed locking deployant clasp. Recognizable across the room only to those that know its distinguishable integrated bracelet design, this unusual, neo-vintage design from Patek is perfect for the discerning collector who wants a truly special piece that flies under the radar and offers a tremendous value!

title: Patek Philippe Ellipse 'Chevron Bracelet'
description: In 1968, Patek Philippe released the Golden Ellipse. Debuting eight years before the iconic Nautilus, the Ellipse—with its distinctive oval shape—was unlike anything else in Patek Philippe’s catalogs. And in the early 1970s, Patek expanded the Ellipse line to include squarish case shapes - immediately dubbed "TV Cases" or "Jumbo" by enthusiasts. But it's the Ellipse that has recently garnered further attention. This particular Reference 4826/19 is once such example. Finished in solid 18K yellow gold, this svelte piece comes in at 23mm in diameter and features a lovely blue 'sigma' dial with applied yellow gold indices and a matching handset, a signed crown, and a fantastic 'Chevron' style bracelet finished in solid yellow gold. Absolutely beautiful. In recent years, collector attention has finally returned to the Ellipse, and these vintage classics are getting the eyes and wrists they deserve. Watches such as this one are fun and wonderful timepieces, and there's no telling if and when one of these in any condition will surface again, so don't wait! *Due to the design of this bracelet, sizing alterations may require custom work. Lead time after measurements are established is 4-6 weeks.*

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava
description: For a brand so closely associated with tradition, Patek Philippe occasionally produces a watch that reminds us it has one eye firmly on the future. The Calatrava has served as the cornerstone of the Patek Philippe collection since 1932. Created during the economic uncertainty of the Great Depression, it distilled the manufacture's values into their purest form: elegance, restraint, and impeccable proportion. Nearly a century later, it remains the benchmark against which all dress watches are measured. Which is precisely why the Reference 6007G-001 feels so unexpected. Introduced in 2023 as part of a trio of boldly accented Calatravas, the 6007G-001 takes one of watchmaking's most traditional designs and injects it with a dose of contemporary energy. While the case and overall architecture remain unmistakably Calatrava, the details tell a different story—one that feels inspired by performance, precision, and modern design. Housed in a 40mm 18K white gold case, the watch combines polished surfaces and classical proportions with a striking dial unlike anything else in the Calatrava family. The ebony-black center features a carbon-pattern motif, surrounded by a circular satin-brushed outer track that creates depth and visual texture. Bright yellow accents energize the composition, highlighting the minute track, central seconds hand, and applied 'Arabic' numerals. The effect is dynamic without becoming loud—a difficult balance that Patek manages with remarkable confidence. White gold hands and luminous markers ensure excellent legibility, while the sporty dial treatment gives the watch a distinctly contemporary character rarely seen from the Genevan manufacture. Inside beats the automatic Caliber 26-330 S C, visible through the sapphire caseback and finished to the exacting standards collectors expect from Patek Philippe. Traditional craftsmanship remains at the heart of the watch, even as the aesthetics venture into new territory. The watch is fitted to a black calfskin strap embossed with a carbon-style texture and accented by vibrant yellow stitching, secured by a signed 18K white gold pin buckle. Accompanied by its complete set, this Reference 6007G-001 represents one of the most distinctive and youthful Calatravas produced in recent years. The Calatrava may have defined the dress watch. The 6007G-010 proves it doesn't have to live in the past, because even icons occasionally benefit from a shot of adrenaline.

title: Cartier Santos de Cartier Galbée Two-Tone
description: Few watches can claim to have changed the course of wristwatch history. The Cartier Santos is one of them. Created in 1904 for Brazilian aviator Alberto Santos-Dumont, the Santos is widely regarded as one of the first purpose-built men's wristwatches. At a time when pocket watches still dominated, Louis Cartier designed a watch that could be consulted mid-flight without removing one's hands from the controls. More than a century later, the Santos remains one of the most important and enduring designs in watchmaking—a rare icon whose appeal has only grown with time. This particular Santos Galbée, dating to the 1980s, represents one of the collection's most charming neo-vintage expressions. Its 29mm case combines stainless steel and 18k yellow gold in a way that feels quintessentially Cartier. The softly curved "Galbée" case profile hugs the wrist beautifully, while the signature exposed screws and seamlessly integrated bracelet create a design that is instantly recognizable from across the discotheque. The dial is pure Cartier. Crisp and elegant, it features a white backdrop accented by printed Roman numerals, a chemin-de-fer minute track, and the maison's signature blued steel sword hands. A sapphire cabochon crown adds a final touch of unmistakable Cartier flair. Together, these elements create a watch that feels equally at home with a tailored jacket, a cashmere sweater, or a simple white T-shirt. Powered by a reliable quartz movement, the Santos Galbée offers all the style and history of one of watchmaking's great icons with the convenience of grab-and-go wearability. The result is a watch that feels every bit as relevant today as it did four decades ago. For many collectors, the Tank may be Cartier's purest dress watch. The Santos, however, is its most versatile—a design that effortlessly bridges sport, elegance, and everyday wear. Few watches do it better.

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava
description: There is a reason the Calatrava remains the benchmark against which all dress watches are measured. For nearly a century, Patek Philippe's most enduring collection has embodied the manufacture's philosophy of elegant simplicity. Free from unnecessary complication and guided by a steadfast commitment to proportion, refinement, and craftsmanship, the Calatrava has become one of the most influential watch designs ever created. While many brands have attempted to define the perfect dress watch, few have come closer than Patek Philippe. This particular example, Ref. 3913/001 dating to 1988, showcases the Calatrava at its most graceful. Crafted in 18k yellow gold, its 31mm case is paired with a beautifully integrated yellow-gold bracelet that flows seamlessly from the case and closes with a signed foldover clasp. The result is a watch that wears more like fine jewelry than a traditional wristwatch, while retaining the quiet sophistication that defines the Calatrava name. The dial is a study in restraint. Executed in a crisp white finish, it features elegant applied Roman numerals in yellow gold that seem to float effortlessly above the surface. Their delicate proportions are complemented by a simple two-hand layout, creating a sense of balance and clarity that feels every bit as compelling today as it did in the late 1980s. There is nothing superfluous here—just exceptional design distilled to its purest form. Powered by a slim Patek Philippe manually wound movement and accompanied by its original Certificate of Origin dated 1988, travel case, manuals, papers, and pamphlets, this example represents a complete and wonderfully preserved expression of the manufacture's craft. Elegant, understated, and undeniably timeless, this yellow-gold Calatrava serves as a reminder that true luxury rarely needs to announce itself. Sometimes, perfection is simply a white dial, a gold bracelet, and the name Patek Philippe.

title: A.Lange & Söhne Lange 1 Moonphase
description: The Lange 1 is one of the defining watches of modern horology. Introduced in 1994 as part of A. Lange & Söhne's celebrated revival, its asymmetrical dial, oversized date display, and unmistakably Saxon character immediately distinguished it from anything else on the market. Nearly three decades later, it remains the watch most closely associated with the Glashütte manufacture and one of the most recognizable designs in all of watchmaking. This particular Lange 1 Moon Phase, Ref. 192.032, elevates that iconic formula with one of the most beautiful astronomical displays ever fitted to a wristwatch. Housed in a 38.5mm 18K pink gold case, it pairs an elegant argenté silver dial with Lange's signature outsize date, power reserve indicator, and off-center time display. At first glance, the moonphase appears familiar. A closer look reveals something far more sophisticated. Unlike traditional moonphase displays, the Lange 1 Moon Phase integrates a day/night indication directly into the celestial disc. During daylight hours, the moon travels across a bright blue sky, while at night it moves against a deep blue firmament populated by 383 individually rendered stars. The effect is subtle, poetic, and uniquely Lange. Behind its beauty lies extraordinary precision: accurate to 99.998 percent, the display deviates by just one day after 122.6 years of continuous operation. Powering the watch is the manually wound Calibre L121.3, visible through the sapphire display back. Comprising 438 components and offering a robust 72-hour power reserve, the movement showcases everything collectors admire about A. Lange & Söhne: untreated German silver bridges, gold chatons, blued screws, and a hand-engraved balance cock executed to the manufacture's exacting standards. Accompanied by its inner and outer boxes, pouch, original papers and pamphlets, Lange guarantee seal, and documentation dated 2018, this example represents one of the most compelling modern interpretations of the moonphase complication. Elegant, technically sophisticated, and endlessly captivating, the Lange 1 Moon Phase reminds us that some of watchmaking's greatest achievements are designed not only to measure time, but also to connect us to the heavens above.

title: A.Lange & Söhne Lange 1 Perpetual Calendar
description: When A. Lange & Söhne unveiled the Lange 1 in 1994, it immediately changed the conversation around modern watchmaking. Introduced as part of the manufacture's celebrated return following German reunification, the watch rejected convention in favor of a bold asymmetrical layout, an oversized date display, and distinctly Saxon design language. More than thirty years later, it remains the defining face of A. Lange & Söhne and is one of the most recognizable watches in haute horlogerie. The challenge facing Lange's watchmakers was simple: how do you add one of watchmaking's most revered complications—the perpetual calendar—without compromising the character of the Lange 1? The answer arrived in 2022 with the Lange 1 Perpetual Calendar, a watch that seamlessly integrates a full perpetual calendar into the collection's iconic architecture while preserving the balance and elegance that made the original famous. This particular example, Ref. 345.033, pairs a warm pink gold case with a sophisticated grey dial, creating one of the most compelling combinations in the contemporary Lange catalog. Measuring 41.9mm in diameter, the case provides ample space for the calendar indications while maintaining excellent proportions on the wrist. The familiar Lange 1 elements remain front and center: the outsize date, the off-center time display, and the beautifully executed moonphase display integrated into the running seconds register. Meanwhile, the day, month, and leap-year indications are incorporated with remarkable subtlety, demonstrating the manufacture's talent for presenting immense complexity with exceptional clarity. Turn the watch over, and the view is every bit as impressive. Visible through the sapphire display back is the self-winding Calibre L021.3, a movement comprising hundreds of components and finished to the exacting standards for which Lange is renowned. Untreated German silver bridges, hand-engraved details, gold chatons, blued screws, and a beautifully executed rotor featuring a platinum centrifugal mass combine to create a movement that is as captivating visually as it is mechanically sophisticated. Accompanied by its inner and outer boxes, original papers, guarantee seal, and accessories from 2022, this Lange 1 Perpetual Calendar represents one of the most important modern creations from Glashütte. Combining the manufacture's signature design language with one of watchmaking's grandest complications, it is a masterclass in thoughtful engineering, mechanical artistry, and enduring design.

title: A.Lange & Söhne Zeitwerk
description: Few watches have challenged conventional notions of mechanical watchmaking as successfully as the A. Lange & Söhne Zeitwerk. When it debuted in 2009, the Zeitwerk felt unlike anything else on the market. While most high-end watchmakers were looking backward for inspiration, Lange introduced a thoroughly modern interpretation of timekeeping—one that displayed the hours and minutes digitally while remaining entirely mechanical. It was a bold concept, but one executed with the precision, ingenuity, and uncompromising craftsmanship for which the Glashütte manufacture is renowned. Inspired by the famous five-minute clock in Dresden's Semper Opera House, the Zeitwerk presents the time through oversized jumping numeral displays framed within a beautifully balanced dial architecture. Behind the apparent simplicity lies one of the most sophisticated mechanisms of the modern era. A patented constant-force escapement manages the substantial energy required to advance the display discs instantaneously every minute, ensuring both precision and reliable power delivery throughout the movement's operation. This particular example, Ref. 140.029, represents the first generation of the Zeitwerk and is housed in a substantial 41.9mm 18k white gold case. Its striking black dial is anchored by a German silver time bridge that frames the jumping hours and minutes, while a power-reserve indicator at twelve o'clock and a constant-seconds display at six provide visual symmetry and functional balance. The result is unmistakably Lange—technical, architectural, and instantly recognizable from across a room. Turn the watch over and the manually wound Calibre L043.1 is revealed through the sapphire display back. Comprising hundreds of meticulously finished components, the movement showcases everything collectors have come to expect from A. Lange & Söhne: untreated German silver plates, hand-engraved details, gold chatons, blued screws, and a level of finishing that borders on obsessive. Fitted to a signed black alligator strap with a matching white gold deployant clasp, the Zeitwerk remains one of the defining watches of twenty-first-century horology. More than a decade after its introduction, it still feels as innovative, daring, and mechanically fascinating as the day it was unveiled.

title: Audemars Piguet "Cobra"
description: There was a time when Audemars Piguet's creativity extended far beyond the Royal Oak. During the 1970s and 1980s, the Le Brassus manufacture produced a remarkable collection of jewelry watches that combined high watchmaking, precious metals, and bold design in ways that feel increasingly distinctive today. Among the most recognizable is the Cobra, a model whose fluid, integrated bracelet and sculptural profile perfectly capture the era's glamour and optimism. Crafted entirely in 18K white gold, this Cobra is a study in texture, light, and form. The softly curved case flows seamlessly into a signed white gold bracelet, creating a unified design that wraps elegantly around the wrist. Like the finest integrated-bracelet watches of the period, the bracelet is not merely an accessory but an essential part of the watch's identity, lending the piece a remarkable sense of cohesion and comfort. The true star of the show, however, is the dial. Executed in a dazzling 'pavé' pattern, its diamond-set surface radiates outward from the center in a striking tiny 'sunburst' motif that transforms with every wrist movement. The intricate geometry catches and reflects light from every angle, creating an effect that is both architectural and undeniably luxurious. Applied sapphire hour markers at three, six, and nine o'clock introduce subtle flashes of deep blue, providing a beautiful contrast against the brilliant white gold backdrop. Powered by a reliable manually wound movement and fitted with its original signed white gold bracelet and foldover clasp, this Cobra exemplifies a period when Audemars Piguet approached watch design with extraordinary freedom. Equal parts jewelry, design object, and timepiece, it remains a compelling reminder that some of the manufacture's most fascinating creations exist well beyond the Royal Oak family tree. Elegant, unconventional, and unmistakably Audemars Piguet, the Cobra is vintage luxury at its most expressive.

title: Jaeger-LeCoultre Gran'Sport Reverso
description: Few watches are as instantly recognizable as the Jaeger-LeCoultre Reverso. Born in 1931 from a practical challenge posed on the polo fields of British India, its ingenious reversible case was designed to protect the crystal during play. What began as a sporting solution quickly transcended its origins, becoming one of the defining designs of the Art Deco era and, ultimately, one of the most important wristwatches ever produced. By the late 1990s and early 2000s, Jaeger-LeCoultre began exploring a more contemporary side of the Reverso. The result was the Gran'Sport collection, a fascinating chapter in the model's history that blended the elegance of the classic Reverso with the durability and versatility of a modern sports watch. Water-resistant, automatically wound, and frequently paired with rubber straps or bracelets, these watches represented a bold departure from the dressier Reversos that had come before. This particular Reverso Gran'Sport is crafted in 18K yellow gold and features a 27mm x 43mm reversible case with the collection's signature stepped gadroons and more muscular proportions. The silver dial is rich in detail, combining oversized Arabic numerals, luminous sword hands, a textured central guilloché pattern, and a date display at six o'clock. A red-tipped seconds hand provides a subtle sporting flourish, while the signed screw-down crown further underscores the watch's everyday practicality. Perhaps the most distinctive element is the signed black rubber strap paired with its matching gold deployant clasp. Unusual on a precious-metal Reverso and emblematic of the Gran'Sport's forward-thinking design, it gives the watch a casual versatility that feels remarkably contemporary more than two decades after its introduction. Powered by an automatic Jaeger-LeCoultre movement and housed within one of watchmaking's most celebrated case designs, the Reverso Gran'Sport occupies a unique place in the model's history. Equal parts sport watch, dress watch, and design icon, it remains one of the most compelling—and increasingly collectible—modern interpretations of the Reverso ever produced.

title: Baume & Mercier 'Lucchetto' Padlock
description: There are watches that tell time, and there are watches that tell stories. This remarkable Baume & Mercier Lucchetto belongs firmly to the latter category. Produced during the golden age of postwar design, it transforms an everyday object—the humble padlock—into an elegant piece of wearable sculpture. Crafted in 18K yellow gold, its distinctive rectangular case is suspended within a graceful arched frame, creating the unmistakable silhouette that gives the Lucchetto its name, the Italian word for "padlock." At just 21mm across, the watch possesses all the refinement one expects from a mid-century ladies' dress watch, yet its unconventional design sets it apart from nearly everything produced during the era.
