The silvered dial is beautifully restrained, featuring applied gold baton indices and matching hands, allowing the unique architecture of the case to remain the focal point. Viewed from the side, the watch feels almost like a miniature piece of modernist jewelry—an object designed as much to delight as to inform. Founded in 1830, Baume & Mercier has long occupied a unique place in Swiss watchmaking, balancing technical expertise with a strong appreciation for design and aesthetics. Throughout the 1950s and 1960s, the firm produced a number of imaginative jewelry watches that reflected the optimism and creativity of the period, and the Lucchetto remains among the most charming examples. Powering this piece is a manually wound movement housed within its 18K yellow gold case, while a black leather strap and matching gold buckle complete the presentation. More than sixty years after its creation, the Lucchetto remains a wonderful reminder that some of the most memorable watches are the ones willing to be a little playful. Equal parts watch, jewel, and conversation piece, it is a delightful expression of mid-century creativity from one of Switzerland's most enduring names.

title: Patek Philippe Gondolo
description: 1989 marked an incredible anniversary for Patek Philippe — 150 years in business. Founded in 1839, Patek Philippe is one of the oldest watch manufacturers in the world with an uninterrupted watchmaking history. Few international luxury brands carry the gravitas of their name, and for good reason. The firm's commitment to excellence in horological manufacture is unflinching, and their track record of innovation in design without peer. They continue to lead the industry, and even their fiercest competitors have nothing but the utmost respect for the company. From the simple elegance of their Calatrava line to the stunning study in miniaturization that is reference 1518 perpetual calendar to the modern reference 5750P chiming watch, Patek’s catalog is chock full of some of the most elegant and complicated timepieces ever made. Family-owned and completely independent, the firm has the freedom to do what it wants — such as discontinue one of the world’s most beloved steel luxury sport watches, the reference 5711 — when it wants. Take this Gondolo for example; a Reference 5024G from the early 2000s. It features a fantastic, 30mm curved 'Art Deco' case with a sapphire crystal, a signed, recessed crown, a beautiful satin salmon dial with applied stylized 'Art Deco Arabic' indices and a matching 'sword' handset, and Patek's Calibre 215 manual winding movement within. Paired to a signed black alligator leather strap with a matching white gold pin buckle, this piece offers something a bit off the beaten path for Patek, for those looking for something a little bit different, but packing a huge punch in the value department. Any old wristwatch can tell the time. Few truly define it.

title: A. Lange & Söhne Saxonia Big Date
description: Where does one turn when the typical, minimalist dress watch fails to inspire? To A. Lange & Söhne, of course. The Glashütte-based manufacture is world-famous for its absurdly beautiful, complicated timepieces, but their simpler watches are similarly the pinnacle of elegance. This Saxonia Outsize Date, with its large case and distinctly Saxon, oversized date complication, sits somewhere in the middle. Executed in a modern 38.5mm rose gold case and dating to 2021, this example features satin black dial with applied rose gold indices and subsidiary seconds at 6 o’clock, plus a matching spear handset. Of course, what makes this particular model stand out is the oversized “digital” date complication below the 12 o’clock marker, controlled via a pusher at 10 o’clock — a holdover from the simply unbeatable Lange 1, which debuted in 1994. With its sapphire crystal and display case back, 18k gold signed crown and polished matching bezel, and matching alligator leather strap with signed 18K rose gold pin buckle, this Saxonia is the type of watch that — at least aesthetically — pairs well with everything from a t-shirt to a tuxedo. The beautifully finished, in-house Caliber L086.8 ain’t bad to look at, either. There’s nothing wrong with a classic dress watch from a member of the “Holy Trinity.” But for a modern stunner in beautiful, nearly new-old-stock condition, this Saxonia is simply unbeatable.

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava
description: Few watches can claim to have defined an entire category, but the Patek Philippe Calatrava is one of them. Introduced in 1932 during a period of economic uncertainty, the Calatrava emerged as a new vision for the wristwatch. Following the stock market crash of 1929 and the Stern family's acquisition of a controlling interest in Patek Philippe, the manufacture sought to create a watch that embodied elegance through simplicity rather than complexity. Drawing inspiration from the Bauhaus movement and its philosophy of functional, uncluttered design, Patek created what would become the archetype for the modern dress watch. Named after the Calatrava Cross—the symbol of the Spanish military order that later became the emblem of Patek Philippe—the Calatrava has served as the foundation of the manufacture's collection for nearly a century. While countless references have followed, the model's core principles of proportion, refinement, and restraint remain unchanged. This particular example, the Reference 5117G-001, dates to the 2000s and offers one of the more distinctive interpretations of the classic Calatrava formula. Its 37mm 18K white-gold case features elegant crown guards and the model's signature Clous de Paris bezel, a detail that adds texture and visual depth while remaining unmistakably Patek Philippe. The crisp white dial features painted black Roman numerals, a matching minute track, and elegant feuille hands, creating a look that is both traditional and highly legible. Powering the watch is Patek Philippe's self-winding Caliber 315, a beautifully finished in-house movement renowned for its reliability and refinement. The watch is fitted to a black alligator leather strap with a signed 18k white-gold pin buckle, perfectly complementing the understated sophistication of the design. Accompanying the watch are its original inner and outer presentation boxes, Certificate of Origin, manuals, and related literature from the 2000s, making it a highly complete example of one of Patek Philippe's most enduring references. Elegant without being ostentatious, traditional without feeling dated, the Reference 5117G embodies everything that has made the Calatrava a cornerstone of fine watchmaking for generations.

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava
description: First presented in 1932 with the Reference 96, the Patek Philippe Calatrava established the template for the modern dress watch. Clean, balanced, and heavily influenced by the Bauhaus principle that form should follow function, the Calatrava represented a radical shift away from the ornate pocket-watch traditions that preceded it. Nearly a century later, its influence can still be seen throughout the watch industry. The Reference 96 was also among the earliest watches introduced under the Stern family's stewardship after their acquisition of Patek Philippe. It became the foundation upon which generations of Calatravas would be built, each preserving the model's commitment to elegance, proportion, and restraint while interpreting those ideals for a new era. This example, Reference 5127R-001, captures that enduring spirit in warm 18K rose gold. Produced during the 2010s, it features a beautifully proportioned 37mm case with classic downturned lugs, a polished bezel, sapphire crystal, signed crown, and screw-down sapphire display caseback revealing the finely finished self-winding movement within. The size strikes a near-perfect balance, offering contemporary presence while maintaining the refined character expected of a true Calatrava. The silvered dial is a study in understated sophistication, furnished with applied rose-gold indices, a delicate dot minute track, matching dauphine hands, and a framed date aperture at 3 o'clock. Every element serves a purpose, creating a display that is remarkably clean, legible, and timeless. Fitted to a signed brown alligator leather strap with an 18k rose-gold pin buckle, this watch is also accompanied by its original Certificate of Origin from the 2010s. Simple, elegant, and executed to an extraordinarily high standard, the Reference 5127R embodies everything that has made the Calatrava one of the most respected dress watches in horological history. It is a watch that never chases trends because it helped define what timelessness looks like in the first place.

title: Patek Philippe Retrograde Perpetual Calendar
description: A perpetual calendar is like a tiny mechanical computer for the wrist. Think about everything involved in displaying the correct date. The watch must know whether a month has 30 or 31 days. It must account for February, including leap years. It must track the day of the week, the month, and often the phases of the moon. Now imagine accomplishing all of that not with software or electronics, but with springs, levers, gears, and cams working together in perfect harmony. It's one of the greatest achievements in traditional watchmaking. Few brands are more closely associated with the perpetual calendar than Patek Philippe. Since the 1940s, the Geneva manufacture has produced some of the most elegant and technically sophisticated perpetual calendars ever made. This particular example, the Reference 5159G-001, offers a distinctive interpretation of the complication that stands apart from almost anything else in the Patek Philippe catalog. Dating to the 2010s, the watch is housed in a 36mm white-gold officer-style case with a stepped bezel, sapphire crystal, and signed crown. The crisp white dial features applied indices, elegant spade hands, apertures for the day and month, a moonphase display above six o'clock, and the defining feature of the reference: a sweeping retrograde date display. Rather than circling the dial continuously, the date hand travels across an arc before instantly snapping back to the first of the month—a wonderfully theatrical mechanical flourish that never loses its charm. What makes the 5159 so appealing is its individuality. While many Patek perpetual calendars share familiar layouts, the 5159 feels entirely its own. The combination of the retrograde display, officer-style case, and compact proportions creates a watch that is unmistakably Patek Philippe while offering something a bit more unconventional for the seasoned collector. Completing the package is a signed brown alligator leather strap fitted with a white-gold Patek Philippe deployant clasp. Accompanying the watch are its original inner and outer presentation boxes, instruction manuals and pamphlets, as well as its Certificate of Origin, providing the kind of complete set collectors are increasingly seeking. With its ingenious complication, distinctive display architecture, and exceptional craftsmanship, the Reference 5159G represents one of the most interesting perpetual calendars of the modern era—a sophisticated reminder that some of the most impressive computers in the world are still powered entirely by gears and springs.

title: Cartier Panthère Diamonds
description: Few watches embody Cartier's ability to blur the line between fine jewelry and watchmaking quite like the Panthère. The panther has served as the maison's unofficial mascot since the early twentieth century, when Louis Cartier bestowed the nickname La Panthère upon Jeanne Toussaint, the visionary designer who would help define the brand's aesthetic. Elegant, powerful, and unmistakably glamorous, the feline motif became synonymous with Cartier itself—and nowhere is that spirit more evident than in the Panthère collection. This Reference 1660 represents the Panthère at its most luxurious. Crafted entirely from 18K white gold, the watch features a refined 22mm case framed by a brilliant diamond-set bezel. An additional diamond adorns the crown, creating a subtle sparkle that catches the light from every angle without overwhelming the watch's elegant proportions. The dial is quintessential Cartier. A warm ivory backdrop hosts bold black Roman numerals arranged around a railroad-style minute track, while delicate sword hands maintain the clean, balanced aesthetic that has made Cartier dials among the most recognizable in watchmaking. Every detail feels intentional, every proportion perfectly judged. Perhaps the loveliest detail of the Panthère is its bracelet. Fashioned from solid 18K white gold and secured by a concealed butterfly deployant clasp, it drapes across the wrist with remarkable fluidity, wearing more like a piece of fine jewelry than a traditional wristwatch. The effect is both luxurious and effortlessly comfortable. Powered by a precise quartz movement, this Panthère places the focus squarely on design, craftsmanship, and wearability. While many luxury watches aspire to versatility, few accomplish it with such grace. Elegant enough for evening wear, refined enough for everyday use, and elevated by its diamond-set details, this white-gold Panthère remains one of Cartier's most enduring expressions of Parisian sophistication. More than a watch, it is Cartier doing what Cartier does best.

title: Audemars Piguet Royal Oak
description: The Royal Oak has long transcended its status as a watch to become a design icon. When Gérald Genta unveiled the model in 1972, its exposed screws, integrated bracelet, and angular architecture challenged every convention of luxury watchmaking. More than fifty years later, the Royal Oak remains the benchmark for the luxury sports watch category it helped create. See a recent international global frenzy over a certain Swatch collab as a reference. This Ref. 15127BA.OO.0789BA.01 demonstrates why the Royal Oak's appeal extends far beyond its most famous jumbo references. Crafted entirely in 18K yellow gold, the watch pairs the collection's unmistakable industrial design with the warmth and richness of precious metal. Measuring 36mm in diameter, it occupies a particularly desirable sweet spot, offering all of the Royal Oak's signature presence while maintaining elegant proportions that feel remarkably contemporary. The white dial provides a striking contrast to the yellow-gold case and bracelet. Decorated with Audemars Piguet's signature Petite Tapisserie pattern in the center, the dial features Arabic indices wrapped around reminiscent of its 'Military Dial' sibling. Matching, luminous hands maintain a clean, balanced appearance, while the date aperture at three o'clock integrates seamlessly into the overall design. Powering the watch is Audemars Piguet's automatic Calibre 2225, visible through the sapphire exhibition caseback. Combining reliable performance with refined finishing, the movement delivers a 40-hour power reserve and serves as a reminder that the Royal Oak's appeal is rooted in substance as much as style. Of course, no discussion of the Royal Oak would be complete without mentioning the bracelet. Machined from solid 18K yellow gold, the integrated design remains one of the greatest achievements in modern watchmaking. Its interplay of brushed and polished surfaces creates a remarkable sense of fluidity, allowing the watch to wear with a comfort that belies its substantial construction. While contemporary tastes often gravitate toward larger case sizes, references such as the 15127 remind us that the Royal Oak was always at its best when proportion was paramount. Elegant, substantial, and endlessly versatile, this yellow-gold Royal Oak is a sophisticated expression of one of the most important watch designs ever created—a watch that feels every bit as relevant today as when it first revolutionized the industry.

title: Breguet Marine
description: Few names in watchmaking carry the weight of Breguet. Founded by Abraham-Louis Breguet in 1775, the maison's influence on modern horology is almost impossible to overstate. Yet while collectors often focus on the brand's classical dress watches, the Marine collection represents an equally fascinating chapter in its modern history. Introduced in 1990, the Marine arrived at a moment when heritage manufacturers were beginning to embrace the growing demand for versatile luxury sports watches. Rather than abandoning its traditions, Breguet did what it does best: it reinterpreted them. The result was a watch that retained the maison's unmistakable design language while introducing a more robust, contemporary character. This Ref. 3460 SA captures that philosophy beautifully. Executed in an enduring combination of stainless steel and yellow gold, the watch possesses a warmth and presence that feels distinctly 1990s while remaining remarkably relevant today. The signature fluted caseband, integrated bracelet design, and sculpted crown instantly identify the watch as a Breguet, even from across a room. The silvered guilloché dial is the undeniable star of the show. Engine-turned by hand, it displays a mesmerizing tapestry of textures that shift dramatically as light moves across its surface. Applied Roman numerals frame a trio of recessed registers, while Breguet's famous blued-steel hands glide across the dial with elegant precision. The result is a chronograph that is highly functional without sacrificing an ounce of refinement. Powered by an automatic chronograph movement and fitted to its original integrated two-tone bracelet, the Ref. 3460 SA offers the best of both worlds: sporting versatility and classical watchmaking pedigree. It is a watch from an era before luxury sports watches became ubiquitous, when brands were still discovering how to blend elegance and utility in their own distinctive ways. Today, early Marine references are increasingly appreciated for exactly that reason. They feel authentic, unmistakably Breguet, and refreshingly different from anything else on the market. Rich in detail, beautifully executed, and effortlessly wearable, the Ref. 3460 SA remains one of the most compelling expressions of Breguet's transition into the modern era.

title: Tudor Black Bay Fifty-Eight
description: There is a reason the Black Bay Fifty-Eight has become one of the defining modern dive watches of the last decade. While many brands spend their time mining the past, Tudor has managed to accomplish something far more difficult: creating a contemporary watch that captures the spirit of its vintage ancestors without feeling like a costume. Introduced in 2018 and inspired by Tudor's first 200-meter dive watch from 1958, the Black Bay Fifty-Eight distilled everything enthusiasts loved about vintage Submariners into a remarkably wearable package. The result was an instant success and, for many collectors, remains the sweet spot of the entire Black Bay family. This Ref. 79030N embodies that formula perfectly. Its 39mm stainless-steel case strikes an ideal balance between vintage proportions and modern capability, offering a fit that works on nearly any wrist. The black dial is clean, highly legible, and free from unnecessary distractions, allowing the warm gilt accents and signature Snowflake handset to take center stage. Of course, no Fifty-Eight would be complete without one of its defining details: the red triangle at 12 o'clock on the bezel. A subtle nod to Tudor's historic dive watches, it adds just the right amount of color and vintage character to the otherwise monochromatic design. Combined with the black aluminum bezel insert, it creates a look that feels both purposeful and timeless. Powering the watch is Tudor's in-house Calibre MT5402, a COSC-certified automatic movement featuring 27 jewels, a silicon balance spring, and an impressive 70-hour power reserve. Robust, accurate, and built for everyday wear, it represents everything modern enthusiasts expect from a contemporary tool watch. Fitted with a black-and-gold NATO-style fabric strap with a steel buckle and accompanied by its original manual and hangtags, this example offers the complete Black Bay Fifty-Eight experience. It is a watch that succeeds because it does not try too hard. Comfortable, capable, handsome, and endlessly versatile, the Fifty-Eight has already secured its place among the great modern sports watches—and this black-dial reference remains the one that started it all.

title: Patek Philippe Annual Calendar Moonphase
description: In 1991, the soon-to-be graduates at the Geneva School of Engineering were presented with their final project prior to receiving their diploma — to simplify the perpetual calendar. Although the task was easier said than done, their work led to the inception of the annual calendar complication, patented by Patek Philippe in collaboration with the bright engineering minds at the GSE. Five years later, Patek debuted the Reference 5035, a watch powered by the world’s first-ever annual calendar movement and one that finally bridged the gap between a triple-date function and the formidable quantième perpétuel . This slightly later annual calendar, a Reference 5146/1J-001 , is housed in a beautifully proportioned 39mm 18K yellow gold case with a sapphire crystal, signed crown, and a smooth, polished bezel. It features a luminous, white dial with applied indices, recessed subsidiary registers indicating day and month, a moonphase aperture and date window at 6 o'clock, and a matching luminous 'feuille' handset. Powered by Patek Philippe's Calibre 324 self-winding movement, it comes complete with an incredible 18K yellow gold bracelet that adds a reassuring heft to the beautiful piece. This piece packs pedigree, elegance, function and outstanding craftsmanship — exactly what you'd expect from a Patek Philippe!

title: Patek Philippe Aquanaut
description: The Patek Philipp e Aquanaut may be one of the most important modern luxury sport watches on the market. The Reference 5060J, launched in 1996 for the 20th anniversary of the Nautilus, was a sort of transitional watch. Borrowing features from the Nautilus but doing away with the famed case “ears” of that porthole-inspired model and adding lugs, it provided the basis for the Reference 5060A in 1997, the first model actually bearing the Aquanaut name. The Aquanaut would go on to form the basis of a full collection of luxury sports watches that provided the entry point into the Patek Philippe catalog. This piece, a Reference 5168G, features a 42mm white gold case with a satin-finished bezel, sapphire crystal, a signed screw-down crown and an incredible blue dial. On the dial you'll find all of the signature Aquanaut features present — hobnail texturing, luminous Arabic indices, a matching luminous handset and a date indicator at 3 o’clock. In excellent condition throughout, this example is fitted to its blue, integrated rubber strap. With more presence on the wrist compared to its older siblings, the 5168 remains one of most highly-coveted sport watches on the market. The 5168 is the ultimate subtle watch for the lover of the Aquanaut looking for a more under the radar approach to the design language. An iconic design from a maison with ultimate pedigree … what more could you ask for?

title: Patek Philippe Nautilus
description: The Nautilus is without question one of the great horological icons of the 1970s, and one of the most in-demand timepiece models on the planet. Collectors and prospectors alike are clamoring to get their hands on Genta's second great luxury sports watch, and with the 5711 having been discontinued in steel, this dramatic rise in popularity shows no signs of slowing down. Interestingly, most demand for Nautilus models is centered around Jumbo models in steel, something we can't fully wrap our heads around given the sheer excellent of smaller variants. This midsize Nautilus, a Reference 3800/1J, embodies all of the porthole-inspired character of its larger siblings, just with a slightly smaller 37mm case, and a perhaps more polarizing metal color. Dating to circa 1989, it features a matching integrated yellow gold bracelet, a signed crown, a beautiful blue dial with an outer 'railroad' minute track, applied yellow gold indices, and a matching handset, and Patek's Calibre 335SC automatic movement inside. It also happens to ship with its Extract from the Archives. The Nautilus has become a true piece of horological history — an icon of icons, it must be experienced to be believed!

title: Patek Philippe Ellipse
description: In 1968, Patek Philippe released the Golden Ellipse. Debuting eight years before the iconic Nautilus, the Ellipse—with its distinctive oval shape—was unlike anything else in Patek Philippe’s catalogs. And in the early 1970s, Patek expanded the Ellipse line to include squarish case shapes - immediately dubbed "TV Cases" or "Jumbo" by enthusiasts. But it's the Ellipse that has recently garnered further attention. This particular Reference 3938/1J is once such example. Finished in solid 18k yellow gold, this svelte piece comes in at 35mm in diameter and features a lovely blue 'sigma' dial with applied yellow gold indices and a matching handset, a signed crown, and a fantastic woven bracelet finished in solid yellow gold. Absolutely fantastic. In recent years, collector attention has finally returned to the Ellipse, and these vintage classics are getting the eyes and wrists they deserve. Watches such as this one are fun and wonderful timepieces, and there's no telling if and when one of these in any condition will surface again, so don't wait! *Due to the design of this bracelet, sizing alterations may require custom work. Lead time after measurements are established is 4-6 weeks.*

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava
description: There are few watches that can legitimately be described as foundational to modern wristwatch design. The Patek Philippe Calatrava Ref. 96 is one of them. Introduced in 1932, the reference established a design language so successful that it continues to influence dress watches nearly a century later. Just as the Cartier Tank defined the rectangular wristwatch, the Ref. 96 defined the round one, setting the benchmark for proportion, restraint, and elegance against which countless watches would be measured. The Ref. 96 was also among the earliest and most important creations produced under the Stern family's stewardship, whose acquisition of Patek Philippe helped redirect the manufacture's focus toward wristwatches at a pivotal moment in horological history. In many respects, the reference laid the foundation for what we now recognize as the Calatrava—not merely as a Patek Philippe collection, but as an entire category of watch design. This example, preserved in 18K yellow gold, dates to March 10, 1959, as confirmed by its accompanying Patek Philippe Extract from the Archives. Measuring 30.5mm in diameter with an elegant 39mm lug-to-lug span, it demonstrates the impeccable proportions that have made the Ref. 96 so enduringly desirable. The dial is particularly captivating. Against a deep black backdrop, faceted dauphine hour markers catch the light beautifully, creating a striking contrast that elevates the watch beyond pure minimalism. The gilt Patek Philippe Genève signature possesses a remarkable warmth and intensity, seemingly glowing from within the dial itself. A recessed small-seconds register at six o'clock provides visual balance while reinforcing the reference's classic mid-century character. Powering the watch is Patek Philippe's manually wound Calibre 12-400, a movement celebrated for its reliability, refinement, and elegant construction. Like the watch itself, it embodies the manufacture's philosophy that true sophistication lies not in excess, but in flawless execution. For many collectors, the Ref. 96 remains the purest expression of the Calatrava ideal. Simple without being plain, elegant without being fragile, and historically important without sacrificing wearability, it stands among the most significant wristwatches ever produced. More than ninety years after its introduction, the Ref. 96 remains not merely a great Patek Philippe, but one of the defining wristwatches of the modern era.

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava 'Calatravone'
description: Among the great dress watches of the twentieth century, few references command the reverence afforded to the Patek Philippe Calatrava Ref. 570. Introduced in 1938 as a larger counterpart to the seminal Ref. 96, the 570 represented a bold step forward for Patek Philippe. At a time when most wristwatches remained modest in size, its 35mm case was considered remarkably substantial, earning the reference the affectionate nickname 'Calatravone' among collectors. More than eighty years later, those proportions feel virtually perfect. The Ref. 570 embodies everything that has made the Calatrava one of watchmaking's purest design expressions. Its flat bezel, elongated tapered lugs, and uncluttered dial create an aesthetic of remarkable restraint, proving that true elegance rarely requires embellishment. The present example is especially appealing, featuring a warm cream dial that has developed a beautiful tone over the decades. Applied gold lapped hour markers are complemented by an outer minute track composed of applied pearl markers, creating a subtle sense of depth and refinement that rewards close inspection. The raised enamel Patek Philippe Genève signature serves as a reminder of the extraordinary attention to detail that defined the manufacture during this period. The case retains the graceful architecture for which the reference is celebrated. Long flowing lugs extend naturally from the caseband, while the slim bezel maximizes dial presence and contributes to the watch's balanced proportions. Visible hallmarks beneath the lugs and along the case flank further underscore the quality and integrity of its construction. Powering this later example is the manually wound Calibre 27SC, one of Patek Philippe's most respected mid-century movements. The introduction of sweep center seconds reflected the era's evolving tastes, offering improved legibility while preserving the clean visual harmony of the Calatrava design. Beautifully finished and mechanically refined, the movement exemplifies the manufacture's commitment to precision and craftsmanship. For many collectors, the Ref. 570 represents the quintessential vintage Patek Philippe. Larger than its predecessors, yet every bit as elegant, it bridges the gap between prewar restraint and modern wearability. Decades after its introduction, the Calatravone remains one of the most important and desirable dress watches ever produced—a masterclass in proportion, execution, and timeless design.

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava
description: First presented in 1932 with the Reference 96, the Patek Philippe Calatrava is the benchmark for classic men’s dress watches. The groundbreaking reference set the stage for nearly every piece Patek has released since, and became the blueprint for other brands’ approaches to classy men’s timepieces. Heavily influenced by the Bauhaus design philosophy, the Calatrava was then considered extremely modern with its minimalist, ‘less is more’ approach to watch design. The Calatrava 96 was also one of the first pieces the brand released after the Stern family purchased a majority share in Patek Philippe in the early 30s. In many respects, the 96 is emblematic of the Stern family’s contributions to Patek. The 96 was one of the earliest round watches Patek ever made, and was also the very first serially produced piece to receive its own reference. In the years since 1932, Patek has released dozens of Calatrava references, each with its own idiosyncrasies. Almost all share the underlying DNA of the 96, prioritizing subtle elegance above all else. In 1985, Patek Philippe was looking to distinguish itself in a post quartz crisis era of the luxury watch market. Patek enlisted help from a brilliant Geneva-based ad man— Renee Bittel— to help Patek define itself for a new customer base. Bittel said Patek Philippe needed a symbol for the brand— something that would capture the classic Patek aesthetic and come to represent the brand. Then Patek President Philippe Stern asked Bittel what this would look like, and legend has it Bittel drew what would later become the 3919, another Bauhaus design, this time incorporating a hobnail bezel. The hobnail bezel first emerged in 1934 on the Reference 96D and Bittel recognized that its distinctive look was eye-catching, and classically Patek. Coupling the hobnail with a cream dial and black printed numerals, the 3919 quickly became the image of Patek Philippe. Today, the 3919 represents one of the best values in neo-vintage Patek Philippe. In 2006, Patek further built upon the 3919’s foundation and released the 5119, which essentially was a scaled up version of the 3919. For those seeking a slightly more contemporary take, the 5119 was a 36mm update to the smaller 3919. Additionally, the 5119 came outfitted with an exhibition caseback, a popular change for collectors. This particular example of the Reference 5119, executed in 18K yellow gold, is in outstanding condition and is ready to class up any modern day collection. Sure, you could get yourself a modern dress watch that tells the time just fine — and more often than not that piece slowly falls out of rotation. But a real Calatrava from the world’s greatest watchmaker is forever .

title: Tudor Oyster Prince Tropical "Tuxedo"
description: Few watches embody the original Tudor mission better than the Oyster Prince. Conceived by Rolex founder Hans Wilsdorf as a rugged, dependable watch for everyday wear, the Oyster Prince combined Rolex's celebrated Oyster case technology with Tudor's more accessible approach to watchmaking. Before its public launch, Tudor famously subjected the model to a series of punishing real-world trials, including a now-legendary test in which construction workers wore Oyster Princes while operating jackhammers. The watches emerged unscathed, helping establish the reputation for durability that remains central to the Tudor name today. This Oyster Prince Ref. 7950 offers a more refined side of that story. Known among collectors as the "Tuxedo" dial, the watch features a striking two-tone design with a rich black center framed by a radiant gilt chapter ring. The contrast creates the formal appearance that inspired its nickname, while also lending the dial remarkable depth and visual character. Decades of aging have softened the surface beautifully, producing the sort of honest patina that collectors spend years searching for. The 'gilt' details continue throughout the dial, from the 'applied' hour markers to the elegant 'dauphine' handset. Fine crosshair lines intersect at the center, drawing the eye inward and enhancing the watch's distinctly mid-century aesthetic. Above six o'clock, the signature "Rotor Self-Winding" designation proudly announces the watch's automatic movement, while the Tudor rose logo serves as a reminder of the brand's earliest years. Measuring 34mm in stainless steel, the Oyster Prince remains a masterclass in proportion. The case is compact by modern standards, but it wears with effortless elegance that feels perfectly suited to both casual and formal settings. Fitted to a tan leather strap with contrasting topstitching and a stainless-steel pin buckle, the watch strikes an appealing balance between vintage character and everyday wearability. Collectors often gravitate toward Tudor's military-issued Submariners and early chronographs, but watches like this reveal why the Oyster Prince remains one of the brand's most enduring creations. Rugged enough for the Arctic, refined enough for a dinner jacket, and blessed with one of the most attractive dial configurations of the era, the Tudor "Tuxedo" remains a timeless classic.

title: A.Lange & Söhne Zeitwerk
description: In the pantheon of modern watchmaking, few timepieces have challenged convention as successfully as the A. Lange & Söhne Zeitwerk. Introduced in 2009, it arrived not merely as a new model, but as an entirely new way of displaying time. At a time when most contemporary watches looked backward for inspiration, the Zeitwerk looked forward, combining nineteenth-century mechanical ingenuity with a display that felt almost digital in its clarity. This second-generation Zeitwerk Ref. 142.025 represents the evolution of that groundbreaking concept. Crafted in 950 platinum and measuring 41.9mm in diameter, it pairs the weight and presence of Lange's most prestigious case material with a rhodium-colored sterling silver dial. The result is strikingly monochromatic, allowing the architecture of the display to take center stage. Dominating the dial is the signature German-silver time bridge, a structural element inspired by the movement itself that frames the oversized jumping numeral displays for the hours and minutes. Unlike conventional displays that rely on rotating hands, the Zeitwerk presents the time through three jumping discs that advance instantaneously. Every sixty seconds, the patented constant-force escapement releases the precise amount of energy required to trigger the jump. At the top of each hour, all three discs can advance simultaneously, a mechanical event that remains one of the most captivating sights in contemporary horology. Powering the watch is Lange's manually wound Calibre L043.6, a movement comprised of 451 components and distinguished by its patented twin-barrel architecture. The redesigned system doubles the power reserve of earlier models to an impressive 72 hours, providing sufficient energy for 4,320 individual minute jumps while maintaining remarkable rate stability. The power-reserve indicator at twelve o'clock now highlights the final twelve hours in red, while a pusher at four o'clock allows the hour display to be adjusted independently, greatly simplifying time-setting. Turn the watch over, and the movement reveals why Lange remains the benchmark for modern finishing. Untreated German silver plates, hand-engraved details, black-polished components, gold chatons, and the intricate constant-force mechanism are displayed beneath a sapphire crystal caseback, transforming the movement into a work of mechanical architecture. The Zeitwerk is often described as a digital watch powered entirely by gears and springs. While technically true, that description undersells what makes it special. More than fifteen years after its introduction, it remains one of the boldest, most original, and most intellectually satisfying watches of the modern era—a watch that reimagined how time could be displayed while remaining unmistakably A. Lange & Söhne.

title: Bulova Stepped Case 'Tank'
description: The 1940s represented a golden era for American watch design. As manufacturers embraced the streamlined aesthetics of the Art Deco and Moderne movements, wristwatches evolved from simple instruments into expressions of style and sophistication. Few companies captured this transition better than Bulova, whose watches combined elegant design, dependable mechanics, and a distinctly American sense of refinement. This handsome Bulova dress watch dates to that period and showcases many of the details that have made the brand's pre-war and post-war models enduring collector favorites. Crafted in 14k yellow gold, the watch features a beautifully proportioned rectangular "Tank" case distinguished by stepped gadrooned detailing at both the top and bottom. These architectural flourishes lend depth and character to the case while reinforcing its unmistakably Deco-inspired profile. The black dial provides a dramatic backdrop for the stylized Arabic numerals, whose flowing forms seem to dance across the surface. Time is indicated by elegant gold-tone hands, while a recessed small-seconds register at six o'clock adds visual balance and period-correct charm. Decades of aging have softened the dial's appearance, creating the kind of character and authenticity that collectors prize in vintage watches. Powering the watch is a manually wound mechanical movement, preserving the tactile ritual that defined watch ownership during the era. It is paired with a black lizard strap and gold-tone pin buckle, a combination that perfectly complements the warmth of the gold case and the richness of the dark dial. Today, watches such as this serve as reminders of Bulova's remarkable contribution to twentieth-century watchmaking. With its sculptural stepped case, striking black dial, and classic small-seconds display, this 1940s example captures the elegance and optimism of an era when wristwatches were becoming true objects of design.

title: Universal Genève Faceted Star Crystal Watch
description: Universal Genève built its reputation on innovation, elegance, and a willingness to experiment with form. While the manufacture is often celebrated for icons such as the Compax and Polerouter, some of its most intriguing creations came in the realm of dress watches, where designers were free to explore shape, proportion, and light in ways that still feel remarkably modern today. This 1960s Universal Genève Faceted Star Crystal is a perfect example. Crafted in 14k yellow gold, the watch centers around a dramatic faceted crystal that transforms the entire dial experience. Rather than serving as a simple protective cover, the crystal acts as an architectural element, creating shifting reflections and geometric distortions that change with every movement of the wrist. The effect is subtle at first glance but endlessly captivating upon closer inspection. Beneath the sculptural crystal lies a clean silver dial fitted with slender applied markers and minimalist hands. The restrained dial design allows the crystal and case architecture to take center stage, resulting in a watch that feels more like modernist jewelry than a traditional timekeeper. Measuring approximately 28mm, the square case wears with the confidence and elegance characteristic of the era's most sophisticated dress watches. Powering the watch is a manually wound mechanical movement, a fitting choice for a timepiece whose appeal lies in its purity and simplicity. The watch is paired with a white top-stitched Saffiano leather strap secured by a gold-tone pin buckle, a combination that complements the warm tone of the case while enhancing its distinctly mid-century aesthetic. Equal parts watch, sculpture, and optical experiment, it serves as a reminder that some of the most compelling vintage watches are not necessarily the most complicated, but the ones willing to see familiar objects from an entirely different angle.

title: Universal Genève Sub Seconds Military
description: Before the Polerouter, before the Compax, and long before Universal Genève became one of the most sought-after names among vintage collectors, the manufacture was producing robust, purpose-built wristwatches for a world defined by uncertainty and change. Watches from the 1940s occupy a particularly fascinating chapter in the brand's history, balancing military practicality with the elegance that would later become a Universal Genève hallmark. This stainless-steel example embodies that spirit beautifully. The original silver dial has aged gracefully over the decades, developing the honest character and patina collectors prize. Large Arabic numerals dominate the display, providing excellent legibility while lending the watch a distinctly military character. Their warm tone contrasts wonderfully against the silver backdrop, while the original handset and small-seconds register at six o'clock complete a design that feels both utilitarian and remarkably refined. The unpolished stainless-steel case retains strong lines and houses a manually wound Universal Genève Calibre 330, a reliable 17-jewel movement from an era when durability mattered as much as precision. A screw-down caseback and internal dust cover further underscore the watch's practical intentions, reflecting the robust construction standards that helped establish Universal Genève's reputation during the period. Perhaps the most intriguing detail lies on the caseback itself. Rather than a formal presentation engraving, the watch bears a deeply scratched inscription that appears to have been added by hand at some point during its life. The crude, almost improvised nature of the engraving gives the watch an undeniable sense of mystery. Was it the mark of a soldier, a serviceman, an owner documenting a memory, or simply a practical identification? Whatever its origin, it serves as a tangible reminder that vintage watches often carry stories beyond those recorded in catalogs and archives. Today, this Universal Genève stands as a compelling survivor from the wartime era—honest, unpretentious, and full of character. The combination of the beautifully aged Arabic numeral dial, robust Calibre 330 movement, and enigmatic caseback inscription creates the sort of authenticity that simply cannot be manufactured.

title: Royce Tiger Eye 'Ellipse' New Old Stock
description: The 1960s and 1970s were a golden age for experimental watch design. As traditional round cases gave way to increasingly bold forms, Swiss manufacturers embraced geometry, asymmetry, and sculptural shapes, transforming watches into wearable works of modern art. This distinctive Royce is a perfect example of that creative spirit. Designed by Eska and inheriting design influences associated with the jewelry house Boucheron, this Swiss-made Royce places style squarely at center stage. The watch is built around an elegant elliptical case, where a polished gold-tone outer frame appears to float around the central dial, creating a striking sense of depth and movement. More jewelry than instrument at first glance, the design feels remarkably contemporary despite being more than half a century old. The focal point is undoubtedly the mesmerizing tiger-eye dial. Rich bands of golden brown and deep bronze shift dramatically as they catch the light, creating a constantly changing surface that brings warmth and character to the minimalist display. Free from numerals or hour markers, the dial allows the natural beauty of the stone to take center stage, interrupted only by a pair of slender white hands and the Royce signature. Powering the watch is a Swiss-made 17-jewel hand-wound movement, reflecting the era's commitment to mechanical craftsmanship. The crown is discreetly tucked into the upper edge of the case, preserving the uninterrupted flow of the elliptical silhouette and further emphasizing the watch's sculptural qualities. Remarkably, this example is preserved in new-old-stock condition, offering a rare opportunity to experience the watch as its original owner would have decades ago. Completing the package is its original, signed burgundy patent-leather strap, paired with a matching gold-plated pin buckle. The glossy, richly colored strap complements the warm tones of the tiger-eye dial beautifully and reinforces the watch's unmistakably luxurious 1970s character. Today, watches like this represent a fascinating intersection of horology, jewelry, and industrial design. With its dramatic shape, captivating tiger-eye dial, untouched condition, and original accessories intact, this Royce is a compelling reminder that some of the most memorable watches were created not to follow convention, but to challenge it.

title: Universal Genève Tank
description: While Universal Genève is best remembered today for its celebrated chronographs and the Gérald Genta-designed Polerouter, the manufacture was equally adept at producing elegant dress watches that reflected the changing tastes of the postwar era. Throughout the 1950s and 1960s, Universal Genève embraced clean lines, modern proportions, and understated sophistication, creating timepieces that remain remarkably contemporary decades later. This handsome rectangular model is a wonderful example of that approach. Executed in stainless steel and measuring a compact 20mm by 28mm, the watch embraces the refined proportions that defined mid-century dress watches. The brushed silver dial is beautifully restrained, featuring elongated 'Roman' numerals that radiate from the center with an almost architectural quality. Paired with slender painted black hands and a minimalist two-hand layout, the design achieves an elegant balance between formality and modernism. The sharply defined rectangular case further enhances the watch's clean aesthetic. Free from unnecessary embellishment, it frames the dial with crisp geometric lines that recall the enduring appeal of classic Tank-style watches while maintaining a distinct Universal Genève identity. The result is a watch that feels equally appropriate with tailoring today as it would have in the 1950s. Powering the watch is a manual wind mechanical movement, a fitting companion to a design that prioritizes simplicity and refinement above all else. Paired with a black leather strap, this Universal Genève offers the kind of incredibly understated sophistication that has become increasingly difficult to find in contemporary watchmaking. Elegant, slightly strict, and unmistakably mid-century, this Universal Genève serves as a reminder that some of the brand's most compelling creations were also its simplest. It really is so chic!

title: Breguet Classique Calendrier
description: Breguet makes the best dials in the biz. Yeah, we said it. Their signature engine-turned dials, individually numbered and hand-finished, are simply beautiful works of art. You’d be hard-pressed to find such fine attention to detail in a watch costing many times what, say, a time-only or time-and-date model from the brand’s Classique line trades for. Take this particular Classique, a Reference 7337BA/1E/AVO from 2022, featuring day, date and moonphase complications housed in a 39mm 18K yellow gold coin-edged case with a sapphire crystal, and gold winding crown. Its dial is comprised of cloud-de-Paris guilloché and silvered tracks, painted black 'Roman' indices, and a blued steel ‘Breguet’ handset. Powered by a micro-rotor automatic winding movement from Breguet, it comes paired to an exceptional yellow gold multi-link bracelet with double folding clasp. In excellent condition, this midsize masterpiece is waiting patiently for its next owner — preferably, someone who appreciates the craftsmanship and patience necessary to execute such a beautifully nuanced dial.

title: A. Lange & Söhne 1815 Tourbillon
description: There are tourbillons that announce themselves — and then there are those, like this A. Lange & Söhne 1815 Tourbillon ref. 730.032F , that quietly assert their authority. Introduced as part of Lange’s most classically minded family, the 1815 Tourbillon is already a study in restraint, but this enamel-dial variant elevates that ethos to something approaching purity. Cased in beautiful rose gold, it pairs one of the brand’s most technically ambitious calibers with one of its most traditional dial-making techniques. What sets the 1815 Tourbillon apart isn’t just the presence of a one-minute tourbillon at six o’clock, but what surrounds it — or rather, what doesn’t. The dial is rendered in a beautiful silver coloring with large Arabic numerals, a chemin-de-fer minutes track, and blued steel hands complete the picture. The result is a dial that feels at once archival and immediate, traditional yet unmistakably Lange. The model distinguishes itself not only through its rarity, but through the clarity of its execution. The tourbillon aperture is framed by a black-polished bridge, drawing the eye without disrupting the symmetry of the design. Despite the presence of a highly complicated regulating organ, the watch remains remarkably discreet — an object that reveals its depth slowly, over time. Housed in a rose case measuring 39.5mm in diameter and just over 11mm thick, it boasts the kind of balanced proportions that define the 1815 line, offering presence without excess. Flipping the watch over, the manually wound caliber L102.1 is on full display beneath a sapphire caseback. Here, Lange’s signature three-quarter plate architecture, hand-engraved balance cock, screwed gold chatons, and even a diamond endstone for the tourbillon axis underscore the brand’s uncompromising approach to finishing. More technically, the movement integrates both a stop-seconds mechanism for the tourbillon and a zero-reset function, allowing the seconds hand to snap precisely to zero when setting the time — an innovation that brings genuine chronometric utility to what is often a purely theoretical complication. This particular example is accompanied by its factory goodies. Paired to a signed brown alligator leather strap with a signed rose deployant clasp, it's a study in Teutonic restraint and quality that signals good taste from across the room. Whether the centerpiece of a larger collection or as the single occupant of an opulent watch box, there's no denying the 1815 Tourbillon's place in the pantheon of great modern timepieces.

title: Vacheron Constantin Saltarello Jump Hour
description: The Holy Trinity of watch brands: Patek Philippe, Audemars Piguet and Vacheron Constantin. Far less understood than either of its respected compatriots, Vacheron Constantin has a legacy of producing some of the very finest haute horlogerie complications in history — and some of the loveliest. What we have here is something different and decidedly more unique. A jump hour complication from the 1990s, this limited edition piece was made in just 200 examples in pink gold with a guilloche dial, hour at 12 in a framed window, and a retrograde minute display below. The case is a unique design on its own. A TV shape, the watch flaunts a multi step bezel and lug profile that reinforces the art deco aesthetic design language that inspires this piece. Flip the watch over, and you're greeted by an automatic winding movement observed through an exhibition caseback. A fantastic blend of retro and contemporary detailing, this watch is not a typical timekeeper, and for that, we love it!

title: A. Lange & Söhne Zeitwerk
description: A classic mechanical movement combined with a modern digital display go together like peanut butter and jelly … who would’ve thought? Well, A. Lange & Söhne did when they developed the Zeitwerk in 2009. At the time, the idea of merging a mechanical watch with a digital display was an exciting concept, and in many ways, was ahead of its time — true to the innovative ethos that we’ve come to identify with manufacture hailing from Glashütte . Equipped with a dual-disc mechanism, the Zeitwerk intuitively displays both the hours and minutes through two separate ‘digital’ display windows and is powered by Lange’s patented constant force escapement. Inspired by the renowned five-minute clock perched high above at the Semper Opera House in Dresden and beautifully balanced in its miniaturized execution, the Zeitwerk is a breathtaking example of mechanical art, with a decidedly German flair. This piece - a Reference 140.032 - is a fine example of the first-generation Zeitwerk, and comes housed in a 41.9mm 18K rose gold case featureing a polished bezel, a signed crown at 2 o’clock, a sapphire crystal and a sapphire exhibition caseback that beautifully frames Lange’s manual-winding Calibre L.043.1 movement. Its satin silver dial features a German silver plate housing both jumping hour and minute ‘digital’ displays, a power reserve indicator at 12 o’clock, and a silver-accented constant seconds sub-register at 6 o’clock. Paired to a signed brown alligator leather strap with a signed rose gold pin buckle, d ubbing this piece a mechanical marvel is not an over-statement … it’s undeniably accurate.

title: Breguet Classique Tourbillon Extra-Plat
description: Breguet makes the best dials in the biz. Yeah, we said it. Their signature engine-turned dials, individually numbered and hand-finished, are simply beautiful works of art. The brand also has equally impressive mechanical watchmaking chops to match. Patented in 1801 by Abraham-Louis Breguet, the tourbillon was designed to compensate for the chronometric inaccuracies gravity inflicts on pocket watch movements. In modern times, tourbillons don't have a practical advantage for timekeeping since wristwatches are always being worn in different positions throughout the day, but nonetheless, the tourbillon is a tribute to the quest for accuracy and excellence in fine watchmaking. The Breguet Classique Tourbillon Extra Plat isn’t merely the proud recipient of an excellent Breguet dial, however — it’s also a masterful blend of complicated simplicity. The timekeeping display is executed with blued Breguet hands at the center, a stunning tourbillon cage at 5 o'clock, and power reserve at 8:30. Measuring 41mm in diameter, the piece is an incredibly svelte 7.1mm to wear comfortably and compactly in spite of its complication. The secret? A brilliant slender automatic winding movement, Calibre 581 DR ticking within, measuring just 3mm in thickness. Simply refined on the top; a complicated dance party on the bottom. Dating to the 2020s, this piece is a work of art, displaying an array of beautiful engravings front and back. Stunning to behold and perfectly sized, this Breguet Classique Complications Tourbillon is stuff horological dreams are made of. Breguet doesn't quite get the attention and love it deserves. Between beautiful dial craft and beautiful movement craft, this watch is everything one could want on a piece of fine complicated watchmaking. Once you try it on, you’ll instantly understand what we mean!

title: Universal Genève Compax
description: There are few names in vintage watch collecting that carry the weight of Universal Genève. Long before the modern fascination with luxury sports watches, the Geneva manufacture established itself as one of Switzerland's premier chronograph specialists, producing elegant, technically sophisticated timepieces that remain highly coveted today. The Compax family stands among the brand's greatest achievements and helped define the modern chronograph as we know it. Offered here is a handsome Universal Genève Compax Ref. 52215, presented in a 33mm 14K yellow-gold case and paired with a striking period 'stretch' brick-link bracelet. Elegant without feeling delicate, the watch exemplifies Universal Genève's ability to blend sporting functionality with refined design. The silver dial features a classic compax layout with running seconds at 9 o'clock, a 30-minute chronograph register at 3, and a 12-hour totalizer at 6. Printed 'Arabic' numerals, slender 'feuille' hands, and a tachymeter scale complete a dial that is both highly legible and wonderfully balanced. The accompanying bracelet deserves special mention. The beautifully articulated brick-link construction drapes comfortably on the wrist and is fitted with an uncommon open-end sliding clasp, a thoughtful period detail that speaks to the quality of the watch's original presentation. Together, the bracelet and case create a cohesive mid-century aesthetic that feels every bit as compelling today as it did decades ago. Turning the watch over reveals a deeply personal engraving: " To M.S. Palmet From Junior Essex Troop. " More than a simple presentation inscription, the engraving connects the watch to a fascinating chapter of New Jersey history. Founded in 1931, the Junior Essex Troop (JET) was a military-style youth auxiliary organization affiliated with the famed Essex Troop of Cavalry, one of the most storied mounted units in the New Jersey National Guard. For generations, the organization provided young riders with instruction in horsemanship, discipline, and equestrian competition, becoming one of the state's premier youth riding programs. The inscription suggests this Compax was awarded to commemorate a significant achievement or milestone, preserving a tangible link to that tradition. Such provenance transforms the watch from a beautiful vintage chronograph into a piece of personal and regional history, carrying a story that extends far beyond the walls of Universal Genève's Geneva-based manufacture. Today, vintage Compax models remain among the cornerstones of serious Universal Genève collecting. With the historic manufacture relaunched in 2026 under the stewardship of Georges Kern's House of Brands Group, renewed attention has been focused on the brand's remarkable archive. This Ref. 52215 stands as a wonderful example of Universal Genève's golden era—an elegant chronograph distinguished by its beautiful proportions, uncommon bracelet, and the sort of character that only decades of history can provide.

title: Universal Genève Brooch Watch
description: Universal Genève occupies a special place in the history of watchmaking, celebrated for everything from groundbreaking chronographs to some of the most elegant dress watches of the twentieth century. Yet among the manufacture's most charming creations are its jewelry watches—objects that blur the line between timekeeping instrument and wearable sculpture. Offered here is a remarkable yellow-gold brooch watch dating to the mid-century period, showcasing Universal Genève's flair for both design and craftsmanship. Executed in warm yellow gold, the piece centers on a diminutive manually wound watch integrated into a sculptural bow motif. The highly stylized ribbon form reflects the optimism and glamour of postwar jewelry design, with sweeping, architectural folds that transform a familiar decorative element into something distinctly modern. Most fascinating is the orientation of the watch itself. Rather than facing outward in a traditional manner, the dial appears to be suspended upside down above the bow, allowing the wearer to read the time with a simple downward glance. Pinned to a lapel, dress, or jacket, the watch would have been perfectly positioned for discrete time keeping—a thoughtful detail that transforms this decorative jewel into a genuinely practical accessory. The silvered dial is signed Universal Genève and accented by applied indices and elegant dauphine hands, while the compact case provides a subtle counterpoint to the bold sculptural form below. Whether worn as originally intended or appreciated as a collectible object, it represents an era when Swiss watchmakers routinely collaborated with the world of fine jewelry to create imaginative expressions of personal style. Today, examples such as this are increasingly appreciated by collectors who recognize that Universal Genève's legacy extends far beyond the Polerouter and Compax. Rarely encountered and undeniably distinctive, this brooch watch offers a fascinating glimpse into a more playful, artistic, and inventive chapter of the brand's history.

title: DOXA 'Anti-Magnetique' Field Watch
description: DOXA's tool watches, particularly of the dive variety, have gained a following among collectors in recent years. We here at Analog/Shift have certainly carried the torch for DOXA's dive watches, and over the years have stocked our inventory (and shamelessly collected for ourselves) exceptional examples of their Sub 300s from the 1960s and 1970s. But while it's DOXA's dive watches that get the most attention, our love for the brand encompasses their whole range of products, rich with impressive timepieces dating to the company's founding. In 1889, Georges Ducommun founded DOXA in that horological hotbed, Le Locle. From the inception of the company, its main stock in trade was dress watches. Their expertly-engineered pocket watches earned a place of distinction with luxury consumers in the early 1900s, and in 1906 DOXA earned a Gold Medal at the International Exhibition in Milan. Throughout the 20th Century, DOXA introduced a wide variety of timepieces. They ranged from consumer grade, time-only watches to ornate ladies cocktail pieces, alarm clocks, precision cockpit instruments (including the first 8-day movement developed for use in automobiles), and military-issued wristwatches. This particular piece is a fantastic representation of the heritage field watch designs that emerged mid-century. A Reference 565, inspired by the Patek 565 Calatrava, this piece features a unique block-like case with the lugs sprouting straight from the midcase. This piece was designed to withstand everything --- it flaunts waterproofing, shock resistance, and anti-magnetic technology. In all cases, the goal was to create a watch that was built to stand the test of time. The result? A lovely 35mm classic piece that you need in your collection.

title: Juvenia Arithmo Calculator
description: What we have here is something truly unique. Made by fine Swiss watchmaker Juvenia, this "Arithmo" calculator watch is one of the coolest watches to come across our desks. Founded in 1860, Juvenia made a variety of beautiful pieces that simply aren't that common these days. The Airthmo is just one example. This piece is unique for its insane calculator functionality hidden under its oversized crystal hanging over the rotating calculator scales. With fixed and rotating slide rules, you can efficiently make precise calculations straight on the wrist. Introduced in the 40s as a practical solution for engineers, in the modern era of smart watches, this was one of the earliest calculator "apps" available for the wrist. If you're on the hunt for a fun vintage piece with loads of history and vintage charm behind it, don't let this beautiful radium-burned dial wind up on the wrist of another and snag this beauty!

title: Breitling Chronomat
description: Breitling has long been purveyor of chronographs to pilots, having designed models such as 1942’s Chronomat from the ground as a no-nonsense instrument for use in the cockpit. The Chronomat has evolved significantly since those days, retaining its aeronautical influence but greatly expanding upon its remit to include features such as dive watch-like water resistance and chronometer-grade accuracy. This particular piece, a steel execution likely dating to the early 2000s, features a very wearable, 39mm case with a sapphire crystal, 'fluted' pushers and a matching crown, a timing bezel, and a signed pill bead bracelet. Inside, it has a beautiful rare mother of pearl dial with contrast subsidiary registers, a matching handset, and Breitling's robust and reliable Calibre 13 automatic winding chronograph movement. Beautifully constructed, robust, and perfectly emblematic of a neo-vintgae timepiece from the brand, how can you go wrong?

title: Girard-Perregaux Vintage '1945'
description: Few watch brands can compete with Girard-Perregaux in the history department. Dating back to the late 1700's, Girard Perregaux has a story filled with innovation that includes pioneering efforts in early wristwatches and invaluable contributions to the engineering of the quartz movement. Like many other brands, GP worked hard during the 1940’s to build simple, robust watches that could be worn day-to-day, the results of which were myriad beautiful timepieces that can still be had relatively affordably. This particular GP, however, is a modern take on a midcentury aesthetic. This gorgeous Reference 2595 is housed in a 28mm x 44mm rose gold case with a signed crown, a domed sapphire crystal, and an exceptional dial. It features a blacked finished with applique numerals and subsidiary seconds. Although this model dates to the 90s, it certainly feels like a 40s or 50s classic. Powered by a manually wound movement, it preserves the classic historical appeal of these timepieces in a surprisingly modern package. Truly, this is a superlative, gorgeous contemporary dress watch that would make an excellent accent to a suit, or for anyone who enjoys a refined look with casual attire. It walks the line between modernity and vintage appeal, and does so in a truly unique way. This one is a keeper!

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava Weekly Calendar
description: There is unusual for Patek Philippe—and then there’s the Reference 5212A-001. At a glance, it reads like a classic Calatrava: clean lines, restrained proportions, and that unmistakable sense of balance that Patek Philippe has spent nearly two centuries perfecting. But look closer, and the 5212A seriousness begins to relax—in the best possible way. Introduced in 2019, this reference brings together a rarely seen complication: the weekly calendar. Alongside the traditional day and date, it tracks the week number, displayed via a central hand against an outer track that corresponds to the months. It’s the kind of function that feels almost academic—until you realize how elegantly it’s been executed. The dial remains airy, legible, and quietly dynamic, a small miracle given the amount of information on display. Then there’s the typography. In a move that feels almost subversive for a brand so rooted in tradition, Patek based the dial text on hand-drawn numerals from the design phase. The result is subtly irregular—each character just slightly different, lending the watch a human touch that’s rare at this level of watchmaking. It’s idiosyncratic, charming, and entirely intentional. Housed in a 40mm stainless steel case—still something of a novelty in Patek’s complicated lineup—the 5212A features stepped lugs, a polished bezel, and a silver opaline dial with blackened gold indices and dauphine hands. Inside, the Caliber 26-330 SC C J SE powers the display with quiet precision, paired to a tan topstitched calfskin strap that leans into its understated personality. This particular Ref. 5212A also includes the original inner and outer boxes, leather folder, and pamphlets. It’s thoughtful. A little eccentric. Deeply considered. Perfectly charming. It proves that even Patek can loosen its tie—just enough to make things interesting.

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava Pilot Travel Time
description: The Patek Philippe Calatrava needs no introduction. Yet every so often, Patek Philippe reminds us that even its most traditional collection can surprise us. The inspiration for the Calatrava Pilot Travel Time can actually be traced back to a little-known chapter of Patek Philippe history. In the 1930s, the manufacture produced a handful of oversized aviator's watches featuring large luminous numerals and highly legible dials for professional use. These rare pieces remained largely forgotten until 2015, when Patek shocked the watch world by introducing the Calatrava Pilot Travel Time Ref. 5524G—a watch that combined vintage aviation aesthetics with one of the brand's most useful modern complications. Traditionalists were startled. Collectors were intrigued. And today, the model has become one of the most distinctive references in the contemporary Patek Philippe catalog. This particular example, Reference 7234G, distills the formula into a more versatile 37.5mm 18K white gold case. Featuring a sapphire crystal, signed crown, and the collection's signature knurled travel-time pushers positioned on the left side of the case, it retains all the charm of its larger sibling while offering proportions that wear beautifully on a wide range of wrists. It also includes boxes, folio, papers, and certificate of origin. The matte blue dial is both handsome and highly functional. Large luminous 'Arabic' numerals and a matching 'sword' handset provide exceptional legibility, while Patek's ingenious Travel Time complication allows the wearer to track a second time zone via a skeletonized local-hour hand. Day/night apertures for both home and local time, a date display at 6 o'clock, and a crisp chemin de fer minute track complete one of the most thoughtfully executed travel watches on the market. Turn the watch over, and the sapphire display back reveals Patek Philippe's self-winding Calibre 324 S C FUS movement, a beautifully finished manufacture caliber that combines everyday practicality with the refinement expected from Geneva's most celebrated watchmaker. The Calatrava Pilot Travel Time occupies a unique place within the Patek Philippe universe. It's sporty without being casual, complicated without being intimidating, and deeply rooted in history while feeling entirely modern. For the collector who appreciates Patek Philippe's willingness to color outside the lines, few references are more compelling.

title: Patek Philippe Annual Calendar Moonphase
description: In 1991, the soon-to-be graduates at the Geneva School of Engineering were presented with their final project prior to receiving their diploma — to simplify the perpetual calendar. Although the task was easier said than done, their work led to the inception of the annual calendar complication, patented by Patek Philippe in collaboration with the bright engineering minds at the GSE. Five years later, Patek debuted the Reference 5035, a watch powered by the world’s first-ever annual calendar movement and one that finally bridged the gap between a triple-date function and the formidable quantième perpétuel . This slightly later annual calendar, a Reference 5146J, is housed in a beautifully proportioned 39mm 18K yellow gold case with a sapphire crystal, signed crown, and a smooth, polished bezel. It features a luminous, white dial with applied indices, recessed subsidiary registers indicating day and month, a moonphase aperture and date window at 6 o'clock, and a matching luminous 'feuille' handset. Powered by Patek Philippe's Calibre 315 S IRM QA LU self-winding movement, it comes complete with a signed black alligator leather strap, signed 18K yellow gold deployant buckle and Certificate of Origin. This piece packs pedigree, elegance, function and outstanding craftsmanship — exactly what you'd expect from a Patek Philippe!

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava
description: First presented in 1932 with the Reference 96, the Patek Philippe Calatrava is the benchmark for classic men’s dress watches. The groundbreaking reference set the stage for nearly every piece Patek has released since, and became the blueprint for other brand’s approaches to classy men’s timepieces. Heavily influenced by the Bauhaus design philosophy, the Calatrava was then considered extremely modern with its minimalist, less-is-more approach to watch design. The Calatrava 96 was also one of the first pieces the brand released after the Stern family purchased a majority share in Patek Philippe in the early 30s. In many respects, the 96 is emblematic of the Stern family’s contributions to Patek. The 96 was one of the earliest round watches Patek ever made, and was also the very first serially produced piece to receive its own reference. In the years since 1932, Patek has released dozens of Calatrava references, each with its own idiosyncrasies. Almost all share the underlying DNA of the 96, prioritizing subtle elegance above all else. This piece, a Reference 5227G-001, is the very image of the elegant Calatrava design, but in a modern silhouette. With a nearly perfect 39mm 18K white gold case and its 9mm case thickness, it’s an incredibly easy-wearing watch. The case features downturned lugs, a polished bezel, a sapphire crystal, a signed crown and an officer-style caseback that when opened, reveals the maison’s Calibre 315 / 190 self-winding movement. Furnished with applied white gold indices, a ‘dot’ minute track, a matching 'dauphine' handset and a framed date window at 3 o’clock set against an ivory tone, the dial is an exercise of simplistic beauty. Outfitted to a signed black alligator leather strap with an 18K white gold pin buckle, this piece is an exceptional example of the traditional Calatrava design and the maison’s artisanship. It also includes the inner and outer boxes, folio, papers/pamphlet, hangtags, and certificate of origin. Simply put, this Calatrava is everything you need, and nothing you don’t.

title: Omega  De Ville 'Emeraude' Tank by Andrew Grima
description: There was a brief moment in the 1970s when watch design became genuinely experimental. Traditional round cases gave way to bold geometric forms, crystals became sculptural elements, and the line between jewelry, industrial design, and watchmaking began to blur. Few brands embraced this shift more elegantly than Omega, particularly through the influence of celebrated jewelry designer Andrew Grima and the avant-garde design language that emerged from the era. This Omega De Ville 'Emeraude' is a perfect example. Housed in a striking 22mm x 46mm stainless steel case, the watch is less a conventional dress watch than a study in proportion and perspective. Its elongated rectangular form is dominated by a dramatic faceted crystal that transforms the dial beneath into something almost jewel-like. The effect recalls a cut gemstone viewed from above, refracting light and adding depth to an otherwise minimalist design. The grey dial is a lesson in restraint. Slim 'baton' markers radiate from the center, while simple hands and discreet De Ville branding let the watch's architecture speak for itself. Free from unnecessary decoration, the dial feels remarkably modern even half a century later. This aesthetic traces directly back to Omega's collaboration with Andrew Grima, whose groundbreaking "About Time" collection challenged conventional notions of what a watch could look like. While the Emeraude was part of Omega's subsequent commercial offerings, it clearly carries Grima's influence: bold geometry, gemstone-inspired forms, and a willingness to prioritize design over timekeeping. Inside beats Omega's manually wound Caliber 620, a reliable and elegantly slim movement perfectly suited to the watch's sleek profile. The piece is fitted to a warm tan leather strap with a signed Omega steel pin buckle, completing a look that feels simultaneously futuristic and unmistakably 1970s. Today, collectors spend enormous sums pursuing the era's most famous design icons. Watches like the Emeraude remind us that some of the most interesting creations came from brands willing to take risks.

title: Harry Winston Premier Chronograph
description: Some watches tell time. Some watches tell a story. The Harry Winston Premier does both. Introduced in 1989, the Premier collection quickly became the signature watch line of the famed New York jeweler, translating the glamour and sophistication of Harry Winston's Fifth Avenue salon into wristwatch form. While many brands borrowed from traditional Swiss watchmaking cues, Harry Winston approached design from a different perspective—one rooted in jewelry, architecture, and visual drama. Nowhere is that more evident than in the case design. This particular Premier Chronograph, Reference 200-MCA37G, is crafted in 18K yellow gold and features the collection's unmistakable triple-arched lugs, inspired by the entrance to Harry Winston's iconic flagship salon on Fifth Avenue. These architectural elements transform the watch from a simple chronograph into something far more distinctive, giving it a silhouette recognizable from across the room. The silver dial is equally well considered. Three recessed registers create a balanced tri-compax layout, while oversized stylized Arabic numerals add character without overwhelming the design. A date aperture at 6 o'clock maintains symmetry, and subtle textural contrasts across the dial surface provide depth and visual interest. The result is elegant, slightly theatrical, and unmistakably Harry Winston. Turn the watch over, and a sapphire display back reveals the automatic chronograph movement within, reminding you that beneath the glamour lies serious Swiss watchmaking pedigree. This is not merely a jewelry house's interpretation of a watch—it's a fully realized luxury chronograph from one of the most celebrated names in luxury.
