title: Piaget Polo Two-Tone Diamonds
description: There’s nothing more classic and appealing than a simple dress watch. Though to be fair, when we say ‘simple’, we mean ‘uncomplicated’ — not unattractive! The 20th century saw a plethora of such watches hit the market. Generally available on leather straps and featuring two or three hands, these reliable wristwatches kept time during the classiest decades of the past 100 years. However, some were more innovative than others. Take this exquisite piece from Piaget, specialists in ultra-thin watchmaking: seamlessly machined such that there’s no perceivable break from watch head to bracelet, it’s as much akin to a piece of jewelry as it is to a more traditional wristwatch. Housed in a 34mm, yellow gold and white gold two tone alternating case with a fantastic, integrated bracelet with a signed clasp, this Polo features a two tone dial with brushed yellow gold components and bands of white gold diamond-set striping. You read that correctly — diamond ... set ... striping . Imagine the looks of curiosity — and envy — that you’ll stir up when rocking this bold Piaget at a cocktail party. With its eye-catching design, fascinating dial, and awesome bracelet, this is a standout timepiece appropriate for virtually any wrist. This piece could easily be mistaken for a bracelet with the design carrying straight onto the dial. That’s really part of the charm of so many of Piaget’s late 20th century watch designs. While these pieces went underappreciated for many years, we have recently seen a well-deserved surge in interest for these avant-garde designs.

title: Enigma Ladies Sports Watch
description: Gianni Bulgari, a watch designer and third-generation member of the famed Greek-Italian jewelry dynasty, feels that women's sports watches should be just as compelling as men's pieces. In 1989, following the sale of his stake in the Bulgari company to his family, he established a new watchmaking firm called GB Enigma in Switzerland to design incredible timepieces with unusual designs. This particular Enigma, an integrated strap sports piece, is emblematic of the firm's bold design philosophy: Housed in a 27mm 18K gold case with an integrated leather strap with matching pin buckle, this piece is completed with a black cabochon crown, a tapisserie dial with applied lume plots a skeletonized 'sword' handset, and a three o'clock date window. All told, this piece would make a great everyday watch. A lesser known brand with a powerful pedigree, an excellent design, and a practical package for everyday applications, don't let this piece slide past you! It's also a great value!

title: Breitling Chronomat
description: Breitling has long been purveyor of chronographs to pilots, and the original Breitling Chronomat models of 1942 were built from the ground up to be no-nonsense instruments for use in the cockpit. The watch that you're looking at here is a contemporary Chronomat model that is equally no-nonsense! Dating to the 2020s, this Chronomat packs 200 meters of water resistance into the 44mm stainless steel case. Set with a polished steel bi-directional bezel, this piece possesses the classic Breitling case and bracelet paring of world renown. Its matte black dial conveys a plethora of information: An outer tachymeter scale and 1/5th-seconds track are joined by an outsized date window between 4 and 5 o'clock, applied luminous indices, and a triple-register chronograph display with running seconds, 12-hour, and 30-minute registers. A luminous 'sword' handset rounds out the feature set. Powered by the automatic Breitling B01 chronograph movement with a 70 hour power reserve, this hardy tool watch comes paired to its correct stainless steel multi-link bracelet with a signed folding clasp. Happily, it also includes its kit. In need of a serious everyday tool watch that you don't have to baby? Look no further!

title: Jaeger-LeCoultre Reverso
description: The Reverso is, in essence, one of the very first sports wristwatches. Despite its refined and elegant appearance, it combined utility with a sleek Art Deco exterior that has become an icon of horological design. But in the case of the Reverso, looks deceive. Though the model appears at first glance a dress watch, it owes its existence to the gentlemanly sport of polo. While touring India in the early 1930s, Swiss businessman César de Trey met a British polo player who'd just cracked the crystal of his watch on the field. De Trey returned to Switzerland with an idea already taken root in his head, which he then discussed with Jacques-David LeCoultre: What if a watch could be made with a case that could reverse? The reversible case, masterminded by designer Alfred Chauvot, was Jaeger-LeCoultre's solution to the problems polo players faced on the field. Once reversed, the delicate components of the case were protected from the shocks sustained while on horseback. No more would polo players crack the crystals or damage the dials of their watches. Chauvot took out a patent for the Reverso in March 1931. Produced chiefly in steel, Jaeger-LeCoultre also released the Reverso in gold, and decorated the case back with engravings or even miniature portraits. This particular Reverso, comes in with a 30mm stainless steel reversible case featuring an exhibition caseback on the reverse side. The front facing dial features a classic 'Arabic' layout with subsidiary seconds and a guilloche dial center. Powered by an in-house manually wound movement, this piece comes fitted to an alligator strap with a signed deployant clasp. In terms of elegant design and horological prowess, this watch punches way above its weight class, and simply cannot be overlooked.

title: IWC Pilot's Watch Mark XVI
description: The IWC Pilot's Watch can trace its history back to the oversized timepieces produced for military aviators in 1940. These enormous pieces were originally designed for maximum legibility in a cockpit setting, and — believe it or not — were meant to be worn on the pilot's thigh! Today, the Pilot's line is perhaps IWC's most identifiable collection, featuring a variety of case and dial configurations suited for any taste — provided your wrist can handle the larger-than-average dimensions. If not, that’s where the Mark series comes in. These watches are contemporary takes on the original Mark X and Mark XI watches from the 1940s. This particular watch, a Pilot's Watch MARK XVI, features a 39mm brushed stainless steel case with a sapphire crystal, a signed crown, and a polished, stepped bezel. It houses a luminous matte black dial with printed ‘Arabic’ indices, a matching ‘sword’ handset, and IWC's Calibre 30110 with 21 jewels and a 41-hour power reserve within. Paired to a beautiful multi-link bracelet, this piece is the essence of a Pilot's watch. With excellent legibility, handsome looks, and utilitarian, military influence, it’s no surprise that the Mark series has become a cornerstone of the IWC collection.

title: Breitling Superocean Automatic 36
description: Breitling has long been purveyor of chronographs to pilots, but in the 1950's, the budding popularity of dive watches such as the Rolex Submariner and the Blancpain Fifty Fathoms pushed it to enter that race. In 1957, the brand released both a time-only dive watch, the Superocean Reference 1004, and a chronograph in the form of the Reference 807. These pieces would form the beginning of a long-lasting and ever-evolving line of nautical watches beloved by many. The watch we’re offering here is a tremendously cool, contemporary take on the Superocean that started it all. Housed in an comfortable 36mm case with a polished, white ceramic timing bezel; a signed, screw-down crown; a sapphire crystal; and a signed, blue rubber dive strap with a matching folding clasp, it's a really comfortable everyday companion to add to your collection. The luminous, blue-white dial features quadrant 'baton' markers and 'square' plots with polished surrounds as well as a stylized, luminous handset with a square-tipped seconds hand. Its attention-grabbing attribute, however, lies within a large, white chapter ring that houses a fully graduated minute track. Powered by Breitling’s COSC-certified automatic Caliber 17, this piece is accompanied by its box, travel pouch, hangtag, and card. If you’ve been on the hunt for a robust diver with some everyday appeal, then this Breitling is the answer to your prayers!

title: Tissot Squelette
description: Oftentimes in the hobby of watch collecting, there can be a bit too much focus on what the hot watch of the moment might be - the piece that no one can get, or the watch that everyone wants to own purely so they can say they own it. But in this frenzy of emphasis on what the next big windfall investment piece might be, there are literally tons of watches and brands which slip woefully under the radar. Tissot is among those brands. This particular Tissot is a modern beauty unlike anything else in the price category. A manually-wound skeleton, this piece has no real dial, with a complete openwork look into the industrial movement design architecture. The midcase is brushed, with a brushed bezel and polished case band. It's particularly exciting to see brands like Tissot investing in manually-wound movements. For a modernist look into traditional watchmaking, you'd be hard pressed to beat this piece at the price point! This one will go fast!

title: Gucci Tiger's Eye Sautoir Timepiece Necklace
description: There’s something irresistibly glamorous about a not-so-secret watch that isn't worn on the wrist. In the 1960s and ’70s, houses like Gucci began to blur the line between horology and jewelry, creating pieces that were as much about presence as they were about precision. The sautoir — a long, draped, and unmistakably elegant necklace with a pendant — became a canvas for that idea. Less about checking the time, more about making an entrance. This Gucci tiger’s eye watch necklace is a perfect embodiment of that moment. Crafted in 18K yellow gold, the long, fluid chain catches the light with every movement, leading to a sculptural pendant measuring just over 4 inches. At its center sits a warm, chatoyant tiger’s eye dial — its natural striations shimmering between golden honey and deep brown depending on the angle. Matching tiger’s eye beads at the ends add a tactile, almost talismanic quality to the piece. Signed Gucci Italy and powered by a manually movement, it’s as thoughtfully made as it is visually striking. But make no mistake, this isn’t about precision timing without numerals or indices. It’s about mood. A louche jet-setting exceptionally Gucci mood! A watch, yes. But more than that, especially with Gucci mining this particular period on the fashion side, it's an ultra-stylish piece of jewelry with a real sense of timing.

title: Patek Philippe Annual Calendar Flyback Chronograph
description: The annual calendar is one of those quietly brilliant complications — the kind that reveals its genius the longer you live with it. Invented and patented by Patek Philippe in the 1990s, it elegantly bridges the gap between simple calendar watches and their more complex perpetual counterparts. Accounting for months of varying lengths, it requires correction just once a year, at the end of February — a small marvel of mechanical logic disguised as everyday convenience. But this is no ordinary annual calendar. The Reference 5905P-001 pairs that ingenuity with a flyback chronograph, allowing the wearer to reset and restart the timing function with a single push. It’s a complication born from utility — timing laps, intervals, moments that matter — yet here it’s executed with the kind of refinement only Patek can deliver. The result is a watch that feels as technically accomplished as it is visually composed. Housed in a 42mm platinum case, this example features a rich blue dial that shifts beautifully in the light, anchored by applied indices and a crisp white minute track framing the chronograph register. The layout is classic Patek: day, date, and month displayed across the top, with a running seconds indication subtly integrated above six. The luminous obelisk hands complete the look, balancing legibility with elegance. Turn the watch over, and the automatic Calibre CH 28-520 QA 24H comes into view through a sapphire caseback — a movement that perfectly encapsulates the brand’s approach to high watchmaking: technically sophisticated, immaculately finished, and built to last generations. Paired with a blue alligator strap and platinum pin buckle, and offered with its full complement of original accessories, this is a piece that delivers on every level. Complicated without being complicated to live with, which, in many ways, is the ultimate luxury.

title: Girard-Perregaux Laureato Chronograph 42
description: There’s a certain confidence in a watch that doesn’t need to reinvent the wheel — it simply refines it. The Girard-Perregaux Laureato has long occupied that sweet spot between sport and sophistication, a design born in the 1970s that remains as relevant today as it was at its inception. Its signature architecture — the interplay between a round case and octagonal bezel, paired with a seamlessly integrated bracelet — remains one of the most quietly compelling shapes in modern watchmaking. This contemporary Laureato Chronograph, Reference 81020-11-431-11A, leans into that legacy with a crisp, steel execution and a striking blue dial. Housed in a 42mm stainless steel case with a domed bezel and screw-down crown, it offers a reassuring sense of solidity on the wrist. The dial itself is rich and dynamic, shifting in tone depending on the light, with applied 'index' markers and luminous hands ensuring clarity at a glance. The chronograph layout is clean and balanced, delivering functionality without sacrificing the design’s inherent elegance. Powered by a Swiss automatic movement and water resistant to 100 meters, this is a watch built for daily wear — equally at home under a cuff or out in the world. The integrated steel bracelet with folding clasp completes the package, reinforcing that fluid, cohesive feel that defines the Laureato line. Sporty, architectural, and effortlessly wearable, it’s a modern classic that knows exactly what it is, and doesn’t try too hard to be anything else.

title: Heuer Calculator Automatic Chronograph
description: There is perhaps no more versatile complication than the chronograph. From race cars to rocket ships, boats to battlefields, you are likely to find a chronograph being employed to measure a plethora of tasks and times. From the Greek khrónos (“time) and gráphō (“to write”), a chronograph is a watch that has the ability to record time, generally via the addition of small sub-counters that register minutes and hours. Though many storied brands produced notable chronographs during the complication’s heyday from the 1930s through the 1970s, numerous other firms fell by the wayside during the Quartz Crisis, folding completely and disappearing or being rolled up into conglomerates that pillaged their stores of parts. Heuer, for its part, is still around today as TAG Heuer, but its pre-TAG period was perhaps its most fertile era of chronograph design. Take the Calculator watch, for example: this special model took advantage of the brand's esteemed automatic chronograph movement technology and paired it with a unique two-part slide rule bezel in what can best be described as a sort of mechanical calculator: Using the bezel, the wearer can easily calculate distance and weight and convert between metric and imperial. Pretty neat! This particular Heuer Calculator watch, a Reference 110.633, dates to the 1970s and features a 45.5mm 'tonneau-shaped' stainless steel case with an outer calculator bezel, dual 'pump' pushers, a left-hand crown, and a stainless steel multi-link bracelet. Its dial is a picture of legibility: Featuring an outer 1/5th-seconds track in white, luminous 'dash' indices, a dual-register chronograph with 30-minute and 12-hour counters, a date window at 6 o'clock, and a luminous orange 'baton' handset, it's easy to use as a time-recording device or for more complex calculations. Powered by the Heuer Calibre 12 automatic chronograph movement and paired to a cool stainless steel multi-link bracelet, this unique tool watch is an awesome vestige of one of the most creative periods in chronograph design. It brings a smile to our faces every time — we're confident that it'll do the same for you.

title: Seiko Speedtimer SRQ057 'Datsun'
description: Seiko makes fantastic watches. Pure and simple. From the rare as hen's teeth Hi-Beat 6159 to the film-famous 6105 and 6309 models to the economy workhorse SXK007, Japanese watchmakers perfected incredibly well-made tool watches decades ago - and at prices that make the most diehard Swiss watch fans question their spending habits. This piece, a Reference SRQ057 , dates to 2025 and recalls one of the coolest pieces of Seiko history. In 1971, a Seiko Datsun was on the wrist of number 11 when he won the East-African Safari Rally, one of the most harrowing races in history. The incredible chrono we have here is a tribute limited edition of the Datsun, sporting the advantages of modern watchmaking including sapphire crystals and an updated automatic movement. The piece measures 42mm in diameter and features an automatic movement within. Built on a reputation for fine chronograph construction, this Seiko is one to save for the ages, recalling one of the coolest moves in Seiko history. These are wonderful timepieces that represent just about everything that we love about Seiko and are overlooked by many. Don't make that mistake!

title: Lucien Piccard Ladies Diamond 'Cocktail' Watch
description: In the 1950s and 1960s, the cocktail watch wasn’t just an accessory, it was part of the occasion. These pieces were designed to disappear into the rhythm of an evening, catching light rather than attention, pairing effortlessly with silk, champagne, and late hours. Small in scale but often extravagant in execution, they balanced mechanical ingenuity with jewelry-level artistry in a way that feels increasingly rare today. This particular example from Lucien Piccard captures that spirit beautifully. Founded in 1923 in Lausanne, the brand built its reputation on elegant, refined dress watches, and this piece leans fully into that heritage. The petite dial sits almost like a secret at the center of a fully diamond-set case, framed by brilliant stones that extend seamlessly into a 'tennis' style bracelet. Tapered 'baguette' accents add structure and geometry, giving the piece just enough architectural edge to balance the sparkle. Look closer, and the charm deepens. The signed crown features Piccard’s signature flourish — a subtle, almost whimsical curlicue that feels delightfully out of step with the otherwise formal design. It’s a small detail, but exactly the kind that gives a watch personality. Finished with a box clasp and safety latch, the diamond 'tennis' style bracelet wears as fluidly as it looks. Light, intricate, and undeniably glamorous, it’s a reminder of a time when watches were made not just to tell time, but to celebrate it.

title: Breguet Classique
description: There are few names in watchmaking that carry the same quiet authority as Breguet — and even fewer that can claim to have shaped the very language of modern horology. Founded in 1775 by Abraham-Louis Breguet, the maison is responsible for some of the most important inventions in watchmaking history, including the tourbillon, the Breguet overcoil, and the 'pare-chute' shock protection system. Just as influential, however, is the brand’s design vocabulary: engine-turned guilloché dials, elegant 'Roman' numerals, and those unmistakable blued 'Breguet' hands. These weren’t just aesthetic choices — they were innovations in legibility and refinement, developed for an elite clientele that included royalty, scientists, and statesmen. That balance of technical mastery and visual restraint remains at the core of Breguet today. This Ladies’ Classique Ref. 8561 is a perfect expression of that enduring philosophy. Crafted in 18K white gold, the 25.5mm case is elegantly framed by a diamond-set bezel and lugs, adding brilliance without disrupting the watch’s elegance. Beneath the sapphire crystal sits Breguet’s signature silvered guilloché dial that is engine-turned by hand, individually finished, and endlessly captivating as it plays with the light. Blued steel hands sweep across 'Roman' numerals with that unmistakable Breguet grace, while a signed crown, marked with the maison’s “B,” completes the overall design. Powered by a manual-wind movement and paired with a complementary burgundy alligator strap, it wears with quiet ceremony and style. Understated, intricate, and deeply rooted in tradition, this is Breguet, not simply a manufacture, but a living blueprint for what fine watchmaking can be.

title: Patek Philippe Twenty-4
description: Patek Philippe may be known for its complicated calendar watches, but it’s equally renowned for the simple, elegant dress watches it makes for both men and women. Take the Twenty-4 line, for example: Released in 1999, this ladies’ collection is geared toward the modern women in search of a superlative timepiece that oozes elegance and class. Available in rectangular and round case profiles in various metals and configurations, it’s one of the best dedicated women’s watch collections on the market today. This particular Twenty-4, a Reference 4910/20G-011 from circa 2004, is a quietly expressive take on one of Patek Philippe’s most enduring designs. Housed in a 25mm rectangular case, it features polished brancards set with two elegant rows of diamonds, framing a soft cream dial with a matching handset. A Calatrava-signed crown and integrated multi-link bracelet complete the look, balancing refinement with everyday wearability. In great condition, showing light wear and powered by a reliable quartz E15 movement, this is a stunning timepiece that has to be seen to be believed.

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava
description: Patek Philippe has long been known for its complicated watchmaking, but following the stock market crash of 1929, fewer clients had the means to purchase these high-end timepieces. After securing a controlling interest in the firm, Jean and Charles Henri Stern decided to create a simple watch that would come in at a lower price point and appeal to the firm’s clientele. Using the principles espoused by the Bauhaus school and its minimalist, function-first philosophy, Patek conceived the Calatrava, taking its name from the Spanish military order established in the 12th century which had become the symbol of Patek Philippe. Since its debut in 1932, the Calatrava has become a byword for a simple, time-only dress watch — even from brands other than Patek itself. This piece, a Reference 6119G-001, builds on the foundational designs of its three-hand predecessors and is housed in a 39mm white gold case with a guilloché Clous de Paris bezel, signed crown, a sapphire crystal and a svelte case profile that will delight any wrist. The dial features a dynamic, vertically satin brushed anthracite tone acting as a canvas for its applied gold indices, the constant-seconds subsidiary register at 6 o’clock, a 'dauphine' handset and a white-accented ‘railroad’ minute track Powered and visible by way of a sapphire exhibition caseback, this Calatrava features a hand-wound Patek Philippe Calibre 30-255 PS and comes fitted to a signed black alligator leather strap with a signed 18K white gold pin buckle. This particular model also comes with its leather folio and Certificate of Origin. A proper Calatrava from the world’s greatest watchmaker is forever.

title: Patek Philippe Aquanaut
description: The Patek Philippe Aquanaut may be one of the most important modern luxury sport watches on the market. The Reference 5060J, launched in 1996 for the 20th anniversary of the Nautilus, was a sort of transitional watch. Borrowing features from the Nautilus but doing away with the famed case “ears” of that porthole-inspired model and adding lugs, it provided the basis for the Reference 5060A in 1997, the first model actually bearing the Aquanaut name. The Aquanaut would go on to form the basis of a full collection of luxury sports watches that provided the entry point into the Patek Philippe catalog. This piece, a Reference 5167/1A-001, dates to 2016 and features a 40mm stainless steel case with a satin-finished bezel, sapphire crystal, a signed screw-down crown and a water resistance rating up to 120 meters. On the dial you'll find all of the signature Aquanaut features present — offered in an ombre anthracite tone that fades to black towards the edges, 'hobnail' texturing, luminous Arabic indices, a matching luminous handset and a date indicator at 3 o’clock. In excellent condition throughout and fitted to a black rubber strap with a signed steel button-deployant clasp, this piece is accompanied by all of its factory goodies including its inner and outer box set, signed leather folio, and a Certificate of Origin, alongside the signed steel multi-link bracelet it was originally sold with. With more presence on the wrist compared to its older siblings, the 5167 remains one of most highly-coveted steel sport watches on the market. Try it on and you'll see why!

title: Longines 'Slim' Tank
description: There’s a particular kind of confidence in doing less, and doing it exceptionally well. Longines has long understood this balance, and pieces like this are a perfect expression of that restraint. Rather than relying on ornament or complication, it leans fully into proportion, surface, and line — the quiet fundamentals that define truly enduring design. Housed in an elongated rectangular 18K yellow gold case, this ultra-slim “Tank” silhouette feels almost architectural on the wrist. The brushed gold dial continues that theme, stripped down to its essence with only a subtle 'crosshair' layout and a simple handset. No numerals, no excess — just a study in symmetry and tone that shifts beautifully with the light. Powered by a manual-wind movement, it stays true to traditional watchmaking while maintaining an almost jewelry-like presence. Paired with a rose-colored alligator strap, the warmth of the gold case is amplified, giving the watch an understated yet unmistakably elegant character.

title: Piaget Jumbo 'Beta 21'
description: There was a moment in the late 1960s when the Swiss watch industry hit reset. The 1969 introduction of the Seiko Astron — the world’s first commercially available quartz wristwatch — sent real tremors through traditional watchmaking. In response, a consortium of major Swiss brands, including Patek Philippe, Rolex, Omega, and Piaget, joined forces to develop their own answer: the Beta 21. Introduced that same year, it was an ambitious electronic caliber, featuring a quartz crystal oscillating at 8,192 Hz, reduced to drive a vibration motor with a smooth, sweeping seconds hand — a detail that set it apart from the “tick” we now associate with quartz. Despite enormous investment, only around 6,000 movements were produced before the project was ultimately abandoned, making surviving examples all the more compelling today. This Piaget reference 14101, dating to around 1970, captures that moment of experimentation and uncertainty with remarkable clarity. Powered by the Beta 21, it’s as much a piece of horological history as it is a wristwatch. The solid 18K yellow gold “Jumbo” case — measuring approximately 40mm by 33.5mm — embraces the scale of the movement with confidence. Its stepped construction and softly rounded rectangular form give it a distinctly sculptural presence, while the black dial, framed by a subtle inner track and accented with gold markers and 'baton' hands, keeps the overall composition clean and intentional. Paired with a black leather strap, it wears with presence but never feels overstated. This is Piaget doing what it does best — taking a disruptive moment in watchmaking and translating it into something elegant, forward-thinking, and unmistakably of its time.

title: Gevril Tribeca 'Paul Newman' Chronograph Re-Issue
description: The ‘Paul Newman’ Daytona — in all its various guises — is one of the most desirable watches in the world. Unfortunately, due to both scarcity and price, not every collector can acquire one. That’s where the Tribeca comes in. Manufactured by Gevril, a Swiss-founded watchmaker currently based in New York City with a history dating back to the mid-18th century, the Tribeca is a love letter to the ‘Paul Newman’ Daytona. Originally produced in 1990 in strictly limited series, the Tribeca models included homages to both steel as well as gold PNDs, making an aesthetic once available exclusively to the most well-heeled (or luckiest) collectors suddenly available to the masses. This particular Tribeca, a Reference R005/1, is housed in a 37mm stainless steel case with holey lugs, screw-down pushers, an acrylic crystal, and a stainless steel bezel with a black tachymeter scale insert. Featuring a white Tritium ‘exotic’ Paul Newman-style dial with black sub-registers, a matching baton handset, and an outer, 1/5th-second track, it’s individually numbered in red text in the 6:00 position. It also comes paired to a stainless steel, solid-link 'Oyster-style' bracelet with a signed blade clasp. In fantastic condition, it even includes its goodies. Inner, outer boxes, and warranty card. If you’re in love with the idea of a ‘Paul Newman’ Daytona but aren’t in the position to, ahem, take out a second mortgage on your home to purchase one — then you owe it yourself to check out this Tribeca. Snag it today!

title: Patek Philippe Calatrava
description: Patek Philippe has long been known for its complicated watchmaking, but following the stock market crash of 1929, fewer clients had the means to purchase these high-end timepieces. After securing a controlling interest in the firm, Jean and Charles Henri Stern decided to create a simple watch that would come in at a lower price point and appeal to the firm’s clientele. Using the principles espoused by the Bauhaus school and its minimalist, function-first philosophy, Patek conceived the Calatrava, taking its name from the Spanish military order established in the 12th century which had become the symbol of Patek Philippe. Since its debut in 1932, the Calatrava has become a byword for a simple, time-only dress watch — even from brands other than Patek itself. This piece, a Reference 6119G-001, builds on the foundational designs of its three-hand predecessors and is housed in a 39mm white gold case with a guilloché Clous de Paris bezel, signed crown, a sapphire crystal and a svelte case profile that will delight any wrist. The dial features a dynamic, vertically satin brushed anthracite tone acting as a canvas for its applied gold indices, the constant-seconds subsidiary register at 6 o’clock, a 'dauphine' handset and a white-accented ‘railroad’ minute track Powered and visible by way of a sapphire exhibition caseback, this Calatrava features a hand-wound Patek Philippe Calibre 30-255 PS and comes fitted to a signed black alligator leather strap with a signed 18K white gold pin buckle. A proper Calatrava from the world’s greatest watchmaker is forever.

title: Patek Philippe Annual Calendar Flyback Chronograph
description: In 1996, Patek Philippe made one of its most brilliant strategic moves— the introduction and development of the Annual Calendar complication. Patek recognized a gap in offerings between the simple and (relatively) accessible Calatrava classic dress watches and the complicated, and in turn, highly expensive, Grand Complications. The so-called "Annual Calendar" bridged the gap between these two price points, offering a natural progression for collectors looking to access a Patek complication at a more accessible price point. The Annual Calendar needs adjusting just once per year. This change enables the movement to be far more economical to produce, easier to service, and more affordable to purchase. The inaugural Reference 5035 Annual Calendar of 1996 was a tremendous success, and ever since, Patek's Annual Calendars have been a popular favorite. Annual Calendars from Patek represent the bread and butter of the brand— perfectly executed, complicated dress watches. In 2006, Patek Philippe introduced the Reference 5960P, a platinum annual calendar featuring a flyback chronograph. Distinguished from the other annual calendars because of its decidedly sporty look, the 5960 stood out from the crowd. It wasn't only noteworthy for the flyback; however, it also featured a modern annual calendar layout. Instead of displaying the annual calendar in subsidiary dials, Patek instead used aperture displays. While apertures have been used by Patek throughout history (as seen in the Reference 3448 perpetual calendar, for example), they are usually displayed in-line. For the 5960, Patek instead made vaulted, framed apertures that follow the curve of the case. This gave the annual calendar a truly modern look and breathed new life into the collection. It's not for everyone, but it's an entirely new look. This particular Reference 5960P-001 is crafted in platinum, featuring an anthracite dial and red accents. The calendar complications and power reserve are positioned at the top of the dial, while the minute and hour totalizers are located at 6 o'clock within a single oversized sub-register. A day/night indicator is easy to miss within the subdial. The case is topped with a sapphire crystal. Several other stylistic choices were made with the 5960 that distinguished it from previous references. Unlike the 5035 and 5146 annual calendars, the 5960 features a concave bezel that helps reinforce its modern look. Additionally, the 5960 was sized at a comfortable 40.5mm—a sporty size for a Patek complication, but one that suits the rest of the watch's look. The 5960 is finished with a signed crown and engraved pump pushers. The aesthetics of this piece are classic and modern all at the same time. The 5960 is one of the most beloved modern Patek Philippe references and a great starting point for those interested in complicated watches, particularly sports watch enthusiasts. Rip off the bandaid with the 5960 and then go full send on a 3940. You'll thank us later.

title: Omega 'Secret' Bracelet Watch by Gilbert Albert
description: There are jewelry watches. And then there are small, subversive sculptures that happen to tell time. This 1960s Omega watch belongs firmly in the latter category. Its elaborate 18K yellow-gold bracelet explodes across the wrist in a nugget-meets-lava formation. An organic, 'coral-like' lattice that feels less fabricated than unearthed. Created during one of Omega’s most adventurous design periods, the piece throws polite Swiss restraint out the window. The result is a watch that behaves more like a sculpture than timekeeper, a small eruption of gold across the wrist where form, texture, and imagination take the lead. The petite champagne dial—complete with slender 'baton' indices and 'sword' hands—has a truly elegant presence in a sea of gold. It’s intimacy by design. The crown is tucked discreetly on the caseback, preserving the uninterrupted sculptural silhouette. Inside beats a manual-wind Omega Calibre , a slim, reliable movement suited perfectly to refined ladies’ watches of the era. Omega has long understood that women’s watches can be mechanically serious and aesthetically daring. This piece proves it. Part avant-garde jewel, part timekeeping instrument, fully wearable art. A wildly confident design period in Omega’s history. One that deserves far more attention than it gets.

title: Cartier Tank Mini Diamonds 'MOP'
description: When you think of Cartier, their longstanding history in jewelry probably comes to mind. But they also have a reputation for making timeless and elegant timepieces, which they’ve been doing for over a century. The Tank Louis is without question the brand’s most well-known model, but the story doesn't end there. Beyond the Louis line are numerous executions — many produced in very limited quantities — that are quite literally some of the most beautiful timepieces ever made. This particular Tank is an extraordinary ladies’ piece from circa the 1990s. It features a striking 15.5mm x 25mm white gold case - set with diamonds on the vertical 'brancards', a mineral crystal, a sapphire cabochon crown, and a stunning mother of pearl dial with a matching 'sword' handset. To top it all off, this piece is fitted to a 18K white gold bracelet with a beads of rice profile. Outstanding. One could spend an entire lifetime just collecting Tanks, nevermind the rest of the staggering Cartier oeuvre . Why not start here, with this rare, stunning piece that you are not likely to catch again. Get this one before it's too late!

title: Breitling Super Avenger B01 Chronograph 42
description: Breitling has long been purveyor of chronographs to pilots. In fact, the original Breitling Chronomat models of the 1940s were built from the ground up to be no-nonsense instruments for use in the cockpit. Since then, Breitling has expanded on its line of aviation watches, moving into more mechanically (and visually) complex chronographs, as well as more straightforward, legible designs such as the Avenger line. This particular piece, an Avenger B01 42 features a — you guessed it — 42mm black stainless steel with dual 'paddle' pushers, a sapphire crystal, a signed crown, and a unique dive bezel with signature 'rider tabs'. Inside, it has a dark green dial with applied luminous 'baton' indices, black chronograph registers, an outer minute track in black and silver, and a luminous 'sword' handset. Paired to a signed stainless steel multi-link bracelet with a signed fold-over clasp, it's powered by the COSC-certified automatic Calibre B01 movement from Breitling. Equipped with 45 jewels and a 70-hour power reserve, this workhorse movement is ready to take on any adventure — just flip the watch over and you'll receive confirmation that it's working overtime via a sapphire caseback. If you’ve been on the hunt for an excellent, serious tool watch watch with some heft, you've found it. What's more, it's from one of the best brands in the game!

title: Cartier Tank Americaine
description: The Cartier Tank Americaine is quite possibly the least understood model in Cartier's lineup. Introduced in 1989, it is, in many ways, a modern update to the classic Cintrée. With an elongated case featuring a gently curved caseback, the collection was designed from the start to be a larger watch to suit American tastes. Initially launched exclusively with quartz movements, it has expanded in the past decades to include a variety of mechanical variants as well as sizes, case materials, and complications that offers something appealing to a wide range of collectors. This particular example is a beautiful ladies' Reference W2620031-2503 cased in 18K rose gold, and features the timeless satin silver guilloché dial with printed 'Roman' indices upon which Cartier was built. Measuring 19mm x 34.8 mm , it boasts smooth brancards , while a sapphire-set cabochon crown and a sapphire crystal complete the picture of a supremely elegant case. The silver guilloché dial — fitted with an inner 'railroad' minute track and blued steel 'sword' handset — is a straightforward picture of pure class. Meanwhile, a handy quartz movement and a stunning scale-link bracelet in 18K rose gold with a hidden butterfly clasp seal the deal. The Tank Louis is all well and good. But for our money, this incredible, elongated Americaine is equally deserving of your attention!

Forget about the Tank Louis for a moment, and spring for something with a touch of sparkle!

title: Cartier Baignoire
description: Ladies' watches, unfortunately, don’t get the attention they deserve. It has seemingly been long assumed that women will be content with shoddily-designed timepieces devoid of soul, providing of course that they are pink and have loads of precious stones set on them. We know this to be nonsense — a lady’s watch shouldn't be any less considered than a man’s, and we seek out examples of watches done right, regardless of intended gender. At Analog:Shift HQ, we are excited to curate a selection of timepieces that provide equally engaging options for ladies as the more common men’s pieces. No watch better captures this philosophy than the Cartier Baignoire. This example, a Reference W15045D8-1954 , features a beautiful case shape, with its soft curves and oblong 'ellipse' aesthetic. Paired with a beautiful 18K yellow gold bracelet with an equally distinct link profile, this watch is anything but boring, and provides an incredible host of details to obsess over. In spite of the unique design, this piece still preserves many of the details of classic Cartier we would hope to see: a 'Roman' numeral dial, blued steel hands, petite Cartier logo, and more all serve as a reminder that this piece is backed by a name with an unrivaled history for fine jewelry making, and yes, watchmaking too. A Baignoire on a leather strap is a solid choice for any occasion. However, a Baignoire on an integrated bracelet is seemingly more our style!

title: Breitling Endurance Pro 44 Chronograph 'IRONMAN'
description: Breitling has long been purveyor of chronographs to pilots, having designed models such as 1942’s Chronomat from the ground as a no-nonsense instrument for use in the cockpit. Since then, numerous Breitling chronographs have seen action in myriad scenarios, not the least of which is on the wrists of athletes and ordinary folks simply going about their business, who need a strong, reliable watch to time everyday events. The Breitling Endurance Pro in particular stands out for its versatile use cases, being equally at home out in the field or simply out for a stroll. This particular Endurance Pro from the 2020s features a COSC-certified quartz movement caliber 82— as if the common battery-powered caliber wasn’t accurate enough, Breitling did you once better! Housed in a 44mm polymer Breighlight case with a sapphire crystal, a signed crown, 'piston' pushers, and a black polymer, bi-directional 'compass' bezel, it features a luminous red fume dial with applied 'Arabic' indices, a matching handset, a triple-register chronograph with a date window at 4:30, and an inner pulsometer scale around the dial periphery. This piece is part of the IRONMAN special edition collection, coming specifically in the red colorway. Powered by the Caliber Breitling 82 thermocompensated SuperQuartz movement and paired to a red rubber strap with a black polymer pin buckle, the Reference X823109A1K1S1 is ready for a lifetime of adventure with its next owner. That owner should be you!

title: Breitling Top Time B01 Chronograph 'Chevrolet Corvette'
description: When Breitling launched the Top Time in the early 1960s, it was meant to be a simpler, more affordable alternative to the brand's higher-end pilot's watch offerings. Aimed at consumers 25 and other, it featured clean lines, an oversized 38mm case in steel or gold, and dials in a kaleidoscopic range of colors, including funky “radio” patterns ideal for the fashion-forward young man (or woman). The modern Top Time is no different. With its uncluttered dial designs and workhorse movement, it's an ideal entry into the Breitling catalog, which features such famous models as the Chronomat and the Navitimer. For those looking for a simpler chronograph devoid of the Navitimer's multiple timing scales, the Top Time is just the ticket. This particular Top Time, a Reference AB0176, celebrates the famous Chevrolet Corvette. Housed in a 41mm stainless steel case with a sapphire crystal, dual 'pump' pushers, and a signed crown, it features a handsome red 'sunray' dial with the Corvette logo situated beneath the Breitling wordmark; an outer multi-color tachymeter scale; a triple-register chronograph with black 'squircle' registers; and luminous 'dash' indices. With its bright orange and yellow accents against a red and black background, it's a beautiful study in chronograph design, and a cool tribute to one of America's most famous muscle cars. Powered by Breitling's B01 automatic chronograph movement and fitted to a black calfskin leather strap with a steel folding deployant buckle, the Breitling Top Time Chevrolet Corvette is the ideal driving watch — though it should do just fine outside a powerful vehicle, as well!

title: Movado Acvatic Dress Watch
description: At a glance, this looks like a simple mid-century dress watch. It isn’t. This Movado Acvatic reference 18141, dating to the 1950s, deserves your full attention. At first, it reads like a classic mid-century dress watch: a well-proportioned 35mm stainless steel case, sharp lugs, 'dauphine' hands, and applied 'dagger' indices set against a warm, aged dial. But look closer, and the details begin to unfold. The dial has developed a remarkable, organic patina — a constellation of speckled aging that transforms the surface into something entirely unique. No two examples will ever age quite like this, and here, it adds depth and character in all the right ways. Then there’s the case. Signed “Acvatic”, Movado’s period spelling for “aquatic,” this model points to its then-novel waterproof construction — and more specifically, its Borgel case. Designed by François Borgel, these early waterproof cases were among the most innovative of their time, featuring a threaded design that improved water resistance well before it became industry standard. While Borgel cases are often seen in smaller, more ornate forms, finding one in a larger, round, more robust 35mm configuration like this is decidedly uncommon. A detail you might miss entirely — until you don’t. Paired with a blue leather strap, the watch balances its rugged, forward-thinking case construction with classic dress sensibility. Uncommon, quietly technical, and full of character, this is a Movado that rewards curiosity.

title: Breitling SuperOcean Heritage Chronograph 44
description: Breitling may be best known for its aviation roots, but by the late 1950s, the brand had its sights set below the surface. As dive watches surged in popularity, led by icons like the Submariner and Fifty Fathoms, Breitling answered with the SuperOcean in 1957, introducing both a time-only diver and a chronograph built for underwater use. It marked the beginning of a nautical lineage that remains central to the brand today. This SuperOcean Heritage Chronograph 44 carries that legacy forward with a modern standpoint. Housed in a 44mm stainless steel case, the watch balances presence with purpose. The unidirectional timing bezel and screw-down architecture reinforce its dive-ready credentials, while the sapphire crystal and signed crown speak to everyday durability. The dark sunburst green dial adds depth and personality — shifting tones in the light — while applied indices with outer lume plots and Breitling’s signature hands ensure clarity in any condition. A day-and-date display adds practical functionality without overwhelming the design. Inside beats the Breitling Caliber 13, a COSC-certified automatic chronograph movement known for its reliability and ease of service. It’s paired here with a black rubber strap, giving the watch a more contemporary, sport-driven feel on the wrist. Offered as a complete set with its box, warranty card, and hangtag, this example checks all the right boxes for a modern tool watch with heritage appeal.

title: Breitling Avenger Automatic 42
description: If you think Breitling is a one-trick pony, it might be time to look a little closer. Founded in 1884, the brand has spent well over a century building some of the most capable aviation watches ever made. But beyond the slide rules and cockpit timers, Breitling has always excelled at something more fundamental: making watches that work. Robust, legible, and easy to service, they’re the horological equivalent of a well-built tool — dependable, no-nonsense, and ready for whatever you throw at them. The Avenger line takes that ethos and pushes it further. Designed with jet pilots in mind, it’s less about nostalgia and more about capability — a modern interpretation of what an aviation watch should be today. This Reference A17328101B1A1, sized at 42mm, delivers exactly that. The black dial is clean and highly legible, framed by a unidirectional rotating bezel with deep, easy-grip knurling. Substantial crown guards, a screw-down crown, and thick, purposeful lugs reinforce the watch’s tool-first mentality. Paired with a steel bracelet, the overall look is tactical without feeling overbuilt. With 300 meters of water resistance, corrosion-resistant construction, and intuitive handling even with gloves, the Avenger is designed to perform in extreme conditions — whether that’s a cockpit, a coastline, or somewhere in between. You don’t need a flight suit to wear one. But it doesn’t hurt.

title: Eska French Chronograph
description: Vintage chronographs are the soul of Analog:Shift. The perfect balance of complication, sophistication, detail in design, and staying power, vintage chronos bridge both sport and dress aesthetic in a brilliant way. As our bread and butter, we're always looking for notable and exciting chronographs for your consideration. What we have here is a great example of this. An Eska Chronograph from the 1950s, this brilliant 35mm piece was years ahead of its time and equally comfortable in the 2020s. Founded in the 1910s in Switzerland, Eska made a name for itself producing some of the most beautiful dress pieces for the market. This chronograph is fashioned from 18K gold and packs a classic manually wound movement within. With twin 'tach' and 'telemeter' scales outbound, the beautiful piece is completed with gold hands and applied numerals, 'grooved' sub-registers, and sharp faceted lugs. Not only is this piece a beautiful testament to 1950s watch design, it's in simply pristine condition throughout. For something dating to this period, it's truly hard to find something in this condition. Lesser known than its natural competition but every bit as capable, this is the type of chronograph that fits in any collection. Snag it before someone else does!

title: Longines Weems
description: In this age of global travel, it’s easy to take for granted the sight of contrails snaking across the sky. And yet in the early years of the last century, airplanes were a new invention. But thanks to the contributions of aviation pioneers like Alberto Santos-Dumont, whose achievements in aviation are matched by those in watches, flying became more commonplace. Since aeronautical navigation posed its own particular challenges, there arose a need for specialized tools and timekeepers. Due to the distance traveled at higher speeds, any error in navigation—even if it was as little as 30 seconds off—would put the pilot off course by as much as seven miles. Therefore, just as John Harrison did for sailors in the Age of Sail with his marine chronometer, so too did Captain Philip Van Horn Weems do for pilots. A native of land-locked Tennessee, Weems must have felt the call of the sea from an early age. At just nineteen, he enrolled at the US Naval Academy in Annapolis. There he developed an aptitude for celestial navigation, and during his tenure with the Aircraft Squadron Battle Fleet, he encountered airplanes for the the first time. Despite the advances undertaken in the century between the development of John Harrison’s marine chronometer and the time Captain Weems joined the Navy, the tools and charts used in navigation were just as primitive. For example, Weems—and many of his fellow navigators—had been trained to use the American Nautical Almanac. This publication used tables, first published in 1757, that called for navigators to take measurements using observations that were so complicated that few navigators could even do them. First introduced in 1929, the Longines Weems Second-Setting Watch was the preferred timekeeping tool for navigators and pilots until the introduction of Charles Lindbergh’s version, the Hour Angle, in 1931. The Second-Setting watch allows pilots to synchronize their watches with radio signals without stopping the movement. The brilliant innovation was instrumental in the history of aviator watches. This particular iteration is one of the most valuable, executed in 14K yellow gold. Dating to the 1940s, the beautiful 28mm piece is powered by Longines manual-winding Calibre 10L and ready for a history lover's collection!

title: Omega Seamaster Planet Ocean 600M
description: The Seamaster 300, introduced in 1957, was Omega's response to the burgeoning popularity of SCUBA diving. Featuring robust steel cases with a 300-meter depth rating, rotating bezels graduated with dive-timing scales, and a metal bracelet with diver's expansion links, the early Seamaster 300s were not only functional divers that would go on to see use in Her Majesty's Navy, but are arguably some of the handsomest sports watch designs of the past century. As it evolved, the Omega Seamaster 300 went on to see numerous evolutionary changes — in fact, nearly innumerable variants in a wide variety of materials and colorways have been produced in the past 60 years. This fact alone has made the Seamaster Professional line incredibly desirable — simply because they don't all look exactly the same . One of the latest additions to the broader Seamaster collection is the Planet Ocean. Introduced in 2005, these watches features a chunkier case, a fresh bracelet design, revised design language on the dial with a 'broad arrow' handset, and increased water resistance — no doubt to compete with that of the Rolex Sea-Dweller. This particular piece, a reference 2900.50.91, is a first-gen Planet Ocean dating to the 2000s that was featured in Casino Royale . Featuring a 45.5mm twisted-lug case, a matte black dial with matching 'broad arrow' handset, a signed stainless steel multi-link bracelet with a signed steel clasp, and the always-controversial helium escape valve at 10:00, these early Planet Oceans are aging quite well and truly hit the sweet spot with respect to design, proportions, and wearability. Although large at the time, it's surprisingly versatile for daily wear. After all: If it was good enough for a certain Agent 007 on the silver screen back in 2006, then it's certainly good enough for us!

title: Audemars Piguet Ellipse
description: This slim and elegant piece couldn't be any further removed from the bulky brute of the Royal Oak Offshore line that the brand is perhaps most commonly known for amongst today's collectors. Hearkening back to a simpler time, it’s representative of an era in which the maison made so few timepieces per year that many were unique pieces, or part of incredibly limited series. This particular watch features a beautiful yellow gold case with a crisp hallmark on the 9 o'clock side, houses a lovely deep navy blue 'sunburst' dial holding a lovely 'golden flaked' patina with printed 'Arabic' indices, a matching 'pencil' handset, and an automatic winding movement within! Following a classic ellipse format, this rare timepiece comes with a date window at 3 o'clock. With its timeless and endlessly appealing looks - combined with extensive pedigree, this is a great opportunity to snag an excellent heirloom quality timepiece from one of the very best in the business! Watches such as this one are fun and wonderful timepieces, and there's no telling if and when one of these in any condition will surface again, so don't wait!

title: Longines 'Salmon' Pointer Date
description: In our opinion, Longines doesn't quite get the respect that they deserve. That isn’t to say that they aren't held in high regard. But the level of innovation, craftsmanship, and design that Longines has demonstrated over the course of their history simply cannot be understated, and certainly extends to a wide variety of timepieces across the board. Take this vintage dress watch, for example: Dating to the 1940s and housed in a 36mm stainless steel case with an acrylic crystal and a brushed bezel, it features one of the most beautiful salmon dials in stellar condition with a pointer date -- a distinctive signature for Longines. The stainless steel Calatrava style case is also in great condition with a concave bezel. For a 1940s piece, this watch was far ahead of its time, and its midcentury pieces like this one that are the inspiration for many of the modern watches the brand makes. This is the type of versatile piece that can be worn everyday, or slipped onto an alligator leather strap for dressier occasions. Perfect for both men and women, it features a stunning dial configuration that simply isn’t found on many modern timepieces, and we love it. This piece reminds us why Longines pieces from this period are becoming increasingly coveted in serious collecting circles.

title: Girard-Perregaux Gyromatic
description: Few names in Swiss watchmaking carry the quiet authority of Girard-Perregaux. With roots tracing back to the late 18th century, the manufacture has weathered revolutions in taste and technology alike — from early adoption of wristwatches to meaningful contributions to quartz engineering. But long before high-frequency oscillators and Laureato hype, GP excelled at something far more elemental: the perfectly judged dress watch. This automatic winding dress watch is an excellent example of what we mean. In the 1950s, the newest developments in watch technology revolved around automatic winding movement development, and GP was at the forefront. In 1950, GP presented the Gyromatic, which replaced ratchet winding with roller clutches that are far more efficient. The Gyromatic allowed Girard-Perregaux to develop slimmer, more efficient compact dress watches. This piece is just one example. Fashioned from stainless steel, this dress swatch features stronger 3,6,9, and 12 indices, with further applied indices for the minor indexes. The dial is fashioned in a silver hue and is topped off with a 'pencil' handset. Slim, elegant, and refreshingly unfussy, this is the kind of watch that makes a strong case for restraint. It also marks an important part in the evolution of watches in general with advanced automatic winding movement systems.

title: Patek Philippe Nautilus Chronograph
description: The Patek Philippe Nautilus is without question one of the great horological icons of the 1970s, and has in recent years once again become one of the most in-demand wristwatch models on the planet. Collectors and prospectors alike have clamored to get their hands on Genta's second great act in luxury sports watch design, and since the legendary stainless steel, time-and-date, Reference 5711 rode off into the sunset in 2021, demand has never been higher. Interestingly enough, most of the demand for Nautilus models are centered around non-complicated models, something we can't fully wrap our heads around when considering the capabilities and expertise in high horology from Patek Philippe. This example, a Reference 5980/1A-001 , resides in the complications camp, boasting a flyback chronograph complication with a mono-counter display. Wrapped in a much-adored stainless steel case as the “A” suggests in its reference designation, this Nautilus features a three-part stainless case spanning 40.5mm in diameter. Displaying a masterful blend of satin and polish finishings throughout, this piece offers a signed screw-down crown, angular chronograph pushers that parallel the case flank, articulating end-links, sapphire crystal and of course, the model’s signature ‘eared’ silhouette. Its dial is finished in a beautiful blue fumé with hallmark horizontal texturing - affectionately referred to as the 'Garage Door' by some collectors. The dial features applied luminous indices, a matching luminous handset, a date window at 3 o’clock and a mono-counter 'bullseye' chronograph register at 6 o’clock, equipped with stacked minute and hour counter hands. Its Calibre CH 28-520 C flyback chronograph movement utilizes a column wheel mechanism and vertical clutch system for dead-on accuracy rating attested by the manufacture , as well as by our measure. This Nautilus makes for a pretty epic daily driver capable of just about anything you can throw at it! Fitted to an integrated stainless steel bracelet which cohesively follows the case taper and culminates with a signed locking clasp, this comes accompanied by its complete factory kit, including its inner and outer box set, leather folio, booklets, adjustor tool, and Certificate of Origin dated April 2007. A stainless steel complicated Nautilus — does it get any better than that?

title: Cartier Tank Americaine Automatic
description: The Cartier Tank Americaine is quite possibly the least understood model in Cartier's lineup. Introduced in 1989, it is, in many ways, a modern update to the classic Cintrée model. With an elongated case featuring a gently curved caseback, the collection was designed from the start to be a larger watch to suit American tastes. Initially launched exclusively with quartz movements, it has expanded in the past decades to include a variety of mechanical variants as well as sizes, case materials, and complications that put it all over the map in terms of value. This particular example is a stunning full-size Reference 1740 cased in 18K yellow gold, and features the timeless satin silver guilloché dial with printed 'Roman' indices upon which Cartier was built. Fitted with a set of blued steel 'sword' hands, an octagonal sapphire cabochon winding crown, an automatic movement, and an absolutely magnificent matching yellow gold bracelet with deployant clasp, it's quite simply one of the most gorgeous (and heavy!) Tanks we've ever had the pleasure of offering for sale. Accompanied by its correct inner Cartier box, this Tank Americaine is the type of spectacular dress watch that will simply never go out of style. If you're jonesing for a hunk of yellow gold on your wrist — that happens to tell the time! — you simply can't go wrong with a Reference 1740.

title: Patek Philippe 'Tank'
description: Though the famous Calatrava is — for good reason — perhaps the best known of Patek Philippe’s incredible dress watches, there are myriad others that deserve recognition. From the rectangular Gondolo to the curvaceous Golden Ellipse, these timepieces, though simple in design, beg a closer look for their classic proportions and strict attention to detail. Patek has been producing such wristwatches for roughly a century, and shows no signs of slowing down. This particular Patek Philippe dress watch is perfect for someone who loves the Tank (and Tank-like) dress watch: A Reference 3405J from the 1960s, it features a beautifully sized, square 27mm x 27mm case with downturned lugs, a smooth bezel, a signed crown, and an acrylic crystal atop a rectangular silvered dial with thin, applied gold 'stick' indices and a matching 'pencil' handset. Powered by the hand-wound Patek Philippe Calibre 23-300 movement and paired to a brown Louisiana alligator leather strap with a signed yellow gold pin buckle, this gorgeous piece is a vestige of a classier time. Strap it on and be instantly transported to midcentury New York City for a bit of Mad Men- esque glamor!

title: Universal Genève Cioccolatone 'J.W. Benson'
description: While Universal Genève may be most famed for its Compax chronographs and the aeronautically-inspired Polerouter, its svelte dress watches are equally compelling. Throughout the latter half of the 20th century, UG designed simple, time-only watches alongside its more complicated brethren that played with shape, color, and design in interesting and novel ways. This particular dress watch is referred to as a 'Cioccolatone' ('big chocolate') after its distinctive, chocolate candy-shaped case that was used by numerous marques beginning in the 1950s. Measuring 25.5mm in yellow gold with beautifully flowing 'scroll' lugs, an unsigned crown, and an acrylic crystal, it features a handsome silver guilloché dial in a C lous de Paris pattern with applied gold faceted indices, a matching gold 'dauphine' handset, and a double-signature: In addition to the Universal Genève wordmark, it also bears the name of J.W. Benson, a well-respected London clock and watchmaker turned retailer, now defunct. Powered by a hand-wound U.G. movement and paired to a lovely brown alligator strap with tone-on-tone stitching and a signed gold-tone steel U.G. pin buckle, this watch is the perfect entryway into Universal Genève for the budding collector. Sure to garner knowing nods of approval from the inner enthusiast circle, it's quite simply a killer piece from one of our absolute favorite brands — full stop.

title: Jaeger-LeCoultre Reverso Classic Duetto
description: The Reverso, Jaeger-LeCoultre's most distinctive watch, certainly has an impressive pedigree. One of the world's first sports watches, the Reverso combined utility with a sleek and elegant Art Deco exterior that has become an icon of horological design. But in the case of the Reverso, looks deceive. Though the model appears at first glance an Art Deco dress watch, it owes its conception to the gentlemanly sport of polo. While touring India in the 1920s, Swiss businessman César de Trey met a British polo player who'd just cracked the crystal of his watch on the field. De Trey returned to Switzerland with an idea that had taken root in his head, which he then discussed with Jacques-David LeCoultre: What if a watch could be made with a case that could reverse? The reversible case, masterminded by designer Alfred Chauvot, was Jaeger-LeCoultre's solution to the impact problem polo players could face on the field. Once reversed, the delicate components of the dial were protected from the shocks sustained while on horseback. No more would polo players risk cracking crystals or receiving damage to the dials of their watches. Chauvot took out a patent for the Reverso in March 1931. Produced chiefly in steel, Jaeger-LeCoultre also released the Reverso in gold, and decorated the case back with engravings or even miniature portraits. But with changing tastes in the 1970s — for round watches as well as quartz movements — Jaeger-LeCoultre ceased production of the Reverso. The model lay dormant for years until its triumphant re-issue in 1982. While those watches contained quartz movements, their success represented a future for the Reverso — which has since returned to its previous tentpole status within the greater JLC lineup. This example, a Reference Q2668432, features a small sized stainless steel 21mm x 34mm reversible case, sapphire crystal, signed crown, and a silver tone dial with printed 'Arabic' indices with a rectangular central minutes track framing a guilloche dial center and blued-steel 'sword' handset. The reverse displays a secondary time display with diamonds at the top and bottom. Powered by a Jaeger-LeCoultre Calibre 844 manual movement, is truly one of the most classic layouts available. This example also comes complete with its factory goodies. In terms of elegant design and horological prowess, this watch punches way above its weight class — offering tremendous looks and street cred with its classic silhouette — the way only a Reverso can!

title: Certina DS-2
description: When it comes to vintage dive watches, we love the heavy hitters just as much as the next guy. The Rolex Submariner, the Blancpain Fifty Fathoms, and the Omega Seamaster 300 all have special places in our hearts - and collections. But for every well-known name in the dive watch world, there’s one or two that make us stop and say, “Now this is why we got into collecting watches in the first place.” In the 1950s and 1960s, lots of brands got into the dive watch game, some using contract cases and movements, while others went down the route of building a purpose built, ground-up, sea going weapon to vanquish its competition. The Certina DS-2 falls into that select group of watches. This brilliantly over-engineered 200 meter diver was made in the 1970s and features a lovely blue dial. Featuring a 40mm stainless steel cushion case housing an automatic Calibre 25-651 movement, its screwdown caseback and rotating bezel assembly are instantly identifiable to dive watch fanatics the world over with a profile that is not easily forgotten. This particular example remains in great condition throughout with a brilliantly patinated dial, timing bezel insert, unsigned screw-down crown, caseback with Certina engravings in deep relief. Its not often that a funky, colorful, 70s diving watch becomes an artifact sought after by dive watch enthusiasts - but the Certina DS-2 is a rare bird that checks all of the boxes!

title: Hamilton Brock
description: The late 19th and early 20th centuries were without question the golden age of American watchmaking. The implementation of mass production and interchangeable parts assured American supremacy. Brands such as Gruen, Elgin, and Hamilton vied against the Swiss to dominate the watch industry — the latter, in particular, was at the top of its game. Specifically, the development of railroad chronometers gave Hamilton a reputation for accuracy and dependability in an age where these qualities were vital in a watch. But the brand's production did not rest on railroad chronometers alone: throughout the 1920s and 1930s and the Second World War, the Lancaster, PA-based brand released a dizzying array of designs. In the 1920s, Hamilton began to deviate from the typical round cases that predominated in the early years of wristwatch production. The company experimented with a variety of shapes, from the square or rectangular “tank” shapes popularized by Cartier to bold asymmetrical designs that subtly foreshadow the Victor, one of the world’s first electric wristwatches. This particular Hamilton Brock, fashioned from 14K yellow gold, features a lovely svelte case profile, stylized numerals, and a lovely black dial with subsidiary seconds. The caseback features an engraving honoring an employee of GM. Whether you follow in the historical provenance by gifting it this Christmas, or adding a charming vintage dress watch to your collection, you really can't go wrong. What more could a collector ask for in a watch?

title: Hamilton Allison
description: The late 19th and early 20th centuries were without question the golden age of American watchmaking. The implementation of mass production and interchangeable parts assured American supremacy. Brands such as Gruen, Elgin, and Hamilton vied against the Swiss to dominate the watch industry—and Hamilton, in particular, was at the top of its game. In particular, the development of railroad chronometers gave the manufacture a reputation for accuracy and dependability, in an age where those qualities were vital in a watch. But Hamilton’s production did not rest on railroad chronometers alone: throughout the 1920s and 1930s, and on into World War II, Hamilton released a dizzying array of designs. In the 1920s, the brand started to deviate from the typical round cases that predominated in the early years of wristwatch production. These watches were often referred to as “Geographic” thanks to their revolutionary case shapes. Hamilton experimented with a variety of shapes, from the square or rectangular “tank” shapes popularized by Cartier, to bold asymmetrical designs that subtly foreshadow the Hamilton Victor, one of the world’s first electric wristwatches. These early wristwatches were named after their shapes: Tonneau, Square Cut Corner, or Cushion were just some of the models Hamilton released in the 1920s. But after a few years, these models were given names that evoked images of success and prosperity. Certain watches were named after famous golf courses or country clubs, such as Meadowbrook (a country club in Northville, MI, outside Detroit) or Oakmont, a golf course near Pittsburgh, PA. The qualities these names evoked became increasingly desirable after the Wall Street crash of 1929. People lost their fortunes, and many businesses were forced to fold. Even Hamilton was not immune to the privations. This particular piece, a Hamilton Allison, is one of the unsung heroes of the Hamilton archive. The Allison features a beautiful tonneau case shape with beautiful applique numerals and subsidiary seconds. In essence, the model captures the aesthetic of American fine watchmaking. This example features light patina and preserves the model's character and personality, telling the story of one of the coolest watches in Hamilton's history.

This particular example has a beautiful champagne dial with Breguet numerals and subsidiary seconds.
